activity: dredging operations at Shifford Lock to make the Thames navigable

te.text:
DREDGING UPPER THAMES.      £50,000 SCHEME.        FH/RW.

Unforeseen difficulties have delayed the famous Conservancy Board's
scheme for making navigable, at a cost of £50,000, 35 miles of the
Thames above Oxford, hitherto choked and silted up by 35 years
neglect. The task has proved more difficult than was anticipated,
and now, after four years work, only half the distance has been done,
though the whole scheme was expected to take between 3 and 5 years.
The river is choked with reeds and mud, and dredging is necessary.
It has also been necessary to "straighten" the river somewhat.

Photo shows - Dredging operations at Shifford Lock, near Oxford,
one of the additional bits of work not anticipated, but now being
carried out to make the Thames navigable.
FOX AUGUST 29th. 34

activity: surrealist image of a girl with eating irons stuck in her garter created for the United Kingdom Cutlery and Silverware Manufacturers' Association

te.text:
REPORTING a curious development in the Back Britain campaign. The
legs on the right are selling British cutlery just to show the naked but
modest girl on the left (who is selling Norwegian tablewear) that ooh-la-la
does not begin at Calais. The journal British Jeweller reprinted the
Norwegian naked lady advertisement with a call to Britain's cutlers to buck
up their own ads. The United Kingdom Cutlery and Silverware Manu-
facturers' Association were stung into action and had the surrealist image
of the girl with eating irons stuck in her garter created.
Handy, I suppose, but it must be murder on her stockings.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
7 FEB 1968
Please return to
ART Library

activity: processed car bodies are tipped from the Rotodip rust-proofing plant

te.text:
'ON THE SPIT'.
...’S FIRST ROTODIP PLANT GUARDS BRITISH CARS AGAINST
                            RUST.

Coventry, Eng:  The turnspit      went out with the stage-
coach but the idea has been revived in the great
Fisher and Ludlow plant -       subsidiary of Standard
Motors - near here to protect bodies of the latest
'Vanguards' from rust.
'Spitted' on a revolving rod 20 feet long by four
inches in diameter, the bodies pass through the world's
first Rotodip plant       of six process tanks, each
holding from five to seven thousand gallons of cleaning
and phosphating liquids.
From this section, the bodies pass into the hot-air
drying oven then into the primer paint compartment.
Throughout the journey the bodies are evenly rotated
until reaching the baking oven.
Full complement of the 300 feet by 20 feet dip is
33 bodies, processed at the rate of       18 an hour.
Treatment time is one hour 47 minutes.
PHOTO SHOWS:  The processed bodies are tipped from
the Rotodip.
       January 20th 1949  PN.g.  Pl corr.

activity: the 'Golden' Lodge High Frequency Spark Plug

te.text:
The "Golden" Lodge High Frequency
Spark Plug

This is the revolutionary new spark plug announced by Lodge Plugs,
Ltd., Rugby, which needs no servicing, cleaning or adjustment
during a working life at least double that of a traditional plug.
Incorporated in the body of the plug is a high frequency converter
consisting of a pellet of special "high K" ceramic coupled with a
series gap. The spark gap is of unique design and provides a
small air gap coupled with a surface gap. These innovations mean
that the plug sparks with a lower voltage than normally and in
consequence there is less erosion of the electrodes.
The plug which retails at 8/6d. is claimed to mark the biggest
single advance in automotive ignition systems for more than half
a century.

1424M)                  A TREE-TOP HOUSE.

22-year-old John Mayall of Acre Lane, Cheadle Hulme,
Cheshire, lives in a house 30-feet up in a tree, at
the bottom of his garden. He and his fiancee, 19-year-
old Pamela Heap will live there when they are married.

modern equipment, two bunks, wardrobe, and all cooking
equipment. John's brother Philip, who is serving with
the Royal Engineers in Cyprus started the house and
John finished it on his return from Korea. He is now
a student at the Manchester College.

activity: A rehearsal for the play 'Who Killed the Squire' in the garden of Ridges Farm, featuring David Green dressed as a chef and displaying decorative 'dressed-up' potatoes.

te.text:
Calcraft   Illus.              28.10.43
Rehearsal in the garden of Ridges Farm, Clifton
Hampden for "Who Killed the Squire". Village boys and
girls play in this Propaganda Play.
OPS 9 Five-years-old David Green wears the chef dress
that won him first prize at a village party. His
mother made it from old sheets. In his tray he
carries samples of dressed-up pota toes made by Joyce
Allmond, a 17-year-old girl. Nobody in Clifton
Hampden ever cooks potatoes in any other way but
their skins. All these dishes were cooked thus,
"dressed-up" afterwards. Note Potatoe ducks with
carrot beak, feet; cloves for eyes. Potat o hedgehog
and fried-bread spines. Potatoe baskets contain
Russian salad. Half potat oes represent boats with
lettuce sails.
After the picture was taken David made sure that
he took tray home. He was going to eat all the
potatoes.

activity: Six-year-old Malcolm Farrant tries his luck with a link-trainer at an RAF Exhibition at Dorland Hall.

te.text:
Nixon   D.H.   27.3.45
A RAF Exhibition was opened today at Dorland
Hall, Regent Street, by Sir Archibald Sinclair,
Secretary of State for Air.  The Exhibition
is being organised by the Daily Herald in
co-operation with the Air Ministry.
   OPS 1   Six-year-old Malcolm Farrant tries
his luck with the link-trainer, with the
assistance of Flight/Lieut. L.F.Gregory, who
is in charge of the Exhibition.  Flight/Lieut.
Gregory was recently re-patriated from a 
German P.O.W. Camp, and is a bomber pilot.

activity: During tests at the Pirbright Institute, an animal under anaesthetic has its tongue marked for inoculation, while men in special rubber outfits handle the cattle and are sprayed with disinfectant.

te.text: FILE: - industry - agriculture, foot & Mouth disease.

FIGHTING FOOT AND MOUTH DISEASE - "THE MOST
EXPENSIVE DISEASE IN THE WORLD"

London:        Although the dreaded foot-and-mouth
disease has just come into the news again,
following further outbreaks of the scourge, and
the cutting-off of large sections of the country
from cattle movements, men at the Pirbright
Institute, in Surrey, near London, are waging a
full-scale, full-time war against the disease.
An international centre, it is called the Institute
for Fundamental Investigation of Animal Virus
Diseases.  At the centre, foot-and-mouth disease
is called "the most expensive disease in the
world".  In Germany, for instance, between 1937
and 1940, the disease cost £90,000,000.
PHOTO SHOWS:-        During tests at the Institute,
an animal under anaesthetic has its tongue marked
where it is to be innoculated.  The men are wearing
special rubber outfits, and they are sprayed from
head to foot with disinfectant after handling the
cattle.
May 9th. 1952.  PN-h.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
RECD. 1 0 MAY 1952
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

COPYRIGHT.
PLANET NEWS LTD
3, JOHNSON'S COURT,
LONDON, E.C. 4.

activity: The North Western Gas Board's use of illustrations of women ('beauties') in its annual balance sheet.

te.text:
H-M-M-M-M! THE GAS BOARD'S
FIGURES ARE IN GOOD SHAPE
HOW can a Gas Board
make figures interesting?
Take a look at the drawing
below. See any interesting
figures there?
This is the way the North
Western Gas Board has de-
cided to brighten up the
dull figures in its annual
balance sheet — which in-
cidentally shows a profit of
£1,027,284. These flashing,
dark-eyed beauties with
swaying hips and flimsy veils
are splashed across the back
page of the balance sheet.
Says the Board: "The fig-
ures dramatise a straight-
forward and serious text.
Financial figures alone are
too tedious to wade through."

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
15 DEC 1955
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

activity: attendance monitoring at Cwm Colliery using an electronic board called the 'Dotto'

te.text:
BY SEVEN-o'clock yesterday morning, it was
plain to see that the Cwm Colliery was in for a
normal Monday. Unlit lamps on a vast three-sided
electronic board at the pithead showed that more
than a quarter of the entire morning shift had not
bothered to come to work.
One section of the panel revealed that colliers—the
men who actually dig coal at the pit face — were
44.6 per cent. under shift strength.
For other face workers, the figure was 36.3. Elsewhere
underground, 25.3.
On the surface 13.5. An average—excluding men registered
as being sick—of 27.8.
The Cwm Colliery at
Llantwit Fardre, nine miles
north of Cardiff, has been
officially threatened with
closure unless there is a
drastic drop in absenteeism.
Lord Robens himself, the
NCB chairman, has blamed
persistent absenteeism for
part of the NCB's deficit.
Yesterday the National
Coal Board reported:
"Despite the warning, this is
a usual Monday with a very
large proportion of the men
absent from work."
The 'Dotto'
The picture can be quickly
assessed from the red bulbs
on the panel, known as the
"Dotto" after a TV quiz
programme popular when it
was installed.
As a man opens his locker,
a red bulb lights up. Another
shows as he takes his lamp
from a special rack. The
third is switched on as he
enters the cage to go below.
Every day at Cwm, many
lights stay unlit. On Monday
morning and Friday after-
noon it is usual to find that
up to half of the colliers
have not reported.
Where were the missing
men? Mainly in the clubs of
the valley. Of the 1,544
miners on the payroll, only
389 live in Beddau, the village
nearest to the pithead.
At the village of Gilfach
Goch, miner Frank Vowles,
aged 52, confessed that he
was one of the absent men
yesterday.
As he sat with a pint of
beer in a club, he said: "I
slept in too late. I had a few
beers last night, but that
wasn't the cause of it. I was
on overtime over the week-
end and just got exhausted."
Blacker..
Mr. Vowles is a repairer
working at the coal face. He
earns £18 for four shifts.
"It's pretty usual for a
man not to work the fifth
shift, but the Coal Board
paint a blacker picture than
the situation deserves," he
added.
"You can work overtime
during the week, or do a
weekend shift, and in fact
put in more hours than a
man who comes in for five
weekday shifts. But you go
down as being absent.
"It's the hardest work in
the world down below, and if
you don't feel up to working
then you are a danger to
your mates to go on shift."
The Friday absenteeism
has a different cause. A man
in a club in the Rhondda
who failed to turn up on
Friday afternoon said: "It
ruins your social life.
"The afternoon shift goes
down at 2.45 pm., and you're
not back on the surface until
10.15 pm. This means you
are too late for a drink."
The men complain that
most pits allow the Friday
afternoon shift to start work
at midday, so that they are
free by 8 pm.
Mr. Bryn Williams, the
NUM lodge secretary at
Cwm, told me as he came up
from the morning shift yes-
terday: "The management
could quite easily allow an
earlier Friday shift here.
"They say that too much
coal would pile up down
below, but we say they could
quite easily put in a couple
of bunkers to hold 2,000 tons
so that it can be brought to
the surface at the normal
rate during the day."
Social life
Cwm has the highest
absentee rate of any British
pit. In two years, more than
100 men have been sacked
for persistent absenteeism.
Mr. Elfed Hughes was dis-
missed two weeks ago at
Cwm. A 26-year-old mar-
ried man, he worked under-
ground as a packer, a man
who stows coal.
"I was off sick for five
weeks, but I didn't get any
medical certificates. I told
them I'd been ill, but was
dismissed nevertheless," he
said.
Another miner who works
at the coalface said: "You
take Friday afternoon off
because you want your social
life, and you take Monday
morning off because you've
had too good a weekend.
"And you feel, 'Why
should I turn up for work
when they won't let me have
Friday off.'"
Men working at the coal-
face can earn up to £35 a
week. But the average pay
for five shifts is £28 for a
collier.
Said one young miner:
"It is hardly worth working
the extra day. I pick up £20
for four shifts, and if I go
for the fifth I pay most of
that in tax.

activity: Mrs. Cole hanging up her washing on the platform of Forty Hill Station, which has been converted into a dwelling.

te.text:
FAMILY LIVES
14 YEARS
IN A STATION

BY A SPECIAL CORRESPONDENT

MRS. COLE lives on the up platform. Mrs. Chilbrook
shares the down. Mrs. Cole’s flat includes the General
Waiting Room. Mrs. Chilbrook and her neighbour have
the Ladies’ First-Class Waiting Room, the Stationmaster’s
Office and the Porter’s Room.

And Mrs. Chilbrook says that
she wouldn't go back to live in a
street if she had the chance.

It is nearly thirty years since the
L.N.E.R. closed that stretch of Essex
railway line, between Edmonton and
Cheshunt to passenger traffic.

During that time only one goods train
a day has run past its three stations,
Churchbury, Forty Hill, and Theobald’s
Grove.

Fourteen years ago Mrs. Chilbrook
took up residence on Forty Hill station
platform. Her husband and Mrs. Cole’s
husband are railway workers. Why
waste good waiting-rooms when a lick of
paint and a few fittings will make them
as good as any flat?

They have done the same at Theo-
bald's Grove station, where offices and
waiting-rooms house three families.

But Forty Hill looks more homely. Mrs.
Cole has seen to that. She came there a
year ago, and Margaret Cole, then two,
was apt to wander on to the line.

So Margaret and her smaller brother,
with their wire netting “pen” on the
platform, now have an all-weather open-
air playground. And the washing dries
nicely in the breeze that blows up and
down the empty railway line.

And if anybody else would like to live
at a railway station there are five from
which to choose down in Devon.

For to-day the Southern Railway is
selling by auction the five stations on
the old Lynton and Barnstaple Railway,
which was closed three years ago.

The five stations, which are being
offered freehold, complete with platforms
and waiting-rooms, are Lynton, Woody
Bay, Blackmoor Gate, Bratton Fleming
and Chelfham.

SAYER      5.10.38
THE STATION IS NOW A DWELLING.
O.P.S. Mrs. Cole hanging up her washing
on the platform which was once known
as FORTY HILL STATION, ENFIELD.
(See Mr. Austin for story).

te.text:
198316      INH
GRIMSBY TRAWLER "ETRURIA" FINED BY RUSSIA -
"ILLEGAL FISHING" CHARGE.
London:  The Master of the Grimsby trawler
Etruria (formerly Lady Elsa), which was
seized by the Russians last week, has been
ordered to pay a fine of 300 roubles (about
£26) for fishing illegally one-and-a-half
miles from the Soviet coast-line.
This information was given in a statement
made by Mr. Davies, the Foreign Affairs
Undersecretary in the House of Commons.
Mr. Davies said that a Note from the Soviet
Ministry of Foreign Affairs claimed that the
master admitted to the charge, and said that
the trawler would be released as soon as the
fine had been paid.
The British Ambassador in Moscow had been
instructed, with the agreement of the owners
of the trawler, to pay the fine on their behalf.
PHOTO SHOWS:  A view of the Grimsby trawler
Etruria (formerly the Lady Elsa) which has
been seized by the Russians.
May 10th 1950.  PN-h.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
RCD. 11 MAY 1950

CROWN COPYRIGHT RESERVED. MINISTRY OF HOUSING & LOCAL GOVERNMENT.
Four prototype houses built for the Sheffield City Council by the
Public Works Department under the 5M system of construction devised
by the Research and Development Group of the Ministry of Housing
and Local Government. This system, which marks a new attempt to
bring the advantages of industrialisation into the field of house-
building, has been derived from the 5M CLASP system used at
Stevenage for a group of old people's flatlets. The new system
is called 5M, because as at Stevenage, it is based upon a planning
grid of 1' 8" (5 x the module of 4"). The object has been to
modify the CLASP system, which has been shown to have advantages
in the reduction of site labour and building time, to suit the
performance standards, and the levels of cost, of 2-storey housing.
Ministry of Housing & Local Government. January, 1963

activity: winning horse ploughing contests

te.text:
THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED

Natural,
they said

Herald Reporter

A SLIP of a girl with brown
curly hair is making
farming history in Cornwall
by winning horse ploughing
contests.
Old-time farmers—more used to
horses than tractors—disapproved
when they heard that 19-year-old
Margaret Hawke, from the hamlet
of London Apprentice, near St.
Austell, was entering these compe-
titions.
"Land girls are all right for
milking and driving these 'ere
tractors," they grumbled, "but
t'aint natural for a lass to handle
a team of hosses."
But there was one exception-
87-year-old Charles Hawke, of
Roche, near Bodmin. He is
Margaret's grandfather. "You'll
see summat that will amaze 'ee
all," he told his cronies. "Mark
my words."
Boast justified
His boast was justified when
Margaret, five-feet nothing in
khaki breeches, gum-boots and
emerald pull-over, went to Cubert
for the Truro and District plough-
ing competition.
She was the first feminine com-
petitor ever known in the horse
section. Smiling, she put her team
into action—her father's bay mare,
Rose, and her cousin's grey, Judy.
And she won second prize in the
under-21 class, beating her brother,
Donald, who was third.
Then, at Gorran and St. Ewe
Young Farmers' Club competition,
she came first, and at Lanreath
Lostwithiel YFC contest she
first again.
[illegible]garet, who was 19 yesterday,
[illegible] just a land girl, but the
[illegible]dant of generations of
[illegible] farmers. She is following
[illegible]r footsteps by helping on
[illegible]er's 50-acre smallholding.
Animals best
[illegible]y be small," she said yes-
[illegible]y, "but I'm strong. Horses
[illegible]y you all right if you are firm
and understand them. That's
more important than being big
and brawny.
"Tractors are useful and I can
drive one all right, but animals
are my choice—horses, dogs and
cats especially, and I have a pet
rabbit, too. My great ambition is
to have a riding horse of my own."

activity: An expert eye checks every blade: an inspector examining razor blades at the Gillette factory.

te.text:
An expert eye checks every blade.

THERE was this man with a thick beard, see,
trying to escape from a razor-blade factory.
Pushing and straining, he was, against the pad-
locked swing doors as though all the Super Silver
blades in creation were closing in on his chin.
  At least, that's how it
looked to amused specta-
tors on the footpath outside.
To me, locked up in the
Gillette factory, the occa-
sion was a first-hand dem-
onstration of just how
carefully Gillette have to
guard their top industrial
secrets.
  At 5 p.m. precisely padlocks
are slammed tight behind the
departing workers. Spies can't
get in. And, unfortunately,
tardy guests can't get out.
  Top secret areas are banned
to all except essential workers,
which is why I can tell you
nothing about the final mys-
tery of a Gillette stainless steel
blade — how it receives an
instant coating of slice-
through plastic that works in
a very mysterious way.

TESTING

  One of the reasons that
Gillette are so concerned about
security is the basic fact that
they consider their product a
cut above all rivals—last year
the Consumers' Association
voted their Super Silver stain-
less blade as the most comfort-
able and longest-lasting of the
blades tested.
  If the Gillette factory had
a motto it would undoubtedly
be " Testing, testing, testing."
Six million blades a day
emerge from the factory at
Isleworth, west of London, and
the firm come as near to test-
ing every one of them as is
physically possible.
  The testing, in fact, begins
before a single machine starts
to roll. Master samples of
ribbon Sheffield and Swedish
steel are taken from their
hermetically sealed drums and
scientifically assessed for
quality before any major ship-
ment is accepted.

PUNCHED

Wound on reels, like those
from a giant film projector, the
soft steel is then fed at speed
into waiting lines of harvester
machines which swallow a con-
tinuous strip of bare steel one
second and spit it out 30 yards
down the factory floor two
minutes later as a stream of
recognisable razor blades.
  In that short time the steel
has been punched, washed,
rinsed, hardened, washed,
rinsed, cooled, tempered,
etched, lacquered, sharpened,
stropped, diamonded, and
finally honed, in one long flow
of continuous action.
  This is when the testers take
over. First the production-line
testers who use microscopes
and other equipment to check
the cutting edge, temper and
strength of the blade.
  Their work is double-checked
by inspectors who use ultra-
violet light and other highly-
sensitive instruments to pick
up any production faults from

by Alan Ross

selected and random samples.
  Next come the appraisal
inspectors who carry out a
further series of high quality
tests to weed out any faulty
specimens that may have
eluded the net.
  The naked blades are then
given their final top-secret
coating and are checked by
yet another battery of all-
seeing instruments to prove
the shaving edge.
  Then, when science has
done its electronic best,
nature's most sensitive instru-
ment takes over—the human
body. Sample blades are taken
home and put to the overnight
shaving test by a body of care-
fully selected volunteer
workers.
  When the final OK is re-
ceived, the coated blades pass
to the packaging department
to be wrapped, either in paper
or plastic dispensers.
  Packaging a razor blade isn't
simply a question of wrapping
the product for easy transport.
The fine cutting edge of the
blade must be prevented from
coming into contact with any
other material which might
damage it.

TUMBLE

  The four spots of petroleum
jelly on the inside wax wrapper
of any blade are designed to
hold it squarely in the centre
of the package. Paper wrapped
blades are submitted to the
tumble test—being whipped
around in a revolving drum—
to make sure that the blade
will not move and pierce the
paper.
  Plastic dispensers, similarly,
are cunningly designed with
interior "pillars" that prevent
the razor edge from ever com-
ing into contact with the
container.
  Says Mr. Jack White, head of
production: "If I want to
change the type of oil on any
of the machinery, for example,
or if I want to keep a window
open on the factory floor, we
have to launch a massive series
of advance shaving test just
to make sure that no adverse
reaction has been set up that
might alter the performance
of a blade."

ST:EL. SUN. 9.8.67.
Gillette factory for advert supplement.

PROPERTY OF

RECD. 2 - MAY 1951
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

A VETERAN AT HOME. xxxxxxxxxx
CW/7262-23. Mrs. Beddow has a cup of tea waiting for husband,
John, when he arrives home from work. At 84 he can look back
on a life of hard work which started when he was 10 at 1/1d.
a week.

THE OLD FOLK OF INDUSTRY
GK/7362. Seeking to prove a man is "not too old at 70"
is the engineering firm of Rubery, Owen and Co, of Darlaston,
Staffs who have started an "Old Folks Workshop" which they
call "Sons of Rest". Situated about a mile away from the
noise and bustle of the main factory, twelve men, all over
the age of 70 work on their own with no young workers beside
them to give them an inferiority complex over their ages.
The veterans start an hour later than the main factory. They
do drilling and assembly work on office equipment and farm
implements for overseas markets. The experiment has been
going on for 10 months and has proved a great success. Doctors
who are urging more active employment for elderly people for
the benefit of their health support it. It is also a means
of saving for industry skilled hands vitally necessary these
days, which would otherwise be lying idle.

PLEASE RETURN TO

A VETERAN GOES HOME.
CW/7262-27. John Beddow is greeted by his wife on arrival
home at the end of his day's work at the "Sons of Rest".
John, at 84, years of age, would rather work than be idle all
day.

THE OLD FOLK OF INDUSTRY
CK/7262. Seeking to prove a man is "not too old at 70"
is the engineering firm of Rubery, Owen and Co., of Darlaston,
Staffs who have started an "Old Folks Workshop" which they
call "Sons of Rest". Situated about a mile away from the
noise and bustle of the main factory, twelve men, all over
the age of 70 work on their own with no young workers beside
them to give them an inferiority complex over their ages.
The veterans start an hour later than the main factory. They
do drilling and assembly work on office equipment and farm
implements for overseas markets. The experiment has been
going on for 10 months and has proved a great success. Doctors
who are urging more active employment for elderly people for
the benefit of their health support it. It is also a means
of saving for industry skilled hands vitally necessary these
days, which would otherwise be lying idle.

activity: High-pressure turbine and lessening gear inside the Bankside Power Station

te.text: Industry - Fuel and Power - Electricity - Power Stns - BANKSIDE.

P.4481   SKI
BANKSIDE POWER STATION: PRODUCTION GETS UNDER WAY

London: An industrial project which has aroused much
controversy from the time of its conception has just gone
into operation. It is the Bankside Power Station, at
which the first 60,000-kilowatt turbo-alternator of
about 80,000 horse-power, has started to supply electricity.
The project was allowed on condition that oil and not
coal was to be burned. Other conditions which had to
be observed were that the building must be set back
far enough from the Thames so as not to interfere with
the projected road and promenade.
Opposition to the power station was so strong that in
January, 1947 a public inquiry was held, with the result
that the scheme was given Government sanction.
On completion the Bankside Power Station will comprise
four 60,000-kilowatt generating sets, the oil
consumption at full-load (16-hour day) being 67 tons
an hour, consuming in one winter's day about 850 tons.
PHOTO SHOWS:- High-pressure turbine and lessening gear.
When completed, the power station will have four turbines
of this kind.
January 1953 PN-b

DAILY HERALD
3 SEP 1952
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

activity: trainee trawlermen being drilled in survival techniques in a lifeboat

te.text:
EDDOM'S COUSIN IS TEACHER
OF LIFE SAVING TECHNIQUES
AT NAUTICAL COLLEGE FOR
TRAINEE TRAWLERMEN

SIX young trawlermen were drilled yesterday in the same basic
survival techniques which only a few hours earlier had saved the
life of Harry Eddom. Their instructor: John Eddom, Harry's cousin.
They are taking training courses at the Hull Nautical College's
Fishing Department, where Harry Eddom once learned the
lessons which kept him alive after the Ross Cleveland foundered.
John Eddom, aged 38, joined the college two years ago after 12
years as a trawler skipper. Yesterday he was putting the six
trainees through their paces in a lifeboat in Hull's Victoria Dock
Basin. "How Harry survived is nothing short of a miracle,"
he said, "but the instruction we give makes something like
this possible even in the roughest conditions, if there is
time for everything to be carried out." Boys can start at the college
at 16 after a minimum of 100 days at sea. They take an intensive
course in every aspect of trawler work and go back to sea with
knowledge of every aspect of deck-hand seamanship. All they
lack is the experience. The principal of the college, Captain Ivan
Allison, said: "We give a very thorough training in trawler
work. Youngsters have to serve a term at sea to confront
them with the conditions. The basic principles of survival and life
saving which Harry Eddom here were probably
responsible for saving his life."

activity: The tumble down cottages from which Mrs. Morten got the villagers removed.

te.text:
EXCLUSIVE.

Denham 2107.    From : Geoffrey F.Hadrill, " Hazeldene,"
                        Lower Road, Higher Denham, Bucks.

Negatives show :--

    (I) The tumble down cottages from which Mrs. Morten got the villagers
        removed.

EXCLUSIVE.
                 Hadrill--Amersham.
             THE VILLAGERS' GRATITUDE.

    One of the busiest women in the Country is Mrs. Richard Morten, of
Denham, Bucks, who even has to take her knitting to various meetings as she
has no time to set aside a special time for it. A member of the District Council,
together with a number of its subsidiary Committees, she is also a Parish Coun-
cillor and a member of most Welfare Committees and bodies in her own village.
    She is never happier than when assisting someone worse off than herself.
One thing that will be a lasting memorial to her is the manner in which she
agitated for the rehousing of many villagers living in decrepit cottages where
their families had been for centuries. After months of hard work she per-
suaded her District Council to build a colony of modern cottages and assisted
with the moving. Out of this she had another brain wave. Troops billeted
in various places needed oil lamps. All the rehoused villagers willingly
gave her theirs when they found themselves with electric lighting.
    Then came evacuation--a tremendous job for a busy woman--and she also took
up the salvage of iron, bones, rags and papers, etcn, in her stride, using
her own car for the work.
    Next she gave up the iron railings round her house for the use of guns,
and with other members of her family granted facilities for the removal of
iron rails round the graves of their ancestors in the Churchyard.
    In gratitude for what she has done the poor villagers voluntarily subscribed
for a present for her. She purchased two ornamental flower pots which she has
placed at her entrance gates. " They can have the pleasure as well as me, "
she told me. Now she is regularly visiting the villagers to make sure they are
comfortable. " God Bless her " is their prayer.

activity: The photograph likely depicts signboards for houses to let in London suburbs, as described in the detailed typed caption about housing costs and estate agents.

te.text:
SOME very strange signboards
are going up outside houses in
London suburbs and neighbouring
towns. They carry a legend that
we haven't seen since before the
war: HOUSE TO LET.
   Wonderful words! True the boards also
say: "A small capital pay-
ment" is required. But
that does not put off frus-
trated house-hunters.
   They are flocking to
the estate agents who
have put up the notices
like thirsty men chasing
a desert mirage.
   A house to let? It seems
too good to be true. AND IT
IS. I have been looking
very closely into this
phenomenon and I warn
anyone who sees one of these
houses as the answer to his
dreams:
   Stop! Think! Work out
the costs for yourself!
   Because I discovered that
one typical house—a small,
three-bedroomed semi worth—
about £3,800 freehold—
would cost you £17,725 by
the time you had finished
paying.

te.text:
LINCOLN.
		SAVING THE FAMOUS ANGEL CHOIR .

An appeal has been made by the Dean of Lincoln for funds to
meet the expenditure of £30,000 to save the Angel Choir in
Lincoln Cathedral from the danger of collapse. The Angel Choir,
according to the report of Sir Charles Peers, is in danger of
collapse. The East Wall has been moving outwards at the rate of
one inch in thirty days and the work of repair is being carried
out without delay. Work is already in hand and every parish
in the diocese is making an effort to send some contribution.

Photo shows- A general view of the interior of Angel Choir
now in splints.
Fox March 16th. 36.

te.text:
12.1.61.

BRITAIN'S SUPER-TRAWLER READY FOR LAUNCHING.

          Towering on the stocks lies Britain's
largest, latest and most powerful super-trawler,
the LORD NELSON, built to the order of Associated
Fisheries Ltd. Her 1,200 tons burthen and 210 ft.
length will dwarf the largest conventional trawlers
of today (about 900 tons, 200 ft long). The super-
trawler which will be launched on Saturday, Janury 14th,
at Bremerhaven, Germany, will be the first fishing
vessel to freeze part of her catch at sea. Her
radio-telephone will enable her skipper to speak to
his home base in Hull from the further side of Greenland,
nearly 3,000 miles away. The Lord Nelson will fish
from the stern instead of from the starboard side and
has separate holds for deep-frozen fish and fresh for the
fresh fish caught at the end of each trip. She will
be based on Hull and is expected to join the fihing
fleet in May.

                    H/Keystone          CD/726051

te.text:
FEBRUARY 2nd 1969
RENT REBELS FIGHT WITH POLICE DURING MARCH TO THE
HOME OF THE HOUSING MINISTER
Rent Rebels from every estate in and around London
converged on the Hampstead Heath home of the Housing Minister
MR ANTHONY GREENWOOD this afternoon, after holding a mass meeting
in Parliament Hill Fields, Highgate. When they arrived at the top
of Downshire Hill, the road in which the Housing Minister lives,
Fighting broke out between the members of G.L.C. Tenants action
association and the police. The march was planned by the Action
Committee as part of a campaign against the GLC rent increases
imposed last October and which were approved by Mr Greenwood.
Tenants have been withholding the increases and they say 'Not
a Penny on the Rents' will be paid by them. The GLC has written
to these tenants warning them that if the increases were not
paid they could find themselves in a lot of trouble.
PHOTO SHOWS A women demonstrator shouting at the police who
stopped the rent rebels from entering the street
were the Housing Minister lives, Downshire Hill,
Hampstead Heath this afternoon.
IS/816031.

activity: Mr and Mrs Peter and Susan Scott in their co-ownership house at Walton-on-Thames

te.text:
SUN YOUNG 3-11-68
Mr and Mrs Peter and Susan Scott in their house at Walton on Thames.
SEE JILL GUYTE HOUSE FEATURE.

PETER and Susan Scott, nearing their fourth wedding anniversary, are now quite settled in their brand new £6,000 house.
It has three bedrooms, a garage, central heating and is situated in the pleasant district of Walton-on-Thames, Surrey.
The Scotts moved in five months ago, as soon as the cement was dry, after a total initial outlay of exactly £147 10s.
They did it by joining one of the co-ownership housing societies which groups of people can set up under the aegis of the Government's Housing Corporation. Surprisingly perhaps, this is still a little known easy route to home ownership.
Co-ownership housing societies build and manage homes without profit-making, therefore slashing costs.
Jointly
Occupiers must all be members, and they own their homes jointly. The Scotts are co-owners with their fellow residents of a group of 18 terraced houses like the one they live in.
The Scotts are typical beneficiaries of such schemes. Peter Scott explained: "To buy a house in this area I would have needed at least £1,000 for a deposit. I could have saved it only by living like a hermit for years, and I wasn't prepared to do it."
Mr. Scott is 29 and an aircraft design development engineer. His 23-year-old wife Susan, works as a secretary.
An analysis of their personal situation illustrates the workings of co-ownership.
Of that crucial £147 10s., the £100 went to the society as a returnable indemnity against depreciation or abuse of the property;
£32 10s. was the first monthly repayment, in advance;
£10 covered legal fees (compare it with the £100-£150 normally payable); and £5 was a fee for society membership.
The Scotts monthly payment of £32 10s. includes paying off the capital loan (spread over 40 years); interest, currently 5 1/2 per cent; £1 society management fees; maintenance of property and grounds (£20 a year); and insurance (£5 a year).
Peter Scott also pays £88 10s. a year rates. The society are currently preparing to battle for re-valuation of the properties at a lower figure.
Susan Scott is delighted with her house, with its 27ft. lounge and dining area, lavatories upstairs and down, wide windows overlooking an open-plan front lawn. And a fenced-off back garden with the Thames riverside a few minutes' drive away.
All schemes like this must be approved by the Government's Housing Corporation, and building is carried out to stringent standards.
One of the Scotts neighbours, George Pearson, now secretary of their Co-owners' Society, says that the cost of each house to the co-owner is just over £5,500. Agents have estimated that on the open market the price would be at least £6,000.
Co-ownership costs vary considerably, depending very much on the type of development, and the area in which it is built.
If the Scotts decide to leave they will be entitled, like all co-owners, to a payment, provided they have been in occupation for at least three years.
This payment consists of the part of the monthly "rent" which has been used to pay off the capital debt, plus the occupier's share of any difference in the value of the house.
The lease can be assigned to a widow or heir in the event of the co-owner's death.
Other big attractions are freedom from worry about obtaining a mortgage. The society borrows on collective credit and the only age restriction is that a co-owner should be over 21.
The 11 members of the society's management committee meet monthly. The sort of things they discuss are rates, refuse disposal and decoration.
"You need to be interested," said Peter Scott. "Your money is involved, and decisions are being taken on your behalf.
Advice
"I would recommend the scheme to anyone. The only advice I would give is this: make sure of the precise cost and remember that the house will never belong to you as an individual."
To date, the Housing Corporation have approved 340 co-ownership schemes all over the country, involving 12,962 homes and £59,142,314.
For information about co-ownership, write to the Housing Corporation, Sloane Square House, London, S.W.1.
by Jill Guyte
These houses would sell for £6,000 on the open market. The Scotts got one for £147 10s. down.

date_info.rationale: A faint rubber stamp with this date and the 'SUN' newspaper mark is visible next to the label.

te.text:
BP PLANS FULL SCALE PROTEIN PRODUCTION

BP plans to build a £2-million plant at the Group's Lavera refinery in France
to produce protein concentrate from a gas oil feedstock. Construction is
expected to start in 1968 and the plant, with an annual capacity in excess
of 16,000 tons, should be in production by 1970. The protein will be marketed
as a component of animal feedingstuffs.

It was at the Lavera refinery, owned by Societe Francaise des Petroles BP,
that M. Alfred Champagnat, leading a team of BP scientists, first realised
the potential of protein manufactured from petroleum feedstocks. The decision
to start full scale production follows eight years of experimental and
development work by BP in France and the United Kingdom.

Extensive tests on the new BP product have been carried out over a period of
years in Holland at the Central Institute of Nutrition and Food Research
(C.I.V.O.) and the Institute of Agricultural Research of Biochemical Products
(I.L.O.B.), two specialist organisations with very long standing experience
in the field of nutrition and agricultural research. C.I.V.O. are conducting
laboratory animal feeding trials to ensure that the protein is completely
free from harmful effects, while I.L.O.B. are assessing the food value of
the concentrate as a protein source in farm animal rations.

activity: Late harvest scene with sacks of wheat hauled up a steep bank overlooking Stoneleigh.

te.text:
E M B A R G O
_________________

NOT TO BE PUBLISHED BEFORE 4.00 p.m. ON MONDAY,
October 1st, 1956
_________________

NEW FERGUSON TRACTOR - the FERGUSON 35 de-luxe (Diesel Model)

The Ferguson 35 de-luxe incorporates numerous entirely new features
resulting from 13 years of intense research. The famous Ferguson hydraulic
system has been revolutionised. In addition to raising and lowering an
implement and automatically keeping a plough or cultivator at a selected
depth on uneven ground, the new hydraulic system gives the tractor driver
perfect control of front, mid or rear-mounted implements.

A new dual clutch gives a "live", engine-driven power-take-off for
power driven implements such as mowers or balers. A six speed gear box pro-
vides a wide selection of gears for every job on the farm enabling full use
to be made of the 37 brake h.p.. An alternative, ground speed p.t.o. in
ratio to the tractor's forward speed provides power for such tasks as planting,
hay making or fertilising, irrespective of the gear selected.

Among the many other important new features are included more
precise and easier steering, two steering brake pedals on the right hand
side of the transmission housing, a new safety starter, safety fuel tank,
instrument panel with a combined tachometer, speedometer and hour meter,
foamed cushion seat and padded back rest. Also new is the styling in two-tone
Ferguson grey and metallic bronze.
=o-o-o-o-o-o-o-o-o=

The new Ferguson 35, with its increased horse power and greater
sensitivity will enable farmers materially to increase their output per man
and per acre. In this late harvest scene sacks of wheat dropped by the com-
bine have been hauled up a steep bank overlooking the village of Stoneleigh,
in Warwickshire.
=o-o-o-o-o-o-o-o-o=

te.text:
DUAL PURPOSE VESSEL LAUNCHED IN ESSEX
February 16th 1960 PAR 82104-1 (PNR-B)

DUAL PURPOSE VESSEL LAUNCHED IN ESSEX

Gracefully sliding into the water at
Brightlingsea, Essex, is the "Boston
Hornet" a dual purpose vessel which
fulfills the role of a Near Water/Drifter
Trawler.
She has been built by James Stone
(Brightlingsea) Limited for the Boston
Deep Sea Fisheries Limited of Lowestoft,
and is thought to be the largest Drifter/
Trawler ever to be built on the Essex
coast.
The vessel has been built to Lloyds 100
Al Class and has an overall length of 99ft.
9 inches, with a breadth of 22 feet and a
moulded depth of 10 feet 6 inches. With
a distinctive 'Look Ahead' wheelhouse and
a well raked bar stem the vessel is ready
to cope with any problem which can be con-
fronted in the fishing industry. The
fishing gear is arranged for operation on
both the Port and Starboard sides for
easy working of the trawl and drifting
gear.
The vessel is of aluminium alloy which
beats the corrosion 'bogey', normally a
constant headache for owners of such
vessels.
February 16th 1960 PAR 82104-1 (PNR-B)

activity: Artist's impression of a new factory and warehouse development for Ranks Hovis McDougall Limited at Wolverton, Bucks.

te.text:
Press Information from I.D.C.

Release No:- 990/023        Date of Issue:- 7 Feb, 1967

NEW FACTORY FOR RANKS HOVIS McDOUGALL LIMITED

     A new 52,000 sq. ft. factory and warehouse is to be built 
shortly to process the well known Ranks 'Blue Cross' range of 
animal foods at Wolverton, Bucks. 

     The project has been designed and will be constructed by 
I.D.C. Limited of Industrial House, Stratford-upon-Avon who are 
Civil, Constructional and Services Engineers, Designers and Contractors.
Construction work will be completed in 46 weeks. 

     The development consists of a six-storey production unit of 
20,000 sq. ft. and a warehouse of 26,000 sq. ft. together with various 
office, workshop and amenity facilities. The production unit, which 
includes a 90 ft. tower, is fully automated and contains precast concrete 
silo and bin stores with special intake and elevator pits. The building 
is steel framed and is clad in light weight asbestos cement and translucent 
sheeting. The 80 ft. clear span portal framed warehouse has a 236 ft. 
long cantilevered loading canopy which projects 30 ft. The walls of the 
warehouse and amenity buildings are formed by exposed aggregate concrete 
panels which are developed and manufactured by I.D.C. Limited. 

END

Photograph attached shows the Artist's Impression of the 
new development.

I.D.C. LIMITED  INDUSTRIAL HOUSE, STRATFORD-UPON-AVON, TELEPHONE 4422

activity: Frank Sinatra shaking hands with H.M. The Queen at the film premiere of 'Me and the Colonel' at the Odeon, Leicester Square.

te.text:
DH. GREAVES.,				27-10-58.
PREMIER OF FILM "ME AND THE COLONEL"
AT ODEON, LEICS.SQ. H.M. The Queen
OPS, Shakes hands with Frank Sinatra.
Frank Sinatra bows as he is presented to the Queen—Herald picture by Frank Greaves.

By Henry Fielding
FRANK SINATRA did NOT fly to London to marry Lady Beatty.
He said it—at last—in front of the Queen, Prince Philip, the Duke and Duchess of Gloucester and two thousand others at the glittering premiere last night of Danny Kaye's new film "Me and the Colonel."
Lady Beatty was not there to hear Sinatra's laughing but significant "I came to England to introduce the stars of this movie and for no other reason. I didn't come here to get married.
"Some people would have me married as often as Farouk."
The Queen and Prince Philip smiled. There was wild applause and then Frank got down to the serious business of introducing Danny, Curt Jurgens and Nicole Maurey.
Back to work
It was a very different Frank who strode to the royal enclosure at the Odeon, Leicester-square, half-an-hour earlier.
Then, he was morose as he stood drawing hard at a cigarette.
"Some people have a hole in their head," he said bitterly. "I came here just for this. I am flying back immediately to start work."
Then he turned away to meet the one man who didn't know who he was.
Somebody said: "I'd like to introduce Lord Nathan." And Lord Nathan said: "I am sure I'd love to know you if only I knew who you were."
So Sinatra, the man everybody knows had to introduce himself.
Lord Nathan, chairman of the executive committee of the British Empire Cancer Campaign, which got £25,000 from last night's affair, said to me: "I knew the name, of course, but I'm afraid I don't go to the pictures."

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
28 OCT 1958
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

te.text:
Fuel & Power
Oil Wells in Britain

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED
UNDAMAGED.

SEEKING OIL WELL UNDER LONDON

"Herald" Reporter
SOMEWHERE near — or
under — London is a huge
reservoir of crude oil.
To find it the D'Arcy Explora-
tion Company is sinking a
2,200ft. bore in the middle of
Gibbon's Recreation Ground,
Willesden, N.W.
Latest American oil-field
machinery valued at £20,000 is
being used, and the cost of bor-
ing will be £8,000, or £4 a foot.
The money is being put up by
the Anglo-Iranian Petroleum Co.
Last night men in overalls
and steel helmets (pictured
above at the head of the bore)
had erected an 87-ft. high steel
derrick.
"If we find it —"
As the sun set they were put-
ting finishing touches to a short
main pipe through which the big
drill can start boring into the
ground first thing this morning.
Mr. Alex Braemner, director of
the D'Arcy Exploration Com-
pany, told me: "Oil sand in the
area points to oil being some-
where near. We are sinking to
get a better idea where it is. If
we find it, it will be a wonderful
discovery for the country."
The company's geologist, Mr.
Arthur Davis, of Croydon-road,
Anerley, S.E., has "great hopes
of tracking down the reservoir,"

NEW PROPELLERS FOR THE QUEEN MARY.           15.7.36.

        Officials of CUNARD, JOHN BROWN and THORNYCROFT today
examined the propellers of the QUEEN MARY for wear as the water
receded in the graving dock at Southampton.  The result was
satisfactory and four new propellers of the same composition
will be built.  An attempt to break the Atlantic record will
probably be made on the liner's next voyage.

O.P.S.  Officials photographed examining the propellers of the
        QUEEN MARY at Southampton today.   73/B. Keystone.

MARY
is to remain in dry dock
at Southampton until
Saturday. Experts, seen
examining her propel-
lers yesterday, have
decided that there is no
need for the four screws
to be replaced. Repairs
to her turbines are being
hurried forward, ready
for her next voyage.

activity: Weeping women relatives awaiting news at the pithead after the Markham Colliery mine disaster

te.text:
60 FEARED DEAD, 39 INJURED AND 50 STILL 
 ENTOMBED AFTER CHESTERFIELD MINE DISASTER. 
 
 Sixty men are feared dead, 39 are injured 
 and in hospital and 50 are trapped half 
 a mile underground following two great 
 explosions at Markham Colliery, near 
 Chesterfield, Derbyshire. 
 Feverish rescue attempts are being made, 
 but it is feared that the death roll 
 will increase. 
 PHOTO SHOWS:- Weeping women relatives 
 awaiting news at the pithead after the 
 disaster.

WEEPING WOMEN WAIT at the pit-head of the Markham 
 Colliery, near Chesterfield, for news of their men who are 
 in the pit. To most of them this vigil is the culmination of 
 the dread that haunts them all their lives. Rescue attempts 
 go on all day but every hour without news brings doubt 
 nearer to certainty. Left, an official consults the list of 
 those rescued for anxious inquirers.

COPYRIGHT. 
 PLANET NEWS LTD 
 3, JOHNSON'S COURT, 
 LONDON, E.C. 4. 
 'PHONE: CENT. 3671 & 3672/3.

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE

THEY WANT TO GO DOWN THE MINE. 
A national recruiting drive for the pits was 
opened in Liverpool on Saturday with an exhibition 
and a Coal Board travelling cinema, and unemployed 
men are already responding to the appeal. 
Recruits have flowed into Myrtle St. employment 
exchange, where Mr. Llewellyn Hughes, Ministry of 
Labour official interviews them. 
He has had as many as 80 inquiries a week, and says 
the men have proved of good physique. 
New recruits receive £4-10-0 a week during their 
three weeks training and afterwards they get £5-15-0 
for a five-days week. 
Starting at Boldmere Colliery, St. Helens, Lancs., 
under the personal supervision of an instructor 
they go afterwards to a mine as near as possible 
to their homes. 
OPS. Alfred Martin one of the first recruits studies 
the poster on the recruiting van.

activity: four women in a damaged room at an old folks' home after a chimney collapse

te.text:
TWO women over 80 were killed and three others
injured when a freak gust of wind blew down
a chimney-stack as they sat round the fire at an
old folks' home last night.
Seven other women, all of them over 75, were trapped under
the debris. Rescuers dug for them with bare hands.
Fifteen old women live in the home, which is on the sea-front at Brighton-road, Lancing, Sussex. Twelve were resting just after tea in the lounge on the second floor, waiting for evening prayers.
There was a thunderstorm with a wind blowing strongly along the sea front.
Then came an extra strong, freak, gust. A chimney crashed on to the roof, shattering the slates and rafters. It made a hole about 10ft. square.
NEAREST FIRE
Bricks, masonry and broken beams crashed through the plaster of the lounge ceiling on to the women sitting beneath.
One of the two killed instantly was Miss Alice Goldring, aged 89, the oldest person in the home. The other was 85-year-old Miss Clara Warren.
Both were sitting nearest the fire and were buried beneath the brickwork of the chimney breast.
The three-ton chimneypiece and the debris fell around the fireplace. Those furthest from it escaped with shock.
Mr. Henry Leeks, superintendent of the home, was downstairs with his staff of four, preparing the evening meal. The crash put out all the lights.
When he got upstairs he found the lounge door jammed. He was struggling to open it as firemen arrived. They put a ladder to a window, and 75-year-old Mrs. Annie Pritchett, who had been sewing near it, opened it for them after she crawled unaided from the debris.

activity: demonstration or announcement of the new Ferguson 35 de-luxe Diesel Model tractor and its technical features

te.text:
Cultivations with the new Ferguson 35 can be carried out faster
and more economically.  The increased horse power, improved hydraulic system
and six forward and two reverse speeds enables the farmer to make the best
use of favourable weather conditions.

E M B A R G O
NOT  TO  BE  PUBLISHED  BEFORE  4.00 p.m.  ON  MONDAY,
October 1st, 1956

NEW  FERGUSON  TRACTOR  -  the FERGUSON  35  de-luxe  (Diesel Model)

The Ferguson 35 de-luxe incorporates numerous entirely new features
resulting from 13 years of intense research.  The famous Ferguson hydraulic
system has been revolutionised.  In addition to raising and lowering an
implement and automatically keeping a plough or cultivator at a selected
depth on uneven ground, the new hydraulic system gives the tractor driver
perfect control of front, mid or rear-mounted implements.

A new dual clutch gives a "live", engine-driven power-take-off for
power driven implements such as mowers or balers.  A six speed gear box pro-
vides a wide selection of gears for every job on the farm enabling full use
to be made of the 37 brake h.p..  An alternative, ground speed p.t.o. in
ratio to the tractor's forward speed provides power for such tasks as planting,
hay making or fertilising, irrespective of the gear selected.

Among the many other important new features are included more
precise and easier steering, two steering brake pedals on the right hand
side of the transmission housing, a new safety starter, safety fuel tank,
instrument panel with a combined tachometer, speedometer and hour meter,
foamed cushion seat and padded back rest.  Also new is the styling in two-tone
Ferguson grey and metallic bronze.

are now pouring not only into our pre-war markets

and Japanese.  We just can't make enough of them.

    a spray.

"QUEENS OF LOVELINESS" ARRIVE AT PARK
LANE HOTEL FOR THEIR STAY IN LONDON TO
APPEAR AT THE "WOMAN'S FAIR" AT OLYMPIA.

women more beautiful, arrived in London yesterday.
Chosen from thousands as the beauties of these industries, they are
the "Queens of Loveliness," who will appear at Woman's Fair,

Belding, Millinery; Miss Olive Carpenter, Silks; Miss Peggy Brabyn,
Perfumery and Cosmetics; Miss Rene Morris, Rayon; Miss Eileen

te.text:
British Petroleum's first drilling barge for North Sea
operations is to begin operating about mid-May this year.

Since last December equipment for 'Sea Gem' has been
arriving at Liverpool docks from as far as Papua and Trinidad.
Transported to the BP North Sea operational base at Eakring,
Nottinghamshire, a complete rig has been assembled on a 'mock-up'
layout of the drilling barge.  Valuable time will be saved by the
crew knowing in advance exactly where every piece of equipment is to
be positioned on the barge which is due to arrive at Middlesborough
from Le Havre on April 30th.

O.P.S.  The 136 feet high derrick which will be mounted on 'Sea
Gem' BP's first drilling platform for North Sea operations.

activity: Mrs. Harding fitting a scalpette on a customer at a wig-makers in West London

te.text:
186475-78  HUM

THE 'CROWNING GLORY' - AS SUPPLIED BY BRITAIN'S
HEALTH SCHEME.

London:  A woman's crowning glory is her hair, so the
mere male is led to believe - but like other feminine
charms these days, it may be false, in part or in whole.
Britain's comprehensive Health Service aids and abets
the deception regarding hair, and teeth, but few would
deny the benefits it confers on both male and female.
Over eight thousand people have taken advantage of free
wigs obtained under the health scheme, and although the
number of women applying is not known, a considerable
number of the applicants are believed to be women who
have lost all or part of their 'crowning glory'.
Of the applicants some 2,600 have so far been supplied
with wigs. One well-known London firm of wig-makers,
who export a considerable number of wigs to the United
States each month, have had 1,500 National Health
Service customers up to date, against their monthly
average of 50 private customers.
The making of wigs is a complicated and skillful art,
needing clever fingers and a sharp eye, for when man
competes with nature, nature usually wins, and to make
a wig which will deceive at close quarters is more than
difficult.
Most of the hair used for wig-making is obtained from
Western Europe, Italy, France and Germany contributing
a great part.  Prices of the hair varies according to
the quality and colour, and this price affects the
cost of the finished wig.  The most expensive wig to
buy, owing to the difficulty of obtaining the hair, is
a white one, the price of which lies between 25 and 100
pounds.

PHOTO SHOWS:  Mrs. Harding fitting a scalpette on a
customer at a well known West London wig-makers.
Customers include many  to whom a neat and presentable
appearance is important in business.
3rd. August, 1949,      PN-d,

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION TUESDAY'S DAILIES

PRINCE PHILIP TO OPEN £26M. STEEL PLANT TODAY
JS 15.10.63.
THE NEW £26,000,000 ENGLISH STEEL CORPORATION WORKS
AT TINSLEY PARK, SHEFFIELD, WHICH WILL BE OPENED
BY PRINCE PHILIP TODAY (TUESDAY), IS CLAIMED TO BE
THE MOST ADVANCED PLANT IN EUROPE FOR THE
PRODUCTION OF SPECIAL ENGINEERING STEELS.
THE PLANT REVOLUTIONISES THE MAKING OF CARBON
AND ALLOY STEELS WHICH PREVIOUSLY HAVE BEEN

NEW WORKS, ON THE 500-ACRE SITE OF A DISUSED

A YEAR WITH AMPLE PROVISION FOR FUTURE EXPANSION.
FOR THE FIRST TIME, THE TINSLEY PARK WORKS
PUT SPECIAL STEEL PRODUCTION ON A FLOW BASIS. ONE-
HUNDRED-TON ELECTRIC-ARC FURNACES MELT STEEL WHICH
CAN THEN BE FED DIRECTLY TO MODERN ROLLING MILLS
IN INGOTS OF 2 1/2 TO 5 TONS - WELL IN EXCESS OF THE
SIZE PREVIOUSLY USED FOR THE ROLLING OF ALLOY AND
SPECIAL CARBON STEELS. EVERY TECHNICAL INNOVATION

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION THURSDAY'S EVENINGS MARCH 17,1949.
      A NEW TUNNEL UNDER THE THAMES.
               17.3.49.
A new tunnel, driven under the river Thames from Battersea
Power Station to Chelsea, will carry cables between the power
station and a new sub-station in north-west London. The
2,500 ft [crossed out] tunnel - one of the most remarkable engineering feats
in London - takes two 500-ft-radius bends to miss the piers of
the Victoria Railway Bridge, but in spite of this it was only
3/8-inch out when it connected with the pit dug at the Chelsea end.
Continuous shifts working day and night since last September have
averaged 60 feet per week, and pressurised air had to be used to
keep the engineers going. At one point the tunnel air pressure
[crossed out] of 10lb per square inch had to be increased to 28lb to stop
the water from bursting through. The internal diameter of the
tunnel is eight feet, and it is being lined with 1,900 tons
of cast-iron lining. It is 76 feet below ground level on the south
bank, and it is 16 feet under the river bed at the highest point.
      This picture shows:
The site of the Chelsea Bridge Road end of the tunnel with
Battersea Power Station (across the river) seen in background.

activity: Mrs Shaw packing one-day-old chicks into cardboard boxes for dispatch at Balbirnie Poultry Farm.

te.text:
JUST IN TIME FOR EASTER
Cow,                                   21.3.51.
The approach of Easter heralds the peak period of the year for
eggs and chickens. At Balbirnie Poultry Farm, near Markinch,
Fife, just now, 2,000 laying pullets and hens lay 1,500 xxxxx
eggs every day. Of these 3,000 a week are put into incubators
for hatching, and the surplus sent to the packing stations.
The eggs are in the incubators for 21days at a temperature of
100 degress Fahr., and 80 per cent hatch out. When they are
one day old and over the chicks are packed in cardboard boxes
and sent all over the country, and this picture shows
Mrs Shaw, wife of the farm's manager, packing some of the
chicks into boxes for dispatch.

COPYRIGHT PHOTO ISSUED BY
CENTRAL PRESS PHOTOS LTD.
119, FLEET STREET, LONDON, E.C.4

activity: The first meeting of the National Economic Development Council ('Neddy') in London, featuring government officials and union leaders.

te.text:
FIRST MEETING OF 'NEDDY'
LE E11676/7 7.3.62.
THE FIRST MEETING OF 'NEDDY' - THE NATIONAL
ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT COUNCIL - WAS HELD IN
LONDON THIS AFTERNOON. THOSE PRESENT INCLUDED
MR. SELWYN LLOYD, CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER,
AND SIX TRADES UNION CONGRESS CHIEFS. THE COUNCIL
WILL ADVISE ON LONG-TERM PLANS FOR MAINTAINING AND
DEVELOPING PROSPERITY.
PHOTO SHOWS: THE MEMBERS OF THE NATIONAL ECONOMIC
DEVELOPMENT COUNCIL SEEN AT THEIR FIRST MEETING THIS
AFTERNOON. THEY ARE (L-R) LORD ROBENS, CHAIRMAN OF THE
NATIONAL COAL BOARD; SIR OLIVER FRANKS, PROVOST OF
WORCESTER COLLEGE, OXFORD; SIR ROBERT SHONE, DIRECTOR
GENERAL OF THE STAFF OF THE COUNCIL, MR. SELWYN LLOYD,
CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER, MR. HARE, MINISTER OF
LABOUR; MR. ERROLL, PRESIDENT OF THE BOARD OF TRADE,
MR. J.N. TOOTHILL, FERRANTI LTD; DR. BEECHING,
CHAIRMAN OF B.T.C., PROF. E.H. PHELPS BROWN, LONDON
SCHOOL OF ECONOMICS; MR. R. SMITH, POST OFFICE WORKERS
UNION; MR. S.F. GREENE, NATIONAL UNION OF RAILWAYMEN;
MR. FRANK COUSINS, TRANSPORT & GENERAL WORKERS UNION;
MR. E.J. HUNTER, SWAN, HUNTER & WIGHAM RICHARDSON LTD;
MR. J.M. LAING, JOHN LAING & SON LTD; MR. W.J. CARRON,
AMALGAMATED ENGINEERING UNION; MR. GEORGE WOODCOCK,
GEN-SEC OF THE T.U.C.; MR. H. DOUGLASS, GEN. SEC OF
THE IRON AND STEEL TRADES CONFEDERATION; AND MR. C.
HARRISON, ENGLISH SEWING COTTON CO LTD; MR. F.A.
COCKFIELD, BOOTS PURE DRUG CO. LTD; AND MR. R.M.
GEDDES.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
- 7 MAR 1962
PLEASE RETURN
TO

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION WEDNESDAY'S EVENINGS, August 20th.
   HARVESTING ON THE SUSSE "PRAIRIES"
                                20.8.47.
The present crisis has brought about the biggest Government drive
for a great increase in the production of home-grown food, and
the Prime Minister has called for a £100,000,000 step-up in this
direction by 1950-51. Since the War Office handed back, a year
ago, many acres of land which had been used for Artillery
training purposes, the East Sussex War Agricultural Committee has
been responsible for over a 1,000 acres [illegible] of corn being
grown. This is now in process of being harvested, and in this
picture, one of the biggest single "fields" in the country,
strecthing for more than 200 acres across the rolling Sussex
Downs, is being harvested of its corn. The binders are starting
on the work which will be taken over by the Combine harvesters
at a later stage.

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

COPYRIGHT PHOTO ISSUED BY
CENTRAL PRESS PHOTOS LTD.
[illegible] LONDON. E.C.4

te.text:
30,000 MULLET NETTED IN CORNISH BEACH CATCH    D/P.1.

In a race against the ebb tide, a catch of 30,000
grey mullet was beached safely with the first seine
shot of the season at Sennen Cove, near Land's End.
After weeks of watching, the cry of "Hevva" went up
in the traditional manner, as the shoals of mullet
were sighted in the bay, and the fishermen rushed the
seine boat out loaded with the net to encircle the
fish. Working all night, the men hauled the catch up
out of reach of the tide, where it was shared out among
the villagers.

PHOTO SHOWS: Sharing out the catch of grey mullet on
the beach at Sennen Cove, near Land's End, Cornwall.

The L.M.S., in an effort to combat the difficulties
of finding lodgings for railway workers, is now
converting caravan camping coaches into "living
trains" to house their men.  The coaches will be
stabled at convenient sidings in Outer London and

men and will consist of three coaches - two as
"sleepers" and one as a self-contained kitchen
and living rooms.  A cook-attendant will "housekeep"
for the "residents" on each train.

activity: John Fain finishing leather hats for Billingsgate fish porters in his workshop.

te.text:
"MY HAT"   FISHY BUSY AT BILLINGSGATE
 COBBLER MAKES PORTERS' HATS        DG/HT

Most unusual hatter in London is  JOHN FAIN
of Lovat Lane  Eastcheap.   He is the only
man in the world, he claims, to make the
well known leather hats for Billingsgate fish
porters.  He has been making them for  over 25 years
It takes  eight hours to make one  and as they
will last for  over 45 years orders for new ones
are not exactly overwhelming.  Mr  Fain  makes and 
repairs shoes when not engaged on  making hats-for
fish-porters-to-carry- boxes-of- iced-fish-on.

PHOTO SHOWS:  There will be no  Billingsgate language
over these two  hats when MR JOHN FAIN  finishes them.
Made of solid leather  with a high rim to keep the cold
water and fish scales off the porter , the hats will
last for years .  A top piece takes the weight of the
fish boxes, a stack of which may easily weigh 1 cwt.
Hats are prized heirlooms in  the market families.

activity: a craftsman beating gold leaf inside a mould

te.text:
"UNDER THE HAMMER"
IT'S STILL THE SIGN OF BEATEN GOLD DG/VAN

The strong right arm of the craftsman
sign of the gold beater of olden times
is still the principal factor in the
making of today's beaten gold, and
the arm of MR E.J. WOODWARD of Harringay
has pounded thousands of fine leaves during
his 50 years at the craft. One of the
finest workmen at the firm of George M.
Whiley (one of the last remaining of London's
gold beaters) Mr WOODWARD is 68 and
looks forward to many more years at his craft.
It is a strange fact that most gold beaters
live to great ages ) . Hammer weighs 8 lb.
British gold leaf is the world's finest
and plays a big part in the export field.
So old are some of the marble benches, that the
beater's left thumb presses a hole in it
as generations of craftsmen come and go.

PHOTO SHOWS:- "Take this gold and beat it"
is what they say to strong armed MR
WOODWARD . The gold leaf is inside the sheets
of this "mould" and beating must be kept up
for five hours.

To maintain a level of production, the British Power Boat Co.,
of Hythe, Hampshire, who have Government contracts, have taken
and equipped as a training centre a large mansion, standing in

activity: Young apprentice ERIC HALLETT watches craftsman JOHN BROWN at work carving rocking horses by hand at the factory at Lee.

te.text:
KT/F28.

A DYING CRAFT IS SAVED.
      Probably the best-known and loved nursery toy
for countless generations has been the rocking horse.
It is a surprising fact that there is only one
genuine wood carving rocking horse maker left in
Great Britain, master craftsman MR.JOHN BROWN who
works at a large toy factory at LEE in South-East
London. MR.BROWN has been with the firm for 40 years,
the last 35 of which he has specialised in hand
carving rocking horses, but he is due to [crossed out] retire
this summer, and it was thought that the craft would
die out completely. Now the situation has been saved,
because 15-year-old ERIC HALLETT of Catford was a
member of a school party being shown over the factory,
and when he saw MR.BROWN at work he became interested,
and as a result he has now joined the firm and is
apprenticed to MR.BROWN and will be taking over from
him.

PHOTO SHOWS.
      Young apprentice ERIC HALLETT watches
craftsman JOHN BROWN at work carving rocking horses
by hand at the factory at Lee.

ONE OF THE OLDEST OF FARMING ARTS.       AW/RS.

58-year-old Mr. Tom Allen Hancock, a smallholder at
Brook, Kent, is one of the few remaining exponents of
the thousands of years old art of flail-threshing.
The flail he uses was used by his father and his
grandfather before him and is nearly 150 years old.
It consists of a club swinging by a leather thong
from the end of a 5ft pole.  The pole is held in both
hands and the club swung to beat the sheaves of corn
laid out on the barn floor.  Tom still relies on it
for threshing peas and beans.  He can remember the
days when his family had six men in the barn working
flails - keeping them occupied most of the winter.

girls are doing their schoolwork at home until

school.

activity: the Brabazon I aircraft surrounded by aircraft workers at the christening ceremony at the Filton assembly hall

te.text:
BRITAIN'S GIGANTIC 'BRABAZON' IS CHRISTENED AT WORLD'S
LARGEST ASSEMBLY HALL.

With the world's biggest aircraft assembly hall waiting
to receive her,              Britain's biggest landplane
was christened 'Brabazon I' at the Filton (Bristol)
plant of the Bristol Aeroplane Company by Air-marshal
Sir Alec Coryton, Controller of Air Supplies of the
Ministry of Supply.
The aircraft is the Bristol Type 167, a 126-ton eight-engined
giant with a fuselage length of 177 feet and wingspan of 230 feet.
The plane had outgrown the assembly hall which gave it birth
and the vast new one was built so that construction
could be completed and the wings attached.
The new assembly hall, which will be used for building
other          gigantic planes, has a capacity of 33,000,000
cubic feet and a floor space of nearly eight acres.
PHOTO SHOWS:- 'Brabazon I' surrounded by thousands of
aircraft workers at the christening ceremony.
Behind the plane is the huge new assembly hall.
             G October 8th 1947 PN. r.

PLANET NEWS LTD.
3, JOHNSON'S COURT,
LONDON, E.C.4.

activity: demonstrating how to hypnotise pigs

te.text: FILE - INDUSTRY - AGRICULTURE - PIGS - (x Filed Hypnotism)

Gentle George tickles
pigs to sleep
By MAURICE FAGENCE
JOYCE and Daisy made their first and positively last
appearance on ITV last night. Some stars make a dozen
farewell appearances before they finally retire. Joyce and
Daisy, two fat little porker pigs, won't have that luck.
Three men who called for them by car while they were doing
their tea-time television
show from the Wood
Green Empire will make
sure of that.
The men asked the stage-
door receptionist: "Are they
ready yet?"
To producer John Irwin, who
is more used to stage-door callers
with bouquets, they said: "Don't
hurry them. Don't hurry them.
We don't need them for bacon
until eight in the morning."
And looking at their visiting
cards (Representing the Letch-
worth Bacon Company) John
Irwin replied: "I've
many artists far more deserving
of such a fate."
A touch
Joyce and Daisy appeared with
George Crocker, a Devon stock-
man in London for the Smith-
field Show which opens at Earls
Court today.
George demonstrated how to
hypnotise pigs.
Viewers saw him send Joyce
and Daisy to sleep by stroking
them near the shoulder. "I
touch a nerve connecting heart
and brain," George explained.
He claims that he can give
pigs up to 20 minutes' deep sleep
with a deft touch and says he
often helps sows to have their
babies with this trick.
"They have to trust you as
somebody who is kind to them
before they'll go off," he adds.
A respite
The bacon company lent him
Joyce and Daisy for the show.
It got them a short respite. For
their final appointment had
been fixed for last Friday.
This morning they meet their
fate with 360 other little porkers.
"We kept the news from their
fellow artists," said an ITV
official. "It was the most we
could do."
Now it's Daisy's turn and
soon another little piggy
is fast asleep. How Mother
must wish she could do the
same with the baby!

activity: aerial view of the tanker 'British Admiral' in a berth at the Vickers-Armstrongs shipyard in Barrow-in-Furness

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION IN DAILIES
OF FRIDAY 5TH FEBRUARY 1965.

BRITAIN'S TWO-SLIPWAY GIANT ALMOST
READY FOR LAUNCHING BY QUEEN.
ERF. H. 2092 3RD FEBRUARY 1965.
THE LARGEST VESSEL EVER BUILT IN EUROPE, BRITAIN'S
FIRST 100,000 TON TANKER, TO BE NAMED "BRITISH
ADMIRAL" WILL BE LAUNCHED ON MARCH 17TH BY
THE QUEEN.
THE HUGE TANKER IS BEING BUILT FOR BRITISH
PETROLEUM AT THE VICKERS-ARMSTRONGS YARD AT BARROW-IN-FURNESS,
AND IS NOW NEARING COMPLETION. IT IS THE FIRST
OF TWO 100,000 TON DEADWEIGHT TANKERS - THE SECOND
IS UNDER CONSTRUCTION AT THE SWAN HUNTER AND WIGHAM
RICHARDSON YARD ON THE TYNE.
SO GREAT IS THE SIZE OF THE NEW TANKER - IT WILL
BE 917 FT 6 INCHES LONG AND 180 FT IN BREADTH - THAT
TWO SINGLE BERTHS, EACH 100 FT WIDE WERE RE-BUILT
INTO A SINGLE BERTH TO ACCOMMODATE THE VESSEL.
ALL THE MACHINERY WILL BE INSTALLED COMPLETE PRIOR
TO THE LAUNCHING AND IT WILL BE THE GREATEST-EVER
LAUNCHING WEIGHT AT BARROW.
AFTER IT ENTERS THE WATER, ONLY A FEW WEEKS
WILL BE REQUIRED TO PREPARE THE "BRITISH ADMIRAL"
FOR FINAL TRIALS.
PHOTO SHOWS:
A STRIKING AERIAL VIEW OF THE MASSIVE
B.P. TANKER, "BRITISH ADMIRAL" -ACCOMMODATING TWO
BERTHS AT THE BARROW-IN-FURNESS YARD OF VICKERS-
ARMSTRONG - DEPICTING IT'S HUGE LENGTH -917' 6" -
AND BREADTH OF 180FT.

activity: The Queen, Prince Charles, and Princess Anne visiting a sawmill on the Balmoral estate, where Prince Charles is shown how to use a machine.

te.text:
QUEEN 'IN DANGER' AT ROYAL ESTATE SAWMILL
Sept 16th 1958 PAR 66157-5 (UP-J)

QUEEN 'IN DANGER' AT ROYAL ESTATE SAWMILL

This picture, taken during a visit by
members of the Royal Family to the sawmill
on their estate at Balmoral, shows the
QUEEN standing in a position of danger,
according to Mr. Thomas McAndrew, general
secretary of the Amalgamated Society of
Wood-Cutting Machinists, writing in the
Society's monthly magazine today (Tuesday).
Mr. McAndrew writes: 'I am appalled at Her
Majesty being allowed to face such danger.
Some years ago we had a man killed in an
Aberdeen saw mill standing in that identical
position.... The saw is not properly guarded....
I dread to think of the result had a
throw-back occurred....'
An official of the Society explained that
the danger occurred if the saw encountered
a hard knot or a hidden piece of metal in
the wood. If the machine was not properly
guarded a piece of wood might 'speed through
the air like a bullet.'
(In the picture, PRINCE CHARLES is being
shown how to use the machine, while PRINCESS
ANNE covers her ears.)
Sept 16th 1958 PAR 66157-5 (UP-J)

PICTURE FROM LIBRARY - Sept 18th 1957

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
17 SEP 1958
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

LUXURY FLATS FOR LONDON WORKERS.

The drab appearance of certain districts of North Kensington,
may soon give place to colour and beauty if the efforts of
the Kensington Housing Trust are carried to fruition. There
have just been completed two blocks of flats of the modern kind
for the housing of working class families at Silchester Road,
North Kensington. They represent a pioneer effort in this country
following the latest continental practice of angle windows, designed
to admit the maximum of air and sunlight. British materials have been
used throughout. The opening ceremony by H.R.H. Princess Louise
takes place tomorrow. *

activity: Workmen unloading casings that will be sunk to a depth of two miles at Portsdown Hill for oil boring.

te.text:
XIH)               BORING TWO MILES FOR OIL

Hundreds of men are now hard at work on the slopes of
Portsdown Hill, near Portsmouth, preparing for the gig-
antic task of penetrating twice as far beneath the sur-
face of England as ever before. In this peaceful spot
engineers are making ready to drill to a point 10,000
feet - or nearly two miles - under the ground in a
search for oil. The hole is to be drilled with the most
modern of machinery, the work being carried out under
the supervision of expert mining engineers who have been
brought from the oilfields of Persia. Portsdown Hill was
decided on as the site for boring after a careful survey
by geologists.

Photo shows:- Workmen unloading casings that will be
sunk to a depth of two miles at Portsdown Hill.

(Topical Press)     H.                    (10)

SUPPLIED BY
“TOPICAL”
AGENCY LTD.

FLEET ST.,

activity: Refrigerated wagons for the transport of bulk meat nearing completion at the Sheffield works of Cravens Ltd.

te.text:
F195102
Industry - Railways - loco & rolling stock

FROM DEEGLAS FIBRES LTD
ARTRITE RESINS LTD

Highly insulated wagons supplied for the transport of
perishables in East Africa have proved so successful that the
manufacturers - Cravens Ltd., of Sheffield - have received
orders for a further eight vehicles with full mechanical
refrigeration equipment. The bodywork is of glass fibre
reinforced polyester resin supplied by Deeglas Fibres Ltd.,
and Artrite Resins Ltd., of Camberley, Surrey, with a foamed
polyurethane insulating core.

In the hot African climate, where meat is liable to rapid
deterioration, these refrigerated wagons are capable of sustained,
efficient cold-storage in transportation. They are 45' 9" long
and 9' 2" wide, have interior framings of aluminium alloy and are
equipped with carcase hanging hooks.

Moulded of GC4/LU102 Artrite resin and Deeglas A106 mat, their
bodywork cannot corrode, requires little painting and the minimum
of maintenance.

CAPTION: Refrigerated wagons for the transport of bulk meat,
nearing completion at the Sheffield works of Cravens Ltd.
The wagons are constructed of reinforced plastics incorporating
Deeglas glass fibres and Artrite polyester resins, and repeat
orders have been received from East African railways where
similar wagons have proved very successful in service.

Further information from
Press Officer, Victoria 3848
Herga House, Vincent Square, London, SW1
Industry . . . Railways . . . Loco and Rolling Stock construction

te.text:
A pile of gearwheels for
the headstocks or gear-
boxes — used on capstan
and auto-turret lathes. The
girl is Cynthia Buckley,
who was once a clerk
in the firm's offices and
volunteered for the factory

STUDIO N
Name Saidman
Date 
File 67161

Saidman and W. J. Passingham photograph and describe the
MACHINES
THAT MAKE
MACHINES
"THE making of machine tools is the
key industry on which practically
all other industries depend."
The words are those of a man who has
laboured a lifetime to create the biggest
British machine tool workshop in all
Europe. I am standing in his vast work-
shop — acres of throbbing, pulsating
machinery — and remembering that
civilization itself is in reality based on
the production of machine tools. Food,

activity: four prototype houses built for the Sheffield City Council using the 5M system of construction

te.text:
CROWN COPYRIGHT RESERVED. MINISTRY OF HOUSING & LOCAL GOVERNMENT.
Four prototype houses built for the Sheffield City Council by the
Public Works Department under the 5M system of construction devised
by the Research and Development Group of the Ministry of Housing
and Local Government. This system, which marks a new attempt to
bring the advantages of industrialisation into the field of house-
building, has been derived from the 5M CLASP system used at
Stevenage for a group of old people's flatlets. The new system
is called 5M, because as at Stevenage, it is based upon a planning
grid of 1' 8" (5 x the module of 4"). The object has been to
modify the CLASP system, which has been shown to have advantages
in the reduction of site labour and building time, to suit the
performance standards, and the levels of cost, of 2-storey housing.

Ministry of Housing & Local Government.   January, 1963
