activity: Construction of the Orient liner 'ORIANA' at the Vickers Armstrong shipyard, focusing on the aluminum superstructure and bulbous forefoot.

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION WEDNESDAY'S DAILIES... 19TH AUGUST, 1959.

NEW TECHNIQUES IN BRITISH SHIP CONSTRUCTION.
LE. 						19TH AUGUST, 1959.
WORK IS NOW WELL ADVANCED ON THE LARGEST ALL-WELDED ALUMINIUM
SUPERSTRUCTURE YET BUILT INTO A BRITISH SHIP, THE 40,000TON
ORIENT LINER, "ORIANA", AT PRESENT UNDER CONSTRUCTION IN THE
VAST YARDS OF THE FAMOUS BUILDERS, VICKERS ARMSTRONG, BARROW-
IN-FURNESS, SHE IS DUE TO BE LAUNCHED THIS AUTUMN AND WHEN COM-
PLETED WILL TAKE UP SERVICE ON THE AUSTRALIA AND PACIFIC RUN IN
CONJUNCTION WITH THE P & O LINER "CANBERRA", ALSO OF 40,000TONS,
WHICH IS TO BE LAUNCHED A FEW MONTHS AFTER THE "ORIANA".
IT HAS BEEN CLAIMED THAT THERE IS MORE ALUMINIUM BEING USED IN
CONSTRUCTION OF THE ORIANA THAN WAS USED IN THE PRIDE OF AMERICA'S
SHIPPING WORLD, FLAG-SHIP OF THE UNITED STATES LINE, THE
53,000TONNER, "UNITED STATES". THE REASON FOR THIS IS THAT PRE-
VIOUSLY WHERE ALUMINIUM HAS BEEN USED TO ANY GREAT DEGREE, STEEL
STIFFENERS HAVE BEEN ESSENTIAL TO HELP WITH THE INTEGRAL RIGIDITY
REQUIRED IN THE CONSTRUCTION OF A LARGE SHIP OF PRESENT-DAY STAN-
DARDS.
THE ALUMINIUM SUPERSTRUCTURE WEIGHING JUST OVER 1,000TONS, COM-
PRISES FIVE DECKS, TWO BRIDGE DECKS, AND ALL UPPER WORKS. THE
TOTAL AREA OF BULKHEAD AND DECK PLATING OF THIS MATERIAL IS ALMOST
350,000 SQ FT.
ABOUT 90% OF THE SUPERSTRUCTURE XXXXXXXXXXXXXX HAS BEEN ASSEMBL
IN A PREFABRICATED FORM IN SHOPS ENTIRELY INDEPENDENT OF THE MAIN
YARDS.
THE COST OF THIS GIANT NEW SHIP, THE LARGEST PASSNGER VESSEL TO
BE CONSTRUCTED IN THIS COUNTRY SINCE THE ALL-TIME RECORD BREAKER,
"QUEEN ELIZABETH", 83,673TONS, IS £12 1/2M.
A MOST INTERESTING FEATURE OF THIS BEATIFUL NEW SHIP IS THE BULBOU
FOREFOOT, THIS, IT APPEARS, ENABLES THE SHIP TO TRAVEL AT A VERY
MUCH HIGHER SPEED WITHOUT THE ADDED EXPENSE OF EXTRA POWER. A
FEATURE WHICH WILL NO DOUBT BE INCORPORATED IN MANY FUTURE BRITISH
SHIPS.
THIS PICTURE, TAKEN RECENTLY IN THE YARDS OF VICKERS ARMSTRONG,
SHOWS

A VIEW OF THE BOWS OF THE ORIANA SHOWING THE SUPERSTRUCTURE OF AL-
UMINIUM RISING FROM THE STEEL HULL, AT THE FOREFOOT CAN BE SEEN THE
BULBOUS DEVICE, REPUTED TO GIVE THE SHIP A REVOLUTIONARY TURN OF
SPEED.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
19 AUG 1959
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

[Reversed stamp] STILL MORE ON
ORIANA SHIP

activity: four-year-old Sylvia and her mother Mrs. Hilda Shoobridge walking along a narrow ledge outside barricaded rooms at a London County Council rest centre during a squatters' siege

te.text:
F192/D3/HOUSING POSTWAR/POST WAR DIFFICULTIES/SQUATTERS/FLATS SEIZED 
 BY HOMELESS - MELCOMBE REGIS COURT MARYLEBONE ETC.

PLEASE RETURN TO 
 'DAILY HERALD' ART LIBRARY 
 AT THE LATEST BY . . . . . 
 AND DATE REQUIRED . . . . . 
 BY WHOM . . . . .

REST CENTRE SQUATTERS ARE TO GO TO PRISON..... 
 
 London:  The three families, who, for a fortnight 
 have barricaded themselves in two rooms on the 
 fourth floor of the London County Council rest 
 centre in Queen's Gardens, Paddington, London, 
 are to go to prison. 
 This new move came as the result of an application 
 by the London County Council, and the order, 
 committing them to prison, came from Mr. Justice 
 Devlin. 
 The siege started because the three 
 families - Mr. and Mrs. George Field, Mr. and 
 Mrs. Patrick Timoney, and Mr. and Mrs. James 
 Shoobridge - refused to go to a London County 
 Council Institution, where the wives and their 
 children would be separated from their menfolk. 
 The three families were firm in their resolution 
 that they would rather go to prison than return 
 to an institution. 
 PHOTO SHOWS: Sixty feet above a milk-roundsman 
 in the road below, four-year-old Sylvia, with 
 her mother Mrs. Hilda Shoobridge, walk along the 
 narrow ledge which joins the two barricaded rooms 
 in which the three families have lived in a state 
 of siege for the last fortnight. 
 September 14th, 1949. PN-h.

COPYRIGHT. 
 PLANET NEWS LTD 
 3, JOHNSON'S COURT, 
 LONDON, E.C. 4. 
 'PHONE: CENT. 3671 & 3672/3.

activity: prototype houses built for the Sheffield City Council by the Public Works Department under the 5M system of construction

te.text:
CROWN COPYRIGHT RESERVED.  MINISTRY OF HOUSING & LOCAL GOVERNMENT.
Four prototype houses built for the Sheffield City Council by the
Public Works Department under the 5M system of construction devised
by the Research and Development Group of the Ministry of Housing
and Local Government.   This system, which marks a new attempt to
bring the advantages of industrialisation into the field of house-
building, has been derived from the 5M CLASP system used at
Stevenage for a group of old people's flatlets.   The new system
is called 5M, because as at Stevenage, it is based upon a planning
grid of 1' 8" (5 x the module of 4").   The object has been to
modify the CLASP system, which has been shown to have advantages in
the reduction of site labour and building time, to suit the
performance standards, and the levels of cost, of 2-storey housing.
                                           January, 1963
Ministry of Housing & Local Government.

These terrace houses have been built in Sheffield by
the Ministry of Housing to illustrate one method of
industrialised building considered particularly suitable for
local authority housing. A skeleton of wood and steel
tubing is built on a sheet of concrete; wall sections are
hung from the flat roof. With this method a kit of parts
is not bought from one particular manufacturer—instead
various firms are invited to tender for different sections.
Minimum economic order would be 500 houses.

te.text: F194   DI   INDUSTRY   FISHING   MARKETS & PORTS

HERRING BY THE MILLION - VAST CATCHES
CAUSE 'NO MORE' ORDER.

The entire East Anglian herring fleet
of 375 boats has been ordered by the
Herring Industry Board to remain in port
at Lowestoft and Great Yarmouth following
the landing of 40,000,000 herring in
four days - catches were five times those
of last year.

activity: a liqueur wine called Korean Ginseng containing the root of the Ginseng plant

te.text:
HAVE a care, you cold-blooded
English lovers! Those wily
oriental gentlemen are ready with
an elixir to make you into modern
Don Juans.
This powerful potion can, according
to ancient legend, turn a Tremulous
Tom or Hesitant Harry into a great
lover.
At first glance it looks like an ordinary
bottle of wine. But be not deceived. Look
closer. Inside the bottle is
something which looks like a
piece of root.
It is a piece of root. It is
the root of the Ginseng
plant which the Chinese
believe has aphrodisiac
qualities.
Already this liqueur wine
called Korean Ginseng, is
on the list of one famous
British wine merchant. It is
described as a “well-known
aphrodisiac.”
None left
With that description it is
little wonder that, when I
tried to buy a bottle this
week, from Matthews Vint-
ners, Ltd., London — the
importers—they didn’t even
have one left in their cellars.
In just two months they
have sold 240 bottles of this
hitherto unknown drink.
Managing director Mr.
Henry Simon, a fourth gene-
ration wine merchant, told
me:
“It’s amazing. I’ve never
known anything quite like
it. For five years we had
these bottles of Ginseng
lying untouched in our
cellars.
“Then two months ago the
word got around about it
and whoosh! it has all
gone.
“We’ve even had to have
some flown in specially by
air, the demand has been so
great.”
And what of its reputed
properties. Has Mr. Simon’s
company put it to the
test? . . .
“Not likely,” he told me.
“If it did work we’d prob-
ably get sued.”

te.text:
THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

191941 QUI
NURSE MAIDS AT A NIPPER NURSERY.

Southampton, Eng: Wanted for somebody's lobster
tea, these nippy nippers from a unique nursery at
Warsash, near here, are gathered by Jack Cross (left)
and Richard "Chalky" White.
The nursery is a half-acre pond that was taken over
derelict by the Crab and Lobster Co. (Warsash),
and with a converted Manx drifter fitted with
storage tanks to carry the shell-fish, cargoes are
collected from coastal districts of the British
Isles and brought to the pond to be fed and "nursed"
until wanted.
The crustacea are kept happy, healthy and clean by
frequent changes of their water from the tide.
They are fed on mussels, herrings and other types
of coarse fish.
Population of the pond runs into thousands, many
of which are destined for export - to be flown by
plane to Belgium, Holland and Switzerland.
29th November, 1949 PN-d.

PLANET NEWS LTD
3, JOHNSON'S COURT,
LONDON, E.C. 4.

activity: lifting operation of a home-made cabin cruiser named Patience

te.text:
CABIN CRUISER COMPLETED IN GARDEN - 15 YEARS LATER     D/MAE

A luxuriously fitted 30-ft. cabin cruiser has just been 
completed in the garden workshop of Mr. G.F. Tarr, retired 
Cheltenham businessman, without professional help.  The 
work was begun in 1937, but, owing to wartime delays, it 
has only just been finished.  Since the job was started, 
hundreds of houses have been built around Mr. Tarr's, and 
the problem of getting the boat out for launching on the 
River Avon at Tewkesbury was solved by the co-operation 
of neighbours who removed garden fences to permit a lorry 
and trailer to come in.  The cruiser, which has an 8 ft, 
6 inch beam and is powered by a 30 h.p. Scripps engine was 
built by following a design published in the New York 
magazine, "Motor Boating".

PHOTO SHOWS:  Mr. G.F. Tarr (with stick) watches the 
lifting operation of his home-made cabin cruiser, aptly 
named Patience.
FOX PHOTOS      470785                 SEPT. 2 ND 1952

RCD.
DAILY HERALD
PROPERTY OF

te.text:
THE Queen arrives at the
London Palladium for
last night's Royal Variety
Show.
With her is impresario
Bernard Delfont, the man
who asked satirists Peter
Cook and Dudley Moore to
cut some of their jokes about
the Queen.
But the Queen and Prince
Philip were highly amused
as the stars of BBC's 'Not
Only But Also' poked fun at
royal life, 'right in the West
End and so handy for the
shops.'
They enjoyed it so much
that Cook and Moore
emerged from the cast of
stars as the undisputed
'Court Jesters' of the
night.
Laughter
The mink and bow-tie
audience who raised £40,000
for show business charity,
laughed with the Queen
right from the start, when
Max Bygraves - "second spot
in a one-night stand leading
the community singing" -
explained how Mr. Delfont
allegedly invited him to
appear.
Said Max: "He told me.
'All you have to do is to
crack a few jokes about Jean
Shrimpton, mention the
schools in Australia, say a
few words about Rhodesia -
and you're bound to get an
MBE.'"
The Queen and Mr. Delfont at the London Palladium last night.

activity: fallen masonry from terraced houses in Blenheim Crescent being surveyed after a collapse

te.text:
WARNER.
D.H.
26.7.56
COPING OF EIGHT HOUSES IN BLENHEIM CRESCENT,
NOTTING HILL, W. FELL TO THE GROUND.
NO ONE WAS HURT.

HERALD REPORTER
ARMY veteran Bill Beck, five times blown up, twice
wounded, escaped death again yesterday—because
he watched the Test on T V.
Every day it is Bill's habit to sit on the front steps of his
house in Blenheim-crescent,
Notting Hill, between 1 and
2 p.m. "Just to watch the
world go by," he says.
But yesterday he broke that
habit to look-in at the match.
And at 1.20 p.m., about 14 tons
of masonry crashed from the
roofs of eight of Blenheim-
crescent's terraced houses. Bill's
was among them.
Said 61-year-old Bill, survey-
ing the rubble on his front
steps later: "That Test match
saved my life — otherwise I
would have been sitting in my
normal place and caught that
packet.
'Like a bomb'
"It was just like a bomb going
off," he added. "The whole
street was covered in dust."
But not one person in Blen-
heim-crescent was injured.
Fire chiefs thought that the
warm spell had made the bricks
expand and crumble in the
coping which overhung the 97-
year-old houses.
Families were evacuated, but
three hours later they were
allowed to go back, and warned
only to use the back rooms.
Gas and electricity were cut
off as a precaution, but nobody
accepted the LCC's offer of
alternative accommodation for
the night.

activity: putting up a barricade to a thirteen roomed house in Havering to prevent eviction by bailiffs

te.text:
HAVERING, Essex:      MR FREDERICK BRUCE (left, background)
and thirteen year old ALBERT ALLEN are pictured putting
up a barricade to their rambling, thirteen roomed house
in the picturesque village of Havering near Romford,
Essex. Bruce and Allen are members of the three families,
who live in house, where they expect bailiffs with orders
to evict them.
			The glass-roofed porch at the back was
jammed with oil drums, branches of trees and iron bars.
			A spokesman for the house agents said.
"These people are squatters and have never paid any rent.
With the consent of the owner, we permitted Mrs Allen to
move into the empty house more than a year ago because she
and her five children - aged six to seventeen - were home-
less and had nowhere to sleep. But we made it clear that
she could not become a tenant, and could only stay a few days.
She has let the other families in. We think we have been
extremely lenient".
				2nd October, 1963-pn-on

te.text:
CALLED BACK TO "HEAD THE GUARDS"        DG/A4

Seventy five year old MR HARRY PATSTON of Southgate
N. 14, has been called back to duty for the benefit of
the entire Brigade of Guards. He is the only man 
in the world who knows the secret of the wicker frames
which go to form the Guards bearskins and he has
been called out of retirement by his old firm
(G. W. Scott and Sons) to pass on his skill 
so that a new contract for bearskins can be filled
He retired last year after 56 years with Scotts who
have done this work since the Crimea
PHOTO SHOWS: "Busby-builder" HARRY PATSTON shows his
pupil Mrs K. Grinham, how to make wicker frames
for the Brigade of Guards' bearskins. The frames 
help to make the bearskins as light and cool as 
possible. Mr Patston makes them at the rate of 12 
a day.
FOX PHOTOS   Mar 12 1951

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
RCD. 13 MAR 1951
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

activity: Miss Ivy Hodge giving evidence at the inquiry into the collapse of the Ronan Point flats in Canning Town.

te.text: Housing - Accidents - Canning Town Flat Disaster

Pictures: Eric Weller & Ken Giller
Stories: David Pringle
48 Station Road, Walthamstow, London, E.17   Phone 01-520 5380   Radio Link Reg 2552 (Blue 1-4-4)

The day the flats collapsed.   June 18 1968
(Picture story : Pringle/Photocall).

MISS IVY HODGE, grey haired and marked
by the memory of Ronan Point flats disaster, was helped
into a packed Newham Town Hall yesterday (Tuesday)
to re-live those moments of horror.
"I went to bed at 10.45 - and read a little,"
said the 55-year-old woman, released especially from
Poplar Hospital to give evidence at the inquiry.
"At 2.25 I was awake and I went into the
kitchen to fill the kettle for a cup of tea ... I
cant remember any more. There was a flash across the
ceiling and then the ceiling began to flake."
The inquiry was hushed as Miss Hodge
who lived in a 19th floor flat at Ronan Point - and
is still alive - chose her words. Asked if she
smelt gas she replied : "I didn't smell nay gas
and I have a good sence of smell."
She sobbed at the end of giving evidence
and was helped back to hospital by two friends.
She is under treatment for burns to her
face arms and legs.
---ends..

Pictures show Miss Hodge giving evidence -
close-up and overall shot.

te.text:
PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
DEC 1955
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

Herald Reporter
SMOG that blacked - out
London yesterday caught
the Queen and the Duke of
Edinburgh on the road in
the Duke's open sports car.
It was the first time the
Duke had driven in smog and
at times his car went at walk-
ing pace on the drive from
Sandringham to Buckingham
Palace.
The sun was shining as the
Queen and the Duke left Sand-
ringham at 2 p.m. but by the
time they reached Stevenage,
Herts. the Duke had to get out
and put up the hood.
With the Queen huddled be-
side him he drove behind a
police escort car through smog
that cut visibility down to 15
yards in places and began
freezing on his windscreen.
It was after five when the
Duke, red-eyed and tense-
faced, swung through the
Palace gates at the end of his
100-mile drive.
Please release
for wire

QUEEN RETURNS FROM SANDRINGHAM

THE QUEEN IS DRIVEN INTO THE GATES OF
BUCKINGHAM PALACE THIS EVENING NOV.30
BY THE DUKE OF EDINBURGH.
THEY TRAVELLED FROM SANDRINGHAM IN THE
DUKE'S LAGONDA SPORTS CAR.
301155H.
RIS.E.21527.
ASSOCIATED PRESS PHOTO FROM LONDON.

te.text:
LONDON SKYSCRAPERS AROUSE CONTROVERSY,   MJH/HT.

Considerable controversy has been aroused by the
£5-million Roehampton Development scheme, under which
15 blocks of L.C.C. flats in "skyscrapers" 11 storeys
high (nearly 100 feet) are being built on 100 acres
skirting Richmond Park, Putney Heath and Wimbledon
Common. Many people particularly local residents, complain
that these towering structures completely ruin what was
once a charming rural district, disfiguring the landscape
and reducing the market value of property in the area.
Undoubtedly this skyscraper experiment does alter the whole
character of the neighbourhood, but on the other hand,
the L.C.C. state that in their efforts to solve the housing
problem, they must build somewhere and sites are
difficult to find. However, they will soon have the
opportunity of pleasing both sides for the Government
recently announced a huge slum clearance drive for the centre
of London, where skyscraper flats could not possibly cause
complaint.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS:  A view of one of the controversial
blocks of flats, now under construction, as seen from
Alton Road, Roehampton.

activity: The gold service which is going on a tour of 25 cities in the U.S.A. and Canada, the heavy gold tray can be clearly seen with its exquisite chasing

te.text:
£9,000 GOLD SERVICE OFF TO NORTH AMERICA
BRITISH MASTERPIECE OF MODERN CRAFTSMANSHIP   DG/own

Flying to North America under armed escort
on Thursday (August 17th) is one of the most
valuable consignments of gold ever to leave this
country. While the amount involved (400 ounces)
is not unprecedented, the form it is taking - that
of an 18 carat gold seven piece TEA AND COFFEE
SERVICE considered to be a masterpiece of
modern craftsmanship
The service which is insured for £9,000 will have
an armed police escort from the BIRMINGHA City
POLICE on its journey from the workshops of the
makers (Adie Brothers Birmingham) to London
Airport. Heaviest piece of the service is the tray
- weighing 220 ounces - probably the largest piece of
18ct gold assayed at the Birmingham Assay Office
since its opening.

PHOTO SHOWS: The gold service which is going
on a tour of 25 cities in the U.S.A. and Canada,
the heavy gold tray can be clearly seen with its
exquisite chasing

FOX PHOTOS Aug 15th 1950

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
RCD. 16 AUG 1950
PLEASE
TO
ART LIBRARY

TURNING GOLD INTO BOOKS.

In spite of thousands of years of scientific research
a machine has not yet been invented to beat gold, with
the delicate manipulation which is essential to success,
and so the job is carried on by hand, in almost the
same way as it was carried on in the time of Queen
Cleopatra, varying only in the fact that the bronze
hammer used by the ancients has been replaced by a steel
one, and that machinery forms a small part of the
early stages of the work.
O.P.S.        A young lady at work trimming the edges from
the finished leaf, after it had been beaten to
about four millionth of an inch in thickness.

British Petroleum's first drilling barge for North Sea
operations is to begin operating about mid-May this year.

activity: Sacks of corn are hoisted to the top of a water-driven flour mill by pulleys.

te.text:
800-YEAR OLD FLOUR MILL STILL DRIVEN BY WATER.  E.M./MABERS.

The village of Winchcombe, Glos., possesses what is believed
to be the only working water driven mill in the country.  It
has been in constant use for grinding locally grown corn
since it was built by some Monks in 1158.  The actual water
wheel was renewed nearly a hundred years ago but the original
millstones and other working parts are still in use.  The
methods at the Winchcombe mill needed no change when wholemeal
flour was introduced, for it has always produced this type of
flour.

Photo shows:-   Sacks of corn are hoisted to the top of the
mill by pulleys driven from the water wheel.  Here the corn
is tipped into hoppers from which it falls into the mills on
the next floor.
FOX.  7th April, 1942.                   272159.

MEN in neat business suits pressed buttons and flicked switches and £150,000-worth of gleaming machinery hummed into rotary action.
Huffing and puffing, sucking and blowing, the armoury of space-age equipment at the First International Cleaning Maintenance Exhibition set about impressing clusters of executives in London's Seymour Hall.
'Note the highly-developed oscillating action,' murmured the salesman. 'See how the rotary sand, scrub and polish, wet or dry.'
Mesmerised by the sheer mechanical inventiveness on glance for a second at the most efficient, effective cleaning machine of them all— 65-year-old Mrs. Minnie Dowling. She was scrubbing her way across the hall on hands and knees.
Her equipment—plastic bucket, brush, dishpan, cloth, brown soap and warm water.
Using a highly-developed form of traditional elbow power, Mrs. Dowling, from Chiswick, West London, put the machinery to shame by cleaning every exhibition stand single-handed.
But at only 6s. 3d. an hour, wearing a cotton shirt, with sleeves rolled up at 6 a.m., she, most of those posh, prestige machines had even before most of those posh, prestige machines had even begun their eye-appeal packaging.
'I wouldn't give you much for any of that lot, dear,' said Mrs. Dowling, flicking her duster at a multi-accessory power-mop. 'They won't get into corners or lift the muck like I can.'
In 15 years as a cleaner of exhibition halls, Mrs. Dowling has observed only one change in the traditional charlady's tools—the scrubbing brush has gone.
'We use the back of a broom and a lump of wool now,' she said. 'It gets the grime up a treat, without too much bending.'
Mrs. Dowling's employers, Curzon Window Cleaning Services Ltd., join her in the claim that Mrs. Mops will never die.
'The kind of small-scale cleaning we do could never justify investment in machines each worth £1,000,' a spokesman said.
DIPLOMA
Which isn't the view of the sponsors of the three-day exhibition, the British Institute of Cleaning Science.
They believe so firmly that domestic cleaning and industrial building maintenance is becoming a highly-skilled profession that they have just sponsored the first City and Guilds Diploma examination in Cleaning Science.
Eight colleges throughout the country offer two-year cleaning and maintenance courses for caretakers, hospital, office and industrial domestics.
Fifty of the first batch of 55 candidates passed the exam this summer and can now consider themselves 'cleaning technologists.'
For any Mrs. Mops who fancy turning to the Institute's new career structure, here is a question from this year's diploma examination paper:
● Adding a detergent to water, rather than the reverse:
(a) maximises foam?
(b) does not affect amount of foam?
(c) minimises foam?
(d) destroys foam completely?
As Mrs. Dowling would have it: 'Spit and polish is the only science I need to know.'

THE VILLAGE THAT LAUGHS AT DEPRESSION.
ALL THE WORLD IS ASKING FOR KILVE'S
HAND WOVEN GARMENTS.

Prosperity is returning with a rush
to the little village of Kilve in
the Quantock Hills, near Bridgwater.

coast of the Bristol Channel, spinning
and weaving are still carried out just
as they were hundreds of years ago.

Italy, France and other countries
has been developed by the craftsmen
of Kilve, who make coats, skirts,
rugs, scarves and other garments in a
way which cannot be imitated anywhere
in the world.
With the growth of the tourist traffic
in Britain Kilve has been provided with
a valuable new outlet, and the
Pardlestone Weavers, as the craftsmen
are known, are staging a great
'come-back'.

10 NOV 1949   QUI
REMOVING THE Q.M.'s CONCRETE PATCH.

Southampton, Eng: Men prepare to remove the concrete
patch 'poured' into the Queen Mary after the vessel
had damaged her hull when running aground in
Cherbourg Harbour during a gale in January of this
year.

plugging the leak broken up by pneumatic drills.

the ship had 50-tons of concrete put in, and

te.text:
MARBLE MASON'S SKILL FOR
WESTMINSTER CATHEDRAL.         MJH/HT.

The Million Crown Fund to defray the cost
of the interior decorative scheme for Westminster
Cathedral has progressed so well that work on
this project, which will take ten years to complete,
is already in hand.    Skilled craftsmen at a Putney
marble masons (Fennings Ltd) are now working on the
carvings for the 12 great bays - each of which will
cost £8,000 - which form part of the project.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS:   MR. VICTOR DALESSENDRO of Putney
seen at work at the Marble Masons carving one of the
marble capitals for the top of a pillar, part of
the decorative scheme for the interior of Westminster
Cathedral.   Mr. Dalessandro has been a marble mason
for over 30 years and it takes him about 6 weeks to
make one of these capitals.

activity: construction of a new tube tunnel for the Bakerloo Line 100 feet below ground at Baker Street

te.text:
SAYERS.  11.4.38.
London Transport Tube Improvements.
The construction of a new tube from Baker
Street to Finchley Road is now in progress
and is likely to be completed by next summer.
O.P.S.
100 feet below ground at Baker Street looking
from the new tunnel on the Bakerloo Line
running south from Watford to Lambeth North.
On the right is seen the existing small
tunnel sheared up by huge planks which allows
the Bakerloo Line to run through these
immense workings, at the junction now called
step plate. This is the biggest tunnel in the
whole of London Passenger Transport Board
underground undertakings.

activity: Advertising campaign 'Breakfast Fortnight' by the Egg Marketing Board, featuring women dressed as 'Egg Chicks' visiting houses in Islington, London.

te.text:
SUN
PROPERTY
19 APR 1966
Please return to
ART Library

Story: PETER HULME

IT was the day the advertising man really
went to work on the Egg.
The day the classless, sex-
less Egg Chicks went into
action to convince Mr. and
Mrs. Britain of the virtues
of egg-eating at breakfast.

Their aim: to boost the
country's egg consumption, the
third highest in the world, by
one egg per person each week.

Their ammunition: premium
bonds as rewards for the egg-
lovers—and half-dozen boxes
of eggs to tempt the cereal-
crunching and anti-breakfast
types.

Plastic

Scene of the first onslaught
by the Chicks was Islington,
London, at 7 am.

Watching from the shadow
of a block of council flats was
34-year-old Michael Talbot-
Ponsonby, the man—or should
it be the egg-head? —behind
the Egg Chicks.

“I go to work on a bike,”
shouted a passing postman as
19-year-old dancer Val Hard-
ing flitted by in orange tights,
plastic feet, and fluffy yellow
nylon bird-suit complete with
tail and felt beak.

Disguise

Old Etonian Talbot-Ponson-
by sighed at the implication in
the postman’s crack. “What
satisfaction to know one’s
slogans have so quickly
become an accepted part of
the vocabulary,” drawled the
architect of “Join the Tea
Set,” and veteran of the
“Drinka Pinta” campaign.

Egg Chick Leila Hart
knocked at a door. “Is that
the gas man?” a voice called
out.

“No, it’s an Egg Chick,
madam,” replied Leila, a music
student in disguise.

After an eternity of door un-
bolting, 78-year-old Mrs. Jane
Grover peered cautiously at the
birdwoman on her doorstep.
“Yes, I always have an egg for
breakfast,” she said. And was
rewarded with a £1 Premium
Bond.

And the Egg Chick crossed
the road. To go to work on the
other side.

Groups

Eighty-four Chicks will be
calling at one house in a
thousand throughout the coun-
try between seven and nine in
the morning during the next
two weeks. “Breakfast Fort-
night,” the Egg Marketing
Board are calling it.

The Chicks work in groups
of three. Each group has a
chaperon, or “momma chick,”
who drives them around in a
“chick car” and arranges
hotel accommodation. Hotel
board and bird-suits are free.

Each Chick is expected to
make calls at 17 homes a day
—18 on Saturdays—during the
breakfast period.

Their pay? About £15 a
week.

Pleasant

The Chicks are supposed to
be classless and sexless. Said
an advertising man connected
with the campaign:

“We have purposely designed
their costumes to make them
pleasant neuters. Housewives
in curlers would be antagonised
if they opened the door to a
too glamorous Chick.”

But when the morning’s
campaigning was over, the
Chicks looked delectable as
they sat down to their own
breakfast.

They had eggs, of course.
Scrambled for Leila, boiled for
Val and fried for a third Chick,
Doris.

And they looked disapprov-
ingly at a man savouring
kippers.

We in Britain have more
ancient buildings to be
sentimental about than the
Americans, but our hysteri-
cal road conditions prevent
us from keeping historical
buildings intact in this
way.
"Streets in the United
States are fantastically
wide," said a heavy haulage
expert at Pickfords.
"Ours are generally so
narrow and cluttered by
overhead wires that it
wouldn't be possible to
drive a house through
them."
The upper storeys of a 16th-
century house were moved last
year to be built into a new
chain store on the same Here-
ford site. But the cost was
£6,000.
A Cambridgeshire woman
had her home dismantled brick
by brick to be rebuilt on an-
other site rather than have it
bulldozed. This cost £8,000.
The American way—but don't try doing this on the M 1

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION THURSDAY'S EVENINGS, MARCH 17, 1949.
A NEW TUNNEL UNDER THE THAMES.
17.3.49.
A new tunnel, driven under the river Thames, from Battersea
Power Station to Chelsea, will carry cables between the power
station and a new sub-station in north-west London. The
2,500ft tunnel - one of the most remarkable engineering feats
in London - takes two 500-ft-radius bends to miss the piers
of the Victoria Railway Bridge, but in spite of this it was
only 3/8-inch out when it connected with the pit dug at the
Chelsea end. Continuous shifts working day and night since
last September have averaged 60 feet per week, and pressurised
air had to be used to keep the engineers going. At one point
the tunnel air pressure of 10 lb per square inch had to be
increased to 28lb to stop the water from bursting through.
The internal diameter of the tunnel is eight feet, and it is
being lined with 1,900 tons of cast iron lining. It is 76
feet below ground level on the south bank, and is 16 feet
under the river bed at the highest point.
The picture shows :- a scene in the 10-ft diameter joint bay

activity: the latest design in stair carpet

te.text:
BRITISH CARPETS TO COVER THE WORLD

Britain's carpet industry is to aim at an export target of 40%
as against 27%, in the new drive to close the gap between imports
and exports.
The accompanying photographs were taken at the Kidderminster
factories of Carpet Trades Limited, the extent of whose trade can be
judged by the fact that it has warehouses and agents in Australia,
New Zealand, USA, Canada, South America, Central America,
South Africa, Scandinavia, Holland, Switzerland, Egypt, Kenya, Uganda,
Zanzibar, Belgian Congo, West Indies, Iceland and Malta.
The designers have to bear in mind the different types of design
which are popular in each country. For instance, the preference in
Australia and New Zealand is for floral patterns and very bright
colours, whilst at the other extreme the Scandinavian market calls
for subdued tones and more severe styles.
Carpet Trades Limited comprises five factories manufacturing
felts and woollen and worsted yarns as well as all types of machine-
made carpet. During the war they turned over to the production of
small-arms ammunition and other items apart from adapting their
textile plants to the manufacture of webbing, duck, blankets, felt
for rubber substitution, etc.
3,000 workpeople - as against 5,000 pre-war - are producing
thousands of yards of carpet alone per week. The picture shows:

11. The latest design in stair carpet. It is part of
an Australian order.

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED

activity: the scene of the old gold mine workings at Milehopeburn

te.text:
2389)    THE LOST GOLD MINE OF YARROW FOUND.

The Ancient workers closed down their Gold mine and
thoroughly camouflaged the workings until every
particle of Quartz was hidden.
Huge stones were erected to mark the place and a
chart would probably be made. Centuries have
passed and now it has been re-discovered by Mr.
John Nicol of Glen Cafe, St. Marys Loch, Yarrow.
In 1933 an article by a German about mining appeared
in a Canadian paper remarking about the Lost Gold
mine of Yarrow. Was this mine worked by foreigners in
long ages past and information handed down through
the generations.
The Gold is both Alluvial and native(ie,in the Sand
of the streams as well as in Reefs)
Back tracking was first noticed in the HENDERLAND
BURN(Backtracking for alluvial mining) as well as the
COM SIKE but particularly in the MILEHOPEBURN where
extensive sluicing had been carried out at two
distinct periods. The Gold is not free in the Rock
area,it is combined with other Reef Ores including
Manganese Copper, Gold and Silver.
Preliminary samples drawn from decomposed back of
Reef Assays showed 2.4 Dwts of Gold per ton of 2240
lbs or 58 grains to the Ton as well as 0.36 ozs of
silver and also included Manganese and Copper.
St. Mary's Loch is a very well known and beautiful
loch and a great many visitors are to be found there
in peace time. The situation is between Selkirk and
Moffat. It is in Selkirkshire and 18 miles from
Selkirk


Photo shows: Milehopeburn, the scene of the old
workings.

20/3/44   Topical Press    (Y.15438)

FILE. INDUSTRY. METALS. GOLD
XR. SELKIRKSHIRE. V

A ROYAL TASK FOR THE VILLAGE BLACKSMITH.	MJH/MAE.

In his tiny forge in the Oxfordshire village of Kingham,
the village 'smith Mr. J. Rathbone, assisted by his two sons,
is busy making a pair of hand-made ornamental wrought
iron gates for the Royal Enclosure at Ascot. These gates, which
weigh about 1 1/2 tons will be fitted early in the new year. Apart
from the usual agricultural work of the village 'smith, Mr. Rathbone
is renowned for his wrought iron craftsmanship and has won First
Prize with his work on two occasions at the Royal Show.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: A close-up of MR. J. RATHBONE, village
blacksmith at Kingham (Oxon), measuring up the partly-completed
wrought iron gate, which he and his two sons are making for the

activity: Mrs. Mary Barker gold-lining a teapot from an 'Appledore' tea service at the Wedgwood factory in Barlaston.

te.text:
WEDGWOOD TEA SERVICE TO BE PRESENTED
TO THE QUEEN.     MJH/RS.

Expert workers at the famous factory of Josiah Wedgwood
& Sons, Ltd. at Barlaston Park, near Stoke-on-Trent, are
now busily working on a bone china tea service which will
be presented to H.M. The Queen when she visits the factory
on November 2nd. The pattern of the Royal tea service
which will be for 12 people, will be one known as "Appledore"
designed in the Wedgwood studios in 1936 and now in current
production and available to housewives all over the country.
It will be decorated with a laurel border, enamelled in
turquoise on an ivory band and an early-Victorian centrepiece
will take the form of a fruit basket, also hand-enamelled.
Her Majesty has requested that her tea service should contain
some specially large cups.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: MRS. MARY BARKER of Newcastle-under-Lyme,
seen at work in the Wedgwood factory gold-lining a teapot
from an "Appledore" tea service, similar to the one which will
be presented to H.M. The Queen.

activity: a large pictorial graph showing the progress of post-war rehousing by Paddington Council, superimposed on a background image of a large house

te.text:
V.44077

HOUSING PROGRESS: LETTING THE PEOPLE KNOW.

In an effort to show the people what ha been done i!
in regard to rehousing, Paddington Council has
produced what is thought to be the first feature
of its kind in any Borough.
    It takes the form of a large multi-coloured
pictorial graph, superimposed on the background of
a large house similar in type to the many that have
figured in the Council's house conversion plan.
    On the extreme left is shown a running total
column marked in units of 100 with a large red
arrow indicating the number of families housed.
On the extreme right is a "monthly output" column
showing the number of families housed each month.
On the graph itself a bold red line indicates the
"climb" from 467 in December 1945, to 1,238 in
January 1947.

File - Housing Post War Figures
- London Paddington.

te.text:
112-TON TURBINE GOES ABOARD THE WORLD'S GREATEST
LINER - THOUSANDS OF TONS OF MACHINERY INSTALLED
IN "QUEEN MARY."

The thousands of tons of machinery necessary to
drive the world's greatest liner, the "Queen Mary",
is being installed at Clydebank, Scotland.
Although rapid progress has been made since the
launch last September, it has mainly been in
connection with the machinery and auxiliary
equipment. This was necessary because until the
enormous components, some of them weighing as much
as 200 tons, had been hoisted on board, the work of
completing the plating of the decks could not proceed.
PHOTO SHOWS: One of the colossal turbines, weighing
112 tons, going aboard the "Queen Mary".
AND March 10th 1935 PN.r.

COPYRIGHT
PLANET NEWS LTD
3, JOHNSON'S COURT,
LONDON E.C.4

LAST "TROOPING" FOR THE 3RD BATTALION
TRV/ODS/MRT.  13.6.59.

TROOP THE COLOUR ON HORSE GUARDS' PARADE BEFORE HER MAJESTY THE

activity: a 10-ton 'GD' road roller being packed ready for export at the Aveling-Barford works in Grantham

te.text:
BRITAIN'S ROLLERS MAKE THE ROADS OF THE WORLD.
                              July 1946
Britain has long been famous in the production of road
rollers and other types of road construction machinery,
and the "Invista" horse of the products of the Messrs
Aveling-Barford of Grantham is to be seen in even the
most out of the way spots of the globe. The latest order
received by this firm is for a million pounds-worth of
road rollers destined for use in all parts of India.
Besides this huge order, they have others in hand worth
threefold for the supply of machinery to all parts -
from Iceland in the far north to New Zealand in the south,
and only the lack of labour and further supplies of raw
materials prevents the acceptance of additional contracts.
These contrasts have not been obtained by sitting at home -
representatives have travelled the world and the result of
their missions is seen today in the increased activity in
the Grantham works, illustrated by the accompanying photos.

xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx.

te.text:
MAN-MADE FOG USED TO BEAT INSECT PESTS.
21.5.47.
A demonstration was held today of
the Todd Insecticidal Fog Applicator, known
as "Tifa", at Thruxton Copse, near Andover.
Tifa is a one-man controlled machine and is
designed to produce a fog of insecticide,
fungicide or hormone. The substance to be
applied is mechanically atomised and introduced
into the atmosphere as a true fog in which the
chemical agent is uniformly distributed, and
provides an entirely new method of applying
insecticides to pests in buildings and open
spaces.
KEYSTONE PHOTO SHOWS. The machine in
operation during the demonstration
today, watched by a party of scientists.

te.text:
“Nice Smiles and Natural Beauty”
have won for each of these twelve girls the title of “Queen of
Loveliness.” They were among 70 girls who, at a London hotel
yesterday, competed for the honour of reigning over an industry
at Woman’s Fair, opening at Olympia on November 2. Ten
judges, including Mr. C. B. Cochran and Miss Frances Day,
selected the twelve you see above for their “nice smiles, quiet
voices, candid eyes and natural beauty,” as Mr. Cochran said.
On the right are the names of the girls and the industries over
which they will reign.

1 RAYON QUEEN:—Miss Renee
Morris, of Flint, North Wales.
2 HAIRDRESSING QUEEN:—
Miss Hylda Wordsworth, of
Leigh-on-Sea.
3 CORSETRY QUEEN: — Miss
Margaret Rutter, of London.
4 MILLINERY QUEEN: — Miss
Ilse Belding, of Luton.
5 PERFUMERY AND COS-
METICS QUEEN:—Miss Peggy
Brabyn, of London.
6 KNITWEAR QUEEN: — Miss
Marjorie Robotham, of
Leicester.
7 FUR QUEEN:—Miss Barbara
Greenfield, of London.
8 STOCKING QUEEN: — Miss
Eileen Barnard, of London.
9 IRISH LINEN QUEEN:—Miss
Maude Clarke, of Belfast.
10 SILKS QUEEN:—Miss Olive
Carpenter, of Birmingham.
11 COTTON FABRICS QUEEN:
—Miss Joyce Bealer, of London.
12 SHOES QUEEN:—Miss Olive
Tilley, of Northampton.

activity: a young lady with her curious net fishing for elvers at Ashleworth near Gloucester

te.text:
THE ELVER FISHERS.    EM/MA.
At this time of the year shoals of Elvers or small eels come
up the River Severn, and hundreds of workers who live near the
river are now busy in their spare time catching them with home
made net scoops of a type used for this purpose from the Roman
days. The Elvers are regarded as a great delicacy in the district,
and there is a ready sale for them over a wide area. With the much
higher prices now prevailing the Elver fisher can collect about
100 lbs. in a night, which becomes a profitable side line. Before
the war Germans collected large quantities from the Severn and
shipped them to Germany for restocking rivers there.
Photo shows - A young lady with her curious net fishing at
Ashleworth near Gloucester.          272772.
FOX APRIL.21st.42.

activity: Alfred Bayley with his orange and lemon plants in his greenhouse

te.text:
CALCRAFT     Illus.           20.1.43
ORANGES & LEMONS GROWN IN ENGLAND.
When Oranges and Lemons were sold at Maidenhead
to aid the local War Prisoners Parcels' Fund
everyone was asking "where did they come from?".
78-year-old Alfred Bayley knew the answer. He
grew them! In his greenhouse at Burnham Buck's
even now he has some still growing.
Formerly a diamond miner in South Africa and friend
of Wells who found the Cullinan diamond, they
both worked at the Premier Mine in the Transvaal.
Bayley had the orange trees sent from South Africa
23 years ago; each year he grafts a bud to another
plant in order to form a further plant. Now he
has over twenty miniature orange and lemon plants.
The original plant cost 2/3, including the freight
charges from South Africa. Bayley thinks more of
his oranges and lemons than he does of the world's
largest diamond. He can afford to smile!!!
O.P.S. Alfred Bayley with his orange and
lemon plants in his greenhouse.

THE NEW CUNARDER will be launched
from her cradle at John Brown's
shipyard on the Clyde on September 20.

Cunarders Queen Mary, Queen Elizabeth
and Aquitania before her, she will be
launched with dignity and grandeur.

the shipyard, detailed the protocol:
the two bands, the seven tugs, the 30,000
selected spectators (mainly shipyard
workers and relatives), the private
luncheon for the Queen, who will launch
the ship, and give her a name (at the
moment she is still called Q4).

A COOL JOB FOR WARM WEATHER, MJH/FM.

te.text:
Saidman Illus.
U.S. REPLACEMENT CAMP. OPS.10. Before the new shipment has finished its
first meal, the individual records are sorted and
filed, and the arrival locator cards are with them
in Depot headquarters. Headquarters can now reach
out and identify each person on the Depot by bed
number if necessary. If all of his records are
correct, a soldier may be on his way out to fill
a requisition before noon. If a soldier's records
are missing, faulty, or incomplete, he can be
issued temporary records, duplicate records, or be
interviewed, tested and reclassified as to aptitude
in military pursuits. In the foreground a coloured
and a white soldier are being interviewed. In the
background, Lt.Ralph E. Dunham,NMB, of Wichita,
Kansas, demonstrates the "reaction" test for drives.
The board drops like the guillotine, and the testee
must stop it with the plunger before it falls one-
third of its length, in order to qualify.

activity: Mrs. Waddicot and her son busy in the front garden sorting out the scrap iron.

te.text:
FOUR TONS OF METAL IN A FRONT GARDEN.        WS/OR
A Surrey business man, Mr. Waddicot, of Kingswood has
organised his own "salvage corps". He and his friends
have collected four tons of metal and it is lying in his
front garden, waiting for a contractor to take it for the
Ministry of Supply. Among the scrap iron are lawn mowers,
garden rollers, baths, bedsteads - and last but not least
- two steel helmets left over from the last war.
Photo shows - Mrs. Waddicot and her son busy in the front
garden sorting out the scrap iron.
FOX   JULY Ist.40.

THE DAILY HERALD
... STREET...

activity: feeding hop-bines into a new hop-picking machine

te.text:
MODERN INNOVATIONS IN THE HOP FIELDS.            MJH/RS.

During this hop-picking season a Kentish firm (Messrs
Strettle and Burr of East Peckham have been working two
of their new machines in the hop-fields. These machines,
a mechanical hop-picker and a hop-cleaner have aroused
a great deal of interest not only in this country, but
also abroad. The mechanical picker is designed for use
in the hop alleys, thus avoiding cutting the bines which
are left on the plant for harvesting in the usual manner.
Quite apart from being a much speedier method than the
"old fashioned" hand-picking, it is found that hops picked
by the machine are much cleaner than those picked by hand
and there is no undue bruising of the hops.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS:       Mrs. Lucy Morgan from Forest Gate
(London) and Mrs. Sharp from Clapham (nearest camera) seen
feeding hop-bines into the new hop-picking machine at work
in Messrs. Truman, Hanbury and Buxton's hop-fields at
Paddock Wood, (Kent).

PROPERTY OF

RECEIVED 20 JAN 1955

TO

In the new 'Terylene' plant at Wilton, polymer chips
are conveyed by suction to the spinning building and then dried
to remove moisture. Afterwards they are put into hopper reservoirs
ready for melting. This picture shows the the polymer chip hoppers
over the spinning machines. The plant covers an area of 30 acres
and the first unit, which has a capacity of 11,000,000 lb. of filament
yarn and staple fibre a year, is now in production. The second unit,
which will be completed during 1955, will double the capacity.

activity: the scene in Henley Street, Battersea, after the collapse of a wall at a slum clearance site that killed four-year-old Anthony Simmons

te.text:
CHILD KILLED
COLLAPSE
O P S

THE SCENE IN HENLEY ST
BATTERSEA - AFTER THE
COLLAPSE OF A WALL
KILLING 4 YEAR OLD
ANTHONY SIMMONS

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
DATE RECEIVED
28 DEC 1957
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

A SMALL boy who left his friends and ran back to a
derelict house where they had been playing, was
killed last night when the wall collapsed on top of him.
But no-one will ever know why Tony Simmons, who
would have been four next Wednesday, ran back.
Five minutes earlier Tony and
11 other children from Oulton-
street, Battersea, had been play-
ing in the partly demolished
house on the slum clearance site
in Henley-street, just around the
corner.
"We had been battering at
one of the walls with iron bars,"
said 13-year-old Robert Kent.
"It was a super game. Then
about 4 p.m. we decided to go
home for tea. Tony, he was
the youngest of us, suddenly ran
back.
TOO LATE
"I didn't hear anything, but I
saw the look on the face of
Tony's sister, Jean. I heard her
scream. And when I turned
round, Tony was lying with a
mound of bricks all over his
legs. He was covered in blood."
Eleven-year-old Jean Simmons
ran screaming back home to No.
14 Oulton-street, to tell her
mother.
An ambulance took Tony and
his mother and father to hos-
pital, but it was too late.
Inside No. 14, Jean nursed
Tony's Hopalong Cassidy black
gun, which had been in his
stocking on Christmas morning.
She had been carrying it for
him when he ran back to the
house of death. She sobbed:
"Why did he go back?"
FAINTED
A neighbour, the mother of
Robert Kent, said:
"As soon as I heard about
the crash I dashed to the build-
ing site. Jean had run in tears
to fetch her mother, shouting
that Tony was dead. Mrs. Sim-
mons came running hard after
me.
"When she saw Tony lying
there under that terrific mound
of rubble, she moaned, 'There is
no hope'—and fainted."

te.text:
WARNER. SUN. 29.1.69.
Winning Designs in the Du Pont Architects Competition.
O.P.S. Ist prize winning model wtih central courtyard.

WARNER. SUN. 29.1.69.
Wi nig Designs h

A model of the winning house—rooms grouped around a courtyard.
Home with a Roman look
By JILL GUYTE

THERE IS a look of ancient
Rome about Britain's 'house
of today' which has won a
£1,000 prize for its archi-
tect.
The house—which would cost
£15,000 to build — is designed
round a courtyard as Roman
villas were. But for northern
winters it has the modern
refinement of a translucent
sliding roof.
This house, designed by Mr.
Frederick Hughes, of Notting-
ham, was chosen from 175
entries in an architects competi-
tion sponsored by Du Pont, the
chemical and synthetic fibre
company, in association with the
Royal Institute of British
Architects.
A model was on show in
London yesterday when Mr.
Hughes received his award. In
March, he will see his house
built and furnished at the Ideal
Home Exhibition.
The competition was to
"encourage advanced and
original ideas in domestic design
which are feasible under today's
conditions."
Thirty-four-year-old Mr.
Hughes, of the Department of
Architecture and Civic Planning
at Nottingham University and a
member of Arthur Ling Associ-
ates, concentrated on adapta-
bility.
He said yesterday: "The
family today is a non-static unit
and this house is designed to
accommodate all the changes
that occur in the family—child-
ren growing up and leaving
home, granny coming to live, or
one child needing his own flat."

te.text:
LEARNING CRAFTS AT COUNTRY HOUSE CENTRE      D/FM

At spacious Victorian Gothic Stoke House, set in
some 60 acres of pleasant grounds at Stoke Hammond,
near Bletchley, Bucks., students of all ages and from
many countries take residential courses, lasting from
a week-end to a month, on arts and crafts. The courses,
under the supervision of principal, Noel Heath and his wife,
with Mr Geoffrey Whiting, an expert potter and Miss Irmgard
Schlafer an experienced weaver, include such things as chalk
stone and wood carving, calligraphy, bookcraft and basketry,
with an emphasis on practicality and an atmosphere of
friendly informality. Entertainment, apart from the
advantage of the demesne itself, include films and a large
and comprehensive collection of classical records. The
class groups are small, insuring individual attention,
and the fees, which cover accomodation, board and tuition
are reasonable. Many authorities make grants to would-be
students at the Centre, and it is particularly valuable to
teachers with emergency training.

PHOTO SHOWS:- Miss Ann Regner of Stockholm, Sweden,
engaged in spinning at the Stoke House Centre, wearing
country 'sabots'.

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION MONDAY'S EVENINGS... 20TH APRIL, 1959.
LUTON TOWN SUPPORTERS MAKE A RUSH FOR BOATERS
LE 20.4.59.
THERE IS ONLY ONE FIRM IN THE WORLD STILL MAKING STRAW BOATERS,
THAT OF A. E. OLNEY, LTD., LUTON, BEDFORDSHIRE. IT IS PROBABLY
NOT SURPRISING THEN THAT AS F. A. CUP-FINALISTS, LUTON TOWN CALL
THEMSELVES THE "HATTERS", THEIR STAUNCH SUPPORTERS SHOULD MAKE A
RUSH FOR BOATERS TO WEAR AT WEMBLEY WHEN THEY COME UP TO CHEER
THEIR TEAM TO ITS HOPED-FOR VICTORY OVER NOTTS FOREST. THIS
SUDDEN UNEXPECTED RUSH HAS CREATED SOMETHING OF A PRODUCTION
PROBLEM FOR THE FIRM, AND TO COPE WITH ALL THESE ORDERS MORE
STAFF ARE REQUIRED, BUT BOATER MAKING AS A VERY SKILLED TRADE,
AND A DYING ONE AT THAT, SO THE FIRM IS MAKING URGENT APPEALS TO
SOME OF ITS RETIRED STAFF TO HELP OUT IN ORDER TO MEET THE DEAD-
LINE OF MAY 2ND.
THIS PICTURE TAKEN RECENTLY AT LUTON SHOWS TRIMMERS AT WORK
WITH (LEFT TO RIGHT) MRS. MARJORIE JOHNSON SEWING IN RIBBON WHILE
MRS ROSE NEE AND MRS GRACE EDWARDS SEW LEATHER BANDS INSIDE THE
CROWN OF THESE DELIGHTFUL STRAW BOATERS.

XM)    CRICKET SEASON KEEPS OPEN FOR MRS WILLOW
Drawing to a close of the Cricket Season means no
respite for 64-year-old Mrs. Nellie Cochrane of Lewes,
Sussex, for her the season of manufacturing Cricket
bats is really just starting.  Turning out 3 dozen
bats a week, Mrs. Cochrane with the help of her husband,
William, claims to be the only woman making cricket
bats in the country.  For 35 years the Cochranes have
been making Cricket bats, 75% of their production
going to Australia, Pakistan, New Zealand and the Tonga
Island.  Some of the Machinery has been hand made by
Mr. Cochrane which he has trained his wife to use.

te.text:
Esten  D.H.  3.4.44
EPSOM PREPARES FOR OPENING OF RACING SEASON
Racing opens at Windsor on Easter Monday and trainers hope that it will be the last wartime season. Victor Smythe of Epsom has 48 horses in training this year, 35 of them untried 2-year olds. The increase is mainly due to a greater allocation of feeding stuffs, but labour is still a problem. Vic Smythe solves this by being assisted by part-time local labour to assist in riding and gallops. One of these is an Irish nurse from a local hospital who rides the horses in gallops with as much nerve as her professional colleagues.
OPS 1  Vic Smythe (on left) supervises a string consisting of 2-year olds. He hopes the Derby will be run on his home ground next year.

te.text:
THE SHAPE OF THINGS TO HUM.
January 19th 1955 PAR 47062-2 (BKS-M)
------------------------------------
THE SHAPE OF THINGS TO HUM.

No, this is not a 'space visitor' being
built for a new television play! But its
place will be in the air, eventually.
It is a Hercules aircraft engine which has
been 'cocooned' at the Bristol Aeroplane Co.'s
works at Filton, Bristol.
The special plastic covering affords the
engine protection against humidity, and an
inserted 'peephole' allows a check to be kept
on a humidity indicator inside the 'cocoon'.
Thus treated, an engine may be stored in the
open for periods of up to two years, although
the plastic covering is only one-twentyfifth
of an inch thick.
January 19th 1955 PAR 47062-2 (BKS-M)

activity: Wives and relatives waiting at the pithead of a colliery during a rescue operation following a subsidence disaster.

te.text:
Wives & relatives
at pithead of No 6.

FOR wives and relatives (above) there is little
to do but wait—and hope. They stand—one
with a child, faces tense—where the rails slope
to the disused Bank Colliery working. On the
surface colleagues squat, time drags.

HERALD REPORTER NEW CUMNOCK, Ayrshire, Friday
RESCUE teams are tonight boring
through a 25ft. wall of coal to reach
128 miners trapped by a huge subsidence
of rain-sodden earth last night into
Knockshinnock Castle Colliery near here.
The coal barrier is also being attacked from the
other side—by the entombed men.  The barrier is
now reduced to 16ft.  Early tomorrow the tunnel
should be finished.
B

DAILY HERALD
RCD. 9 SEP 1950

KEEPING TIME FOR 100 YEARS        18-1-51

General Caption for £26000. Diamond Case at Clerkenwell

diamonds +

diamonds, part of a £26,000
consignment seized by the
Customs in the post. Two other
bagfulls are in the packages
shown.

to have been illegally exported,

appeal.

CH/HT

      A MONSTER JOB OF SHIP SURGERY.

Pieces of machinery weighing as much as 70 tons are now
being removed from the motor ship "Laguna" in King George
V. Docks London. It constitutes the biggest marine job ever
carried out by Harland and Wolff and will take many months.
They are lifting out one set of cylinders to get at broken
crankshafts, both of which are fractured. The machinery is being
lifted through deck.

Photo shows- The three-cylinder block, weighing 70 tons, being
lifted clear of the ship by the Mammoth crane.
FOX Dec 31st. 34.

vehicle - the HOVERTRUCK Mark 1, near Ely. It is basically
a Land-Rover fitted with two engines and a Nylon rubber
'skirt'. One engine drives the vehicle while the other
generates a cushion of air beneath - which - trapped by the
'skirt' - takes four fifths of the weight off the wheels -
thus stopping the vehicle from becoming bogged down.
A farmer can drive over the softest and muddiest fields
while spraying crops etc..

KEYSTONE PHOTO SHOWS: - One of the HOVERTRUCKS spraying
                  the fields - with another in the background -
                  during the demonstration near ELY today.
                  JSS/KEYSTONE        RC/754954..

activity: aftermath of a colliery explosion at Hapton Valley Colliery

te.text:
Industry - Fuel and Power - Coal - Accidents - Hapton Valley Colliery, Lancs.
March. 1962

HAPPY VALLEY

HERALD REPORTER

SIXTEEN miners were killed and 30 injured in an explosion 750ft. undergruond in a colliery yesterday.
Last night National Coal Board experts picked their way among the debris at Hapton Valley Colliery, near Burnley, Lancs, to try to find out what caused the disaster.
The explosion came at 9.45 a.m., when 46 men were working at the pit's No. 2 coal face.
FLAME
All 46 pitmen were hurled several feet by the blast. Then the survivors and men from other parts of the pit ran to help the casualties.
A sheet of flame seared along the face, which is 150ft. long and 3ft. 6in. high. None of the men who were crouching over their work could escape. Rescue teams rushed to the scene of the explosion. As they started work news of the disaster spread to the colliery homes.
Wives of the men down the mine — known locally as “Happy Valley” — gathered silently at the pithead for a long, agonising wait for news.
The rescue work went on for four hours. First the injured were brought to the surface.
Many of the miners were carried past the waiting wives with faces covered to hide their burns.
A eet of ambulances stood waiting to take the injured pitmen to hospital.
Then the dead were brought up. One of the first to be named was 19-year-old Jimmy Cummings, of Rowley-avenue, Burnley.
He was to have bee nmarried tomorrow.
STUNNED
A survivor, coal face “captain” Jack Murray, aged 35, said: “I was working at the end of the line. We werefilling coal [tubs] but not drilling.
“Suddenly there was a bang, and I felt a blast of hot air. It threw me several feet and I was stunned.
“When I looked up everything was in darkness. The light from my helmet picked out bodies lying in front of me.
“I knew then that some of my pals who were nearer the source of the explosion must have died.”

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
23 MAR 1962
PLEASE RETURN TO
ART LIBRARY

This Is How Cardiff Feeds 
 Its Needy Children 
 THIS picture was taken in one of the 14 
 "canteens" in various parts of Cardiff 
 in which free meals are served to necessitous 
 children who are entitled to them. 
 Under the scheme by which the city 
 council attempts to carry out its statutory 
 obligation to feed nearly 4,000 children, at 
 midday, contracts are let out to a number 
 of private caterers. 
 About 90 children are fed in the canteen 
 in which this picture was taken. 
 Labour members of the city council have for 
 long complained about the unsatisfactory 
 features of the present efforts to feed the 
 poor children of the city. 
 They have urged that special accom- 
 modation should be provided, where the 
 children can take their meals in comfortable 
 surroundings, and that the city council 
 should, as other councils do, itself undertake 
 the catering and arrange for proper super- 
 vision by the council's staff. 
 Medical experts recently investigated con- 
 ditions in the present canteens and their 
 report is expected to contain recommenda- 
 tions for improvement.

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE 
 "DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY 
 AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

activity: Michael Leyser trying a fashion adaptation on model Jane Davis in a London factory.

te.text:
IT'S rush-time at this Lon-
don factory, where they're
working late to bring you
high fashion at low prices.
Only three weeks ago, Michael
Leyser, one of the firm's
designers, saw the Italian
fashion collections at Flor-
ence.
Linzi dresses which reflect the
cream of what he saw there
are already rolling off the
pilot plant machines.
Here you see him trying one
of his adaptations on model
Jane Davis.
Slung on rails by his right
elbow are hundreds of bright
orange cardboard pattern
pieces.
Fabrics
He leaves the model, broods
over sketches from his
travels, then begins cutting,
placing the cardboard on a
length of cloth to see how it
will fit—if it will work econo-
mically as well as fashion-
ably.
In the building are stored
thousands of yards of the
fabrics he'll work with.
In an office across the street, a
young graduate of the St.
Martin's School of Art car-
ries through his instructions
into even more sketches and
drafts.
At a factory in Slough, giant
cutting machines are waiting
to start on orders from the
big buyers.
So in a matter of weeks,
fashionable 4-guinea dresses
with a 40-guinea look will be
on sale all over Britain.
The dress Jane Davis is wear-
ing here is in the more ex-
pensive 10-guinea line.
But there are similar versions
at around 4 guineas.
SERENA SINCLAIR

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
11 FEB 1959
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

activity: A bomb-site on Hill-lane, Acton, used as a Labour hall (concrete and asbestos hut) before being sold to an oil company for a petrol station.

te.text:
DAY by day, evidence is piling up of
fantastic fortunes being made by
speculation in land.  The latest story
will bring the lesson sharply home to
the Labour Party Executive today, when
it meets to consider the draft of its
new Home Policy aimed at curbing the
land speculator.
   For the latest people to benefit from the
building land boom are not speculators at all.
They are the Acton Labour Party.
   In 1948 this local Labour and trade union movement
in West London scraped up £1,500 to buy a bomb-site.
It was just the place for a Labour hall—a corner site
45 feet deep with a 90ft. frontage on Hill-lane, a busy
main road.
   Labour volunteers
cleared the site and got
the money together to
build a concrete and
asbestos hut.
   They dreamed of the day
when they would have
enough cash to put up a per-
manent building.
   But rising building costs
beat them every time. Now
they have sold the site to an
oil company for £42,000—
28 times what they paid for
it. A petrol station will be
built on the site.
   They hope to find another
place — less valuable, of
course — in the borough
where their unexpected
wealth will enable them to
[illegible] the land and put up a
[illegible] class building.

DAILY HERALD 
 Copyright 
 Photograph 
 BY R. BURTON 
 NUMBER 1961/876
Housing - Misc. Property & Land Speculators deal

activity: knotting hairs through a silk net foundation at a wig-making department

te.text:
REVIVING THE DYING ART OF WIG-MAKING

he free supply of wigs under the National Health
scheme has increased the demand for them and brought
to light the problem of lack of labour in this trade.
A craft which requires patience, skill, and pains-
taking application, it does not easily attract young
people who can earn more elsewhere, and so most of the
wig-makers are elderly. Wigs are made from women's hair,
costing as much as five pounds an ounce, and the hair
is knotted 2 or 3 strands at a time onto a foundation
of French silk net. Infinite care is then required to
achieve the correct shape and the necessary shading to
give the hair the semblance of authentic growth.

INP PHOTO SHOWS: The knotting department at Wig
Creations, Ltd., London. One of the
workers is here seen at the painstaking
job of knotting the hairs, with a sort of
crochet hook, through the foundation of
silk net.

te.text:
248957   BRI
HUSBANDS AND WIVES ARE BUILDING THEIR OWN HOMES
Ruislip, Middlesex: Because they were tired of waiting for
homes, 30 young men and their wives of South Ruislip
got together and decided they would build their own.
While waiting for council approval on the question of
a building site, the men and their wives formed themselves
into a 'self-help building group' and began to practice
the technique of laying bricks.
At week ends the group meets at the home of their 66-year-old
president, Councillor Walter Matthews, where, besides
getting in some practical work they also listen to lectures
given by building experts.
Next month the group plans to start putting up its first house.
PHOTO SHOWS:- The wives cheerfully lend a hand in the building
practice their husbands are getting in at Councillor
Matthews' South Ruislip home. From left are: Mrs Vera Penfold,
Mrs Edith Norman, Mrs Josephine Hone, Mrs Phyllis Onwin and
(right), Mrs Violet Rogers.

te.text:
KT/VAN.
24-HOUR-A-DAY BATTLE AGAINST FOOT-AND-MOUTH.

      Currently working flat out in the battle against the
current outbreak of Foot-and-Mouth disease are the 30
men and women employed on the production of disinfectant
at the Jeyes Group factory at Plaistow in East London.
      Working a 24-hour day in three shifts, production at
the factory has been increased by about 20 times to a
massive 1,000 gallons an hour to keep pace with the
current huge demand from farms and authorities all over
the country.
      Jeyes are the largest manufacturers of Ministry
approved disinfectant in this country.

PHOTO SHOWS.
               Cans of Jeyes Fluid being stacked in readiness
for despatch from the factory at Plaistow this morning.

activity: a general view of BP's operational base at Eakring, Nottinghamshire, showing a drilling rig for the 'Sea Gem' platform and other research rigs

te.text:
British Petroleum's first drilling barge for North Sea
operations is to begin operating about mid-May this year.

Since last December equipment for 'Sea Gem' has been
arriving at Liverpool docks from as far away as Papua and Trinidad.
Transported to the BP North Sea operational base at Eakring,
Nottinghamshire, a complete rig has been assembled on a 'mock-up'
layout of the drilling barge.  Valuable time will be saved by the
crew knowing in advance exactly where every piece of equipment is to
be positioned on the barge which is due to arrive at Middlesborough
from Le Havre on April 30th.

O.P.S.  A general view of BP's operational base at Eakring,
Nottinghamshire, showing the drilling rig which will
be mounted on 'Sea Gem' BP's drilling platform for North
Sea operations, and two other rigs, one of which is being
used by BP for research into new drilling techniques.

activity: Len King and Bill Clark go over layout plans under floodlights used for building homes at night.

te.text:
PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
REC 8-APR 1954
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

LN 269017    TEA    LONDON BUREAU
BUILD HOMES IN SPARE TIME.

LONDON: Clerks, building workers, printers and
lorry drivers are among the 25 members of the
Camberwell Enterprise Housing Club, who are
building their own homes on a site at Crystal
Palace (South London). The idea was born two
years ago, now every night, and at weekends
and holidays, the men work on the houses.
Neighbours lend a hand and much of the work
is done at night with the aid of floodlights.
Special features of the homes will be a modified
form of central heating; a garage to each house;
and a new 'Acotile' plastic tile flooring
throughout. Skilled, unpaid foreman is Bill
Clark, who with Len King, a building representative
during the day, works in the 'site' hut with the
plans. Bill will be the first to move into one
of the new homes - in May. The project is expected
to be completed in two years' time.
PHOTO SHOWS: LEN KING (left) and BILL CLARK go
over the layout plans under one of the floodlights
used for building at night.

Planet News Feature Service, 1954 PN-d.

Jews, Nightingale Lane, S.W.  With solemn
invocation intoned in Aramaic the language used
by Jesus, aged Jews last night sat down to their
meal of unleavened cakes, the roasted shankbone
of a lamb, and an egg, etc.  The shankbone of the
lamb is a symbol of the Paschal sacrifice, the
egg recalls the individual offering of the
Temple worshipper.

chair surrounded with cushions.  The custom demanding
that he shall sit at ease to celebrate the fact that
the Jews are now released from the captivity which
they were in in ancient Egypt. Note. This man is a
refugee and has only been in this country a few weeks.

activity: A cow named Rosie and her bull calf Ferdie in the sale ring at the English-Ayrshire Cattle Breeders Association Show.

te.text:
ESTEN D.H.                  4/2/44.

ROSIE TAKES FAREWELL OF HER YOUNG OFFSPRING.
Cattle show and sales were before the war an excuse
for the farmer and the farm hands families, for a
day out.  Now all you will see at the sale ring is
a hard bitten auctioneer together with the buyers,
keen farming experts and cattle dealers.
Untouched by the little acts of pathos that take
place in the sale ring.  In former years the buyers
family would have reacted and father would have
been persuaded to buy calf as well as cow.
OPS.  Rosie in the ring taking a last farewell
glance at her young bull calf "Ferdie" as she was
led out after being sold for £90.  Ferdie was born
at the sale some four hours previous and was sold
to a seperete buyer for £4, and that was the last
Rosie saw of her offspring.  This Lilliput melodrama
was enacted at the English-Ayrshire Cattle Breeders

activity: Mrs. Simpson, the last resident of a stolen pre-fabricated bungalow, pictured in her new flat.

te.text:
OPS, Mrs. Simpson, the last resident of the stolen pre-fab. in
her new flat today.

DAILY HERALD March 20 1959 5
Stolen—
a house
and all
mod. con.
Herald Reporter
FOUR cheerful young men
took a pre-fab bungalow
to pieces, loaded it in to a
lorry, and drove away.
And that led to the strangest
entry that police at Croydon,
Surrey, have ever put in their
log-book. It reads.
"Stolen; one prefab, with two
bedrooms, lounge, kitchen and
bathroom, fitted cupboards and
all mod. con."
The prefab is — or WAS — in
Firtree - avenue, Shrublands,
Croydon. It was empty, and had
been sold by Croydon council to
a man in Suffolk, who was ex-
pected to take it away.
But the four young men beat
him to it.
'A ROW'
As they worked, unhurriedly,
neighbours watched, thinking
they were contractors' men.
Mr. Charles Jones, a plasterer,
who lives in the next house,
said yesterday: "I was an inno-
cent witness to the crime. I had
a row with one of the men for
flinging bits and pieces into my
garden."
Police admit they haven't a
clue—not even a finger-print.

activity: keel-laying ceremony for an Oberon-class submarine being built for Canada at Chatham Dockyard, involving a team of women 'keel-haulers' led by Mary Hogg

te.text:
THEY started building a new sub- marine at Chatham dockyard in Kent yesterday. And with one of those touches of sentiment that soften the normally no-nonsense world of the sea, the keel was winched into position by a team of women. Some of the women were wives of officers at the dockyard. Others were wives of officers in the Royal Canadian Navy: the submarine, of the Oberon class, is being built for Canada.

Mrs. Mary Hogg, wife of Rear-

Admiral I. L. T. Hogg, Admiral Super- intendent of Chatham dockyard, was in charge of the " keel-haulers ", and officially pronounced the keel " well and truly laid. "

Keel - layers traditionally get a symbolic payment for their work. Mrs. Hogg received a newly minted Canadian dollar set in a casket of English oak lined with Canadian cedar. Her helpers each received a silver half dollar.

PICTURE BY DOUGLAS EATWELL

activity: the kitchen of a demonstration house at Northolt featuring modern gas appliances including a cooker, water-heater, wash-boiler, and refrigerator.

te.text:
DEMONSTRATION HOUSES AT NORTHOLT.

Along one wall of the kitchen is a gas cooker of
the latest type, horizontal, with hotplate fitted [crossed out word] 
beside the oven and hot closet below for keeping
food warm. Next to it is the sink, with double
draining boards, and small recessed instantaneous
gas water-heater, providing an independent hot water
supply for washing-up when necessary. This system makes
for fuel economy, as well as for added convenience,
since in summer the circulator need only be lighted
when hot water is required for baths. A cupboard,
conveniently placed under one of the draining boards,
contains the portable gas wash-boiler, with wringer
attached. When required, this is pulled out and placed
alongside the sink. On the opposite wall is a gas-
operated refrigerator, built in at a convenient
height, with cupboard above and below, a draw leaf
table, and a store cupboard.

SUPPLIED L.N.A.

te.text:
THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
'DAILY HERALD' ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

PRINCESS ELIZABETH VISITS COVENTRY
WEARING NEW FASHION SHE WORE IN PARIS.      22.5.48.

Princess Elizabeth had on one of her outfits
she wore in Paris when she visited Coventry today,
to open a new square. It was the lime green coat
and with it she had a lime green straw hat with
green veiling, white shoes, hand-bag and gloves.
When she got there she examined new cars, labelled
for export, of one car which was marked for export only
she said, "Lets* hope the home motorists will be able
to have some before long.

I.N.P. PHOTO SHOWS.  Little Janet Parbury, representative of
                     Coventry Brownies presenting Princess
                     Elizabeth with a bouquet, which con-
                     sisted of green peas of the "Lady Godiva
                     Variety" and bound by a piece of ribbon
                     made in Coventry to the order of the
                     Government of South Africa on the occasion
                     of the visit of H.M.H. with their majestie
                     the King and Queen in 1947.

Picture BY J. Waldorf.
I8I58.H.              INTERNATIONAL NEWS PHOTOS.

INTERNATIONAL [NEWS PHOTOS]
72, FLEET STREET, LONDON

activity: Thousands of strips of rubber which go to make a golf ball hanging p ready for use

te.text:
MAKING GOLD BALL.
          Golfers who regularly play their golf taking a new ball and
perhaps loosing it immediately rarely realise the intricate work
going to the making of a golf ball. The ball starts as a little
ball of rubberwhich is dipped into rubber latex, they are then weighed
a few inches of rubber tape is then wound on to them with the core
still soft. The ball is then placed on to a machine for winding
on several feet of rubber, they are then put through a gauge for
size and passed through a test for hardness and from then to a
machine for compression, from there the ball receives a coating of
a creamy solution of gutta-percha after a drying trip which takes
a day and a half, the ball is shot through the moulder to get the
pattern. The ball is then plunged into first a hot bath and then
a cold one, it is then stamped with the name, weighed and tested
several times.
O.P.S. Thousands of strips of rubber which go to make a golf
       ball hanging p ready for use.        HD/B. Keystone.

SUPPLIED BY
[illegible] KEYSTONE VIEW-COMPANY
[illegible] LONDON, E.C.4.

FRENCH
DRESSING
WITH YOUR
MEALS

A dash of French
dressing adds
piquancy to chef as
well as meal, it seems.
Hence the apron. Its in-
gredients are British-gay
floral prints from Liberty
and John Lewis-but the
flavour is definitely Pro-
vencal.
The range has been specially
made for Divertimenti, Mary-
lebone, London, in sage greens,
poppy colours and thistle blues.
French kitchen ware is also
catching on. Demand is over-
taking supply of items like the
double-funneled sauce boat in
white porcelain (bottom left in
the picture).
The vegetable steamer next
to it, in brown-glazed fire-
proof porcelain, keeps the
flavour in the food where it
belongs, instead of allowing it
to boil away.
The crust casserole, which
the model is holding, is for
chicken or game and has a
novel two-headed lid. Fire-
and oven-proof, it is table-
attractive as well as kitchen-
practical.
The huge wine or oil jar is
in more ornamental mood.
Prices: Aprons from 19s. 11d.
to 25s.; sauce boat 23s.;
steamer 32s. 6d.; casserole
£6 4s.; wine jar 15gns.

SUN
PROPERTY
3 0 AUG 1966
Please return to
ART Library

activity: Mrs. Susan McGarvey in a room in Notting Hill where her six children sleep, illustrating overcrowded housing conditions.

te.text:
IS LONDON's Notting Hill like a monkey
house? In a recent book authors William and
Claire Russell describe it as a place where
people living in overcrowded tenement flats
often react violently to the appalling con-
ditions. Sometimes they even maltreat their
chidren.
  They say that human behaviour compares with
that of monkeys who, cramped and caged behind
bars at the zoo, become cruel and aggressive.
  The Russells lived for
10 years in Notting Hill,
scene of the race riots of
the 50s, and now, they
declare, a "human
monkey house."
  I spent two days in the
district, which comes under
the Royal Borough of Ken-
sington and Chelsea, to find
out how people do react
and what they think of the
Russels' allegation.
  SUSAN McGARVEY is only
21. Every morning from her
front window she sees scrawled
on the grey corrugated fence
opposite—her only view apart
from the dustbins—the words,
The sky has died.
  It is a slogan of the anguish
and futility of life in an over-
crowded city.
  "A little of me dies," sighed
Susan, "every time I see it."
  Behind that window in Cam-
bridge Gardens in two rooms—
with 15 sharing one toilet and
a kitchen whose walls weep
every time she cooks — Susan
and her husband, Patrick,
32, bring up their six children
—the four eldest, all boys, of
her husband's former marriage.
  The children are clean, well
dressed, happy and polite. The
five eldest sleep in bunks in
one room, their own clothes on
top of their parents' under-
neath for lack of hanging
space.
  Baby Susan, six months
sleeps in her pram.

SUN BALNDFORD 4-11-68
O.P.S. Mrs. Susan McGarvey photographed in the room where her six
children sleep
Overcrowding in Notting Hill Gate
