activity: the last yards of a 16-mile length of submarine power cable being coiled in a specially constructed shed at a factory

te.text:
138,000 VOLT SUBMARINE POWER CABLE FOR VANCOUVER.

At their Trafford Park, Manchester, factory, British
Insulated Callender's (Submarine Cables) Ltd., have
completed the first stage of an order valued at over
three-million dollars, for the supply and installation
of 138,000-volt submarine cable for the British Columbia
Electric Company of Canada, who are linking their high-
voltage system in the southern part of Vancouver Island
with the unlimited hydro-electric resources on the mainland
of British Columbia. The cable system consists of single core
cables, each 16 miles in length, with similar cables 3 1/2 miles
long for the inter-island section. At four inches diameter and
weighing 50lbs a yard, this will be the largest continuous
long-length power cable ever installed. Special loading and
transport arrangements are necessary for cable of this size
and weight and a special Coiling Down Shed has been constructed
for it's storage.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: The last yards of a 16-mile length of
cable being coiled on one of the huge cable stacks in the
specially constructed coiling down shed at the Trafford Park,
Manchester, factory of British Insulated Callender's (Submarine
Cables), Ltd. who have manufactured it for the British
Columbia Electric Company.

FOX PHOTOS MAY 2ND. 1956 32623

A PRESS VISIT TO THE TRAFFORD PARK, MANCHESTER, FACTORY
OF BRITISH INSULATED CALLENDER'S CABLES, LTD. HAS BEEN
ARRANGED FOR TODAY.

activity: Looking along the keel of a new ship at the yards

te.text:
BRITAIN'S SHIPYARDS ARE WINNING AGAINST THE U-BOATS.   Y
Despite the savage U-boat warfare on our merchant vessels,
figures since the outbreak of war show that our shipbuilding
industry is more than making up for losses incurred.  New
ships, captures and conversions have given our Mercantile
Marine more tonnage than ever - although thousands of tons
of shipping has been sent to the bottom of the seas.  The
Mercantile Marine has mobilised and ships are being turned

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION

SPINNING THE ARTERIES OF OUR CIVILISATION.
61.. 141.
This is one of a remarkable new series of photo-
graphs taken mainly by the natural light of the
process by which a British ironworks produces
mile upon mile of cast iron pipes for the public
services of gas [illegible] and water which are a prime
necessity of civilised life. A large percentage
of these pipes are spun by a centrifugal process
which eliminates defects and gives a close-grained
metal, easily worked and with a high degree of
resilience and resistance to impact. In addition
to its own requirements, the plant also produces
pig-iron for steel manufacture, contributing largely
therefore to the country's output of armaments.

iron into the hopper for the centrifugal casting
of pipes for gas, water and sewage, etc.,

British shipyards are launching merchant vessels with

activity: modernising British collieries with new haulage arrangements and pithead at New Hucknall Colliery

te.text: INDUSTRY - FUEL + POWER - COAL - PIT VIEWS.

NEW HUCKNALL COLLIERY, Huthwaite, Nottingham.

Handling improvements save manpower.

One of the most important factors in modernising
British collieries has been the speeding up and increasing
the capacity of the haulage arrangements so that more
coal can flow from the production faces. A brand new
pithead has been installed at this colliery, and two-ton
mine cars which have replaced the old small tubs, are now
brought to the surface, pneumatically decked, tipped and
returned to the pit cages with only two men controlling
the operation. Men who used to be employed on these
operations are now available for work underground, and
many have been upgraded to more productive work on the
coalface.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
12 MAY 1958
PLEASE RETURN

activity: two new merchantmen at a British shipyard, one in a 10% stage of completion and the other ready for launching

te.text:
BRITISH SHIPBUILDERS V THE U-BOATS
28.2.41.
As the war proceeds it becomes apparent - as Hitler himself
has proclaimed in his latest harrangue - that the main hopes
of the Nazis are centred in an intensification of the U-boat
attacks on our life-lines across the seas, particularly from
America, the "Arsenal of Democracy". More than ever, there-
fore, is Britain dependent upon the magnificent efforts of
her shipbuilders to back up the heroic work of the Royal Navy
by replacing losses of merchantmen, and it is comforting to
know that our rate of production at the present time is already
higher than the corresponding figures for 1915 and 1916 in the
last war. This is one of a new series taken at a British
shipyard, and shows :-
1. Two of Britain's answers to the U-boats - new merchantmen
at a British shipyard. The one on the left is in a 10%
stage of completion; the other is ready for launching.

activity: Mrs. Esther Clara Garrett, chairwoman of a tenants' committee, addressing a meeting of tenants in Whitechapel to demand rent reductions and repairs.

te.text:
“IT’S more than you dare do,
Garrett,” said the land-
lord’s agent.
“Is that so?” replied Mrs.
Esther Clara Garrett, of Irene
House, Flower and Dean-street,
Whitechapel, E.
She is the chairwoman of the
committee formed by 180 tenants of
tenements there, to demand rent re-
ductions and repairs.
With no schooling except that
which comes from going to work at
eight years of age and bringing up a
large family, Mrs. Garrett yesterday
made her first “public appearance.”
She left the two-room flat for
which she pays 13s. a week rent and
spoke to 250 men, women and
children.
They cheered as she told them,
“I’ll go to the landlord and whatever
there is to say, I’ll say it.”
The meeting followed a procession
from Flower- and Dean-street, with
drums playing and banners flying.
Organised by the Stepney Tenants’
Defence League, the meeting decided
to send the landlord a suggested
scale of rents and repairs, with a rent
strike ultimatum if there is no satis-
faction or negotiation in seven days

KENT MINERS SHATTER TARGET ON EVE
OF NATIONALISATION
Miners of the Snowdown Colliery, Nonington,
near Dover, Kent, have just completed their best
weekly output - and have smashed their target by
over forty per cent. Total tonnage for the week
was 13,863 tons - which works out at 30cwt of
useable coal for every man employed at the colliery
or 7 tons per man employed at the coal face - each
man per day!
PICTURE SHOWS:
Jack Wood and L.Turner, two of the miners
in charge of operations underground who helped
in this effort - beneath the score boad.
19953 17/12/46 John Topham, Sidcup, Kent.

activity: View of the site as the Tower Crane is used - at Norwich

te.text:
NEW TOWER CRANE USED TO SPEED HOUSE BUILDING.. 
 
 5-12-52. 
 MR. ERNEST MARPLES the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Housing and Local Govern- 
 ment, paid a visit to NORWICH today to examine progress 
 in the Norwich Housing Scheme, which is an experiment 
 in mechanisation in house building.. A new huge unique 
 rail tower crane is being used on the site. The crane 
 belongs to the Department of Scientific Research - is 
 mounted on rails and travels around the estate for the 
 lowering of prefabricated house sections. The use of 
 this crane has enabled the "roofed-in" stage of the 
 32 houses to be reached in about half the time normally 
 required (700 hours against the normal 1,300).. 
 
 KEYSTONE PHOTO SHOWS:- View of the site as the Tower 
 Crane is used - at Norwich , today.. 
 JSS/KEYSTONE BIR/599500.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
REC. 11 JAN 1952
PLEASE RETURN
TO

THATCHED ROOF TROLLEY BUS PRESENTS PROBLEM TO    D/HT
PLANNERS

The East Suffolk Planning Committee have been
presented with a tricky problem. A converted trolley
bus, once used in Ipswich streets, is now occupied
by 72-year-old smallholder, Mr. W. Steward and his
wife, in a field at Greeting St. Mary. Under plan-
ning regulations it would have to be moved, but Mr.
Steward has turned the bus into a "cottage" by that-
ching the roof. Now the Committee have to decide if
this constitutes a permanent dwelling.

PHOTO SHOWS: With bus notices still on the walls,
Mrs Steward makes a cup of tea for her husband on
the upper deck of their trolley bus home.

te.text:
A DAY IN THE LIFE OF A GIRL WITH AN
UNUSUAL OCCUPATION.

AT 21-YEARS-OLD AGE, MISS MYRTLE TOPE IS BELIEVED TO BE THE
ONLY GIRL PIG FARMER IN ENGLAND. FROM SEVEN EVERY MORNING UNTIL
DUSK EVERY EVENING THIS VIVACIOUS RED-HAIRED GIRL MANAGES HER
FATHER'S PIGGERY AT YELLAND, NEAR TOTNES, DEVON WHERE SHE HAS
650 PIGS UNDER HER CARE. ALTHOUGH THE NATURE OF HER OCCUPATION
ENTAILS OF THE WEARING OF BREECHES ALL DAY, MISS TOPE IS A VERY
FEMININE PERSON, AND AT THE END OF HER LONG DAY DONS MORE
FEMININE ATTIRE. CLEANING OUT THE PIGGERIES, CARRYING HALF A
HUNDREDWEIGHT OF PIG MEAL ON HER BACK FROM THE STORE ROOM TO THE
FEEDING BARROWS AND THEN PUSHING THE BARROWS ROUND THE FARM TO
FEED 650 HUNGRY PORKERS IS HARD WORK FOR A YOUNG GIRL, BUT MISS
TOPE IS ENTHUSIASTIC ABOUT HER WORK. GROOMING THE PIGS FOR SHOW
PURPOSES IS ONE OF HER MANY TASKS, WHILE THE PIGLETS HAVE TO HAVE
SEED OIL RUBBED INTO THEIR SKINS TO PREVENT SUNBURN AND PAINFUL
CRACKING THROUGH DRYNESS. BREEDING PEDIGREE PIGS IS NO EASY JOB,
BUT MISS TOPE KNOWS ALL THE SECRETS OF HER TRADE.

O.PLS.   MANUAL LABOUR IS ALL IN THE DAY'S WORK.  HERE IS
MISS TOPE CARRYING A HALF HUNDREDWEIGHT OF PIG
MEAL ON HER BACK FROM THE STORE ROOM TO THE FEEDING
BARROWS.        365/B. KEYSTONE

activity: one of the machines used in the book production process, designed to produce the concave front and the convex back and hinge

te.text:
Sheet of 64 pages printed on each side
coming off the printing machine

ROPER                                     16.3.39

50 to 100,000 FULLY BOUND BOOKS PER WEEK.
Some of the largest Perfector printing
machines in Europe:  Printing 64 pages on
each side of the sheet.
The copy from the author goes to Linotype
machines - they have a keyboard similar to
that of a typewriter - which transforms the
printed word into metal type.  The type is
made up into a page form which has a
facsimile taken off it in paper flong, from
which the metal cast is produced.  Plates
are assembled in special order on the bed
of the printing machine and after the
application of ink, the printed sheet is
produced.
The printed sheet goes through nearly a
dozen operations such as folding, gathering,
sewing and cutting, when it is transformed
into the bound copy sold to the public.
Real leather is used for the making of cases.
Real 22 carat gold is applied to the lettering.
Above is one of the machines used in the
process.  Its object is to produce the concave
front, and the convex back and hinge.

activity: The winning student designers discussing various points of their models

te.text:
XML)      NEW DESIGN FOR PART OF OLD CANTERBURY
      ARCHITECTURAL STUDENTS CARRY OUT NOVEL EXERCISE

Sixty-five architectural students from various parts of
Kent have pooled their ideas to suggest how a clearance
area in the heart of old Canterbury could be re-
constructed for business and community purposes.  They
are students of the Canterbury School of Architecture,
where potential architects from a wide area carry out
a five-year course of professional training.  These
young people have produced a series of designs for
re-developing with modern premises the area of the city
bounded by Beer Cart Lane, Stour Street and Jewry Lane,
near the well-known Franciscan Gardens.  Part of this
district was damaged by bombs during the war.  The Head
of the School, Mr. R.W. Paine, has pointed out that
this is nothing more than a collective exercise in
design, but it does show the potentialities of a site
which one day will be re-developed.  The exercise
has taken a month.  Three-dimensional table models as
well as drawings of the suggested new buildings have
been prepared by the students.

Photo shows:-  The winning student designers discussing
various points of their models from left to right
they are - Mr. P.L. Johnson, of Snodland; Miss Margaret
Baker of Rye; Mr. A.K.W. Morgan of Strood; Mr. J.M.
Simmonds of Eythorne, near Dover; and Mr. M.R. Monk of
Gravesend, Kent, they are all students of the Canterbury
School of Architecture.

22/4/53           Topical Press       (Y 79842)

te.text:
LN 266995 AND LONDON BUREAU
EUROPE'S LARGEST FURNACE GETS LIGHTED
217 FT. HIGH
SCUNTHORPE, ENG: A new blast furnace - the largest
in Europe -was officially 'blown-in' at the
Appleby-Frodingham Steel Company's works,
Scunthorpe. The ceremony, which was attended by
hundreds of workers who had helped to build
the furnace, was performed by Sir Walter Benton
Jones, chairman of the United Steel Companies Ltd.
Built by Messrs. Ashmore, Benson, Pease and Co.,
the blast is provided by turbo blowers, and it
is hoped that outputs of well over 6,000 tons
a week will be regularly obtained.
PHOTO SHOWS:- Standing at the base of the
huge furnace - it is 217 feet high -a workman, cap
in hand, chats with SIR WALTER BENTON JONES
at the ceremony of 'blowing-in' the furnace.
The audience includes men who helped to build
this vast project.

activity: scientific farming demonstration at the Somerset Farm Institute in Cannington

te.text:
JACK SMITH          ILLUS.          15.6.42
The 201 acre Somerset Farm Institute at Cannington
Nr.Bridgwater, was the stage for the greatest three
demonstration in scientific farming ever held in this
country. Thousands of farmers from neighbouring
counties and the Minister of Agriculture,Mr.R.S.
Hudson, M.P., came to see for themselves. Many were
prepared to be critical. All, including the Minister,
q went home impressed.
In an address to his farmers the Minister speaking
from a platform in the farmyard,told them, "Britain
must grow more food - we have got to see that every
ounce of labour is economically employed."
Minister and farmers saw these words already in
practice at the demonstration that covered 201 acres.
6,000 farmers came from neighbouring counties,
including Devon,Dorset,Cornwall Warwick, Hereford,
Gloucester.

THEY SHOUTED "DOWN WITH THE FASCISTS"
CROWD INVADE ALBERT HALL MEETING
            13-3-46

Shouting "Down with the Fascists", members of the
Communist Party and men who fought with the
International Brigade in Spain invaded the Albert
Hall platform this evening and broke up a meeting
organised by the Britons' Vigilantes Action League.
They took over the microphone and addressed the
meeting until 20 police officers walked on the platform
and ordered them to stop.
Mr.John PREEN who opened the meeting had shouted himself
hoarse against the clamour and gave up. - One man
declared: XXXXXXXXXXXKXXXXXXXXXX "I am the Governor of the
Brighton Vigilantes. I am dead against this meeting".
KEYSTONE PHOTO SHOWS:

A large crowd with anti-Fascist banners
gathered outside the Albert Hall and tried to
enter the hall forcibly. Here police is seen guarding
the entrance.

te.text:
BUILDING ADVISERS GET DOWN TO BUSINESS.
12 - 12 - 47

_____________________________________

The first meeting of the Advisory Council on Building
and Civil Engineering Research and Development
took place at the Ministry of Works , London
today. The Council will keep under review the
whole field of building research and development,
suggest subjects which need attention and advise
on methods of putting scientific findings into
practice by the industry. Its members include
trade union leaders, employees, an economist,
a professor of anatomy, a psychologist, architects,
civil engineers, a physicist, a statistician and a
professor of public health.

I.N.P. PHOTO SHOWS:- The Council in progress at the
Ministry of Works today.
At top table, from left to right,
are :-
Mr. B. SANDERCOCK, O.B.E.,
Vice-President of National
Federation of Building Trade
Operatives;
Captain A.M. HOLBEIN, B.Sc, Civil
Engineering Contractor, London;
SIR HAROLD EMMERSON, K.C.B.,
The Chairman, who is Permanent
Secretary Ministry of Works;
SIR GEORGE GATER, Vice-Chairman, who
is Chairman of the Building
Apprenticeship and Training Council;
and SIR CHARLES J. MOLE, Director
General of Works.

Picture by J. Bennett. INTERNATIONAL NEWS PHOTOS.
D/13202.

activity: Skilled oxyacetylene burner James Beveridge cutting up the 15-inch gun barrels of the decommissioned battleship HMS Revenge for scrap at a shipbreaking yard in Inverkeithing.

te.text:
"WARRIORS GRAVEYARD"
MAKES "FOOD" FOR BRITAIN'S STEEL MILLS    DG/PRI

With plans for re-armament under consideration
the shipbreaking yards of THOMAS WARD, Inverkeithing,
Scotland, are working at top speed to cut up
the veterans of two world wars. Hissing oxy-acetylene
torches are carving up such famous ships as
"Royal Sovereign", "Revenge", "Nelson" and "Rodney",
and hundreds of tons of valuable scrap are sent to
the ever-hungry steel mills-perhaps to sail again
in a new warship. For seven months breakers have been
at work on this ship - the REVENGE.
PHOTO SHOWS: Skilled oxyacetylene burner JAMES
BEVERIDGE cuts REVENGE'S 15 inch gun
barrels into "cheeses" for removal as valuable scrap.
Tenth ship to bear her name, she saw service in World
War 11 in the Indian Ocean and the Far East .

men are clearly using their loaf.

activity: copper wheel engraving being performed by Peter Dreiser in a workshop

te.text: COPPER DEVELOPMENT ASSOCIATION   55 South Audley St., London, W.1

for further Information contact:
S.C. BRANDER

GLASS ENGRAVING BY COPPER

One of the few crafts surviving in this age of mass
production, copper wheel engraving, is carried out in a small
workshop in the heart of London's West End.  Mr. Peter Dreiser
of Thomas Goode & Company Glass and China merchants, South
Audley Street, W.l, is one of the few glass engravers in Britain.

The tools of his craft are very simple and have hardly
altered since the times of the Romans.  A small lathe, a spindle
fitted with a copper wheel and some carborundum powder.  Ally
these tools with the sensitive steady hands of a craftsman such
as Mr. Dreiser and a plain piece of glass is transformed into an
item that would grace the sideboard of any stately home.

The copper wheel is the basic item of Mr. Dreiser's equip-
ment; many other metals have been tried, but copper is the only
one with the right degree of hardness and capable of retaining
the cutting agent, carborundum, when the wheel is revolving.

The most remarkable feature of Mr. Dreiser's work is the
amount of detail he can produce in his designs.  Ornate heraldic
coats of arms, animals of every shape and size, buildings and
elaborate floral arrangements are engraved with accuracy and
realism.  Because of the wide range of design he is called upon
to engrave, Mr. Dreiser has a large collection of copper wheels
varying in diameter and gauge.  Apart from his hands these are
the most valuable tools of his craft.

-ENDS-

activity: Margaret Redden, a 19-year-old worker, cutting steel castings with a ferro-gas cutter at a new steel foundry in Scotland.

te.text:
F9172 DH 33 F194-D4
D4
Industry : Iron + Steel Misc

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION SATURDAY'S DAILIES. MAY 23rd.

GIRLS MAKE STEEL TANKS AND SHIPS.
22.5.42.
When the Ministry of Supply decided to open a new
steel foundry in Scotland to meet the demands for
tanks for Russia and plates for ship repairs, it
was discovered that there were not enough men at
hand to work it. Local women and girls, therefore
determined that the running of the new foundry
should be their special war effort, with the
result that they are now doing everything there
except the actual smelting of the iron ore into
steel, They are even learning to to this. The
picture is the first to be taken at the new foundry
and shows MARGARET REDDEN 19-year-old former dairy
assistant, now cuts up steel castings with a ferro-
gas cutter. Censor No. 200213.

[illegible]
ISSUED BY
PHOTOS LTD.
[illegible]
LONDON, E.C.4.

FILE INDUS METALS
IRON + STEEL
MISC

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNHARMED.

activity: Three young girls evacuated from London (Yvonne Bibb, Betty Gibbons, and Vivienne) visiting a local market and a Ministry of Food advice centre in the British countryside during WWII.

te.text: THE CHILDREN SET OFF TO MARKET. MRS. BIBB LIFTS LITTLE VIVIENNE INTO THE FARM CART THAT IS TAKING THEM INTO THE NEAREST TOWN TO DO THE WEEK'S SHOPPING FOR THEIR MOTHERS
THREE LITTLE GIRLS WENT TO MARKET

THE Bibbs and the Gibbonses are two of the
families evacuated from London who have no
wish to return to city life. They love the
country and, as Mrs. Gibbons says: "We wouldn't
like to be restricted to a garden again." They
hope that after the war their husbands will find
jobs that will enable them to stay in the countryside.
Certainly Betty Gibbons and Yvonne Bibb and her
little sister Vivienne, or Vivie as every one calls her,
are fine advertisements for rural upbringing. They
are healthy, they are natural, not shy but at the same
time not precocious. They appreciate the country and
little Vivie loves to pick the flowers, while Betty tells
her to look at the lovely St. Bernard, which is her
name for laburnum.
Vivie is a real country girl, the only one of the three
who is country-born. Yvonne and Betty are both
seven and go to the village school, and will later go on
to the secondary school in the nearby town. Betty's
two older brothers are already there.
The children know that nearby town quite well, for
sometimes they go there to do the shopping for their
mothers. ILLUSTRATED cameraman went with them
one market day and found that the first place they
visit is the Ministry of Food stall in the market place
where they ask for advice about their shopping.
Set up in market places all over the country these
advice centres tell shoppers the correct controlled
prices they should pay for vegetables and other goods.
They tell them point values. They give them counsel
about cooking. They distribute leaflets giving advice
on how to make the most of country produce, carried
In the market places of Britain the
Ministry of Food are setting up head-
quarters where shoppers may get expert
advice. Pictures on these pages show
how Yvonne, Betty and Vivie take
advantage of this service
meals, snacks and sandwiches, vegetable cookery,
cheese dishes and how to make the most of the meat,
all subjects that affect the country folk more perhaps
than they do the city dwellers.
Yvonne, Betty and Vivie enjoy their days at market.
Clutching ration books they peep over the butcher's
counter as if they were very used to it. Even three-year-
old Vivie can hand money across a counter with the
best of them. Yvonne looks after her little sister as
well as tending to the shopping. Betty knows just
what she wants.
The children leave home early, usually going into
town by a farm cart that has to go that way. They
return by bus, clasping baskets laden with all the goods
their mothers want, often including such unrationed
things as tripe or liver that they have been lucky
enough to get from the butcher.
When they arrive home they hand over their baskets

title: A photographic print of Queen Elizabeth II, Opening New Forth Bridge, September, 1964

date_info.rationale: This date appears in multiple Daily Herald rubber stamps, likely indicating the publication date or date of processing in the archive.

activity: Bridge worker Pat McAteer speaking with the Queen during the opening ceremony of the Forth Road Bridge.

te.text:
THOUSANDS of cars were pouring across Scotland's new £20mil- lion road bridge spanning the Firth of Forth last night.
Said bridge-master Robert Wilson: "It's amazing. There must be the whole of Scotland's traffic queueing up to cross."
Traffic was allowed on the bridge at 5.30 p.m after the Queen performed the opening ceremony in the morning.
FOG
Queues of cars stretched back more than two miles on either side.
And in the first hour 6,000 cars — paying 2s. 6d. each — had passed through the six toll booths on the south side.
The 100,000 proud Scots who flocked to see the opening nearly missed it all because of fog.
With visibility down to six yards, plans for an RAF fly-past over the bridge at South Queensferry, West Lothian, were scrapped.
SALUTE
And the Queen's inspection of the bridge from the last of the ferry-boats, Queen Margaret, was threatened.
But suddenly the sun shone for the Queen, chased away the mist and uncovered the 500ft. towers of the engineering marvel.
As the haze lifted 25 flag-decorated ships of the Home Fleet blasted out a 21-gun salute.
The Queen, in royal blue, declared that both the new Road Bridge and the old Forth Railway Bridge represented the latest ideas and techniques of their time.
"They demonstrate that Scotland is not content to rely on past achievements, but is determined to remain among the leaders in all branches of the technology," she went on.
It would benefit the economy of the whole of Scotland.
The Queen, who was with Prince Philip, drove on to the bridge cheered by more than 1,000 spidermen and their families who were lining the 3,300ft. centre span.
FREE BEER
At the north end she set 74-year-old gang boss James McLaughter into a fit of laughter.
He had told her how his men had blasted the ways for the approach roads.
She replied: "A fine thing, at your age, to be blowing up bits of Scotland!"
Then the pipe bands of the 1st. Gordon Highlanders marched across the new bridge from north to south.
Last night South Queensferry, the little fishing village on the south side, was in holiday mood.
Pubs stayed open until midnight. Queues thronged outside the post office for souvenir stamps specially franked for opening day. And a milk bar in Fife, across the Firth, served free beer.
Voice of the Herald — Page 6.
"We built it this way" .. bridge worker Pat McAteer tells the Queen

activity: Miss Eve Cherry spinning wool taken from her pet poodle Marcus into yarn while the dog sits beside her.

te.text:
SPINNING A YARN ......... 12.1.65.
DOG BREEDER MISS. EVE CHERRY OF AYTON ROAD,
IRTON NEAR SCARBOROUGH, HAS FOUND A USE FOR
SPARE POODLE HAIR.
EACH TIME SHE COMBS THE MAGNIFICENT COAT OF HER
70 POUND WHITE POODLE "MARCUS", WHO LOOKS
LIKE LENNIE THE LION, SHE SAVES THE HAIR......AND
LATER ON A SWEDISH SPINNING WHEEL SPINS IT INTO
YARN TO MAKE SCARVES, GLOVES BEDSOCKS AND EVEN
EVENING DRESS STOLES.
MISS CHERRY, WHO BREEDS CHIHUAHUAS, HAS EVEN
SPUN YARN FROM THE SPARE COAT HAIR OF THESE TINY
DOGS. THE AUTHOR OF AN AUTHORITATIVE BOOK ON
HANDWEAVING SHE SAYS :" I FOUND THAT POODLE WOOL WAS
EVEN BETTER THAN MANY OTHER FIBRES TO TURN INTO YARN.
IT HAS SUCH A SOFT FINISH. I SPIN WHILE WATCHING
TELEVISION. IT'S INTRIGUING".
SAID 25-YEAR-OLD BLONDE-HAIRED BUNTY RUFFELL
OF SCARBOROUGH, WEARING ONE OF MISS CHERRY'S
STOLES, "NO MORE EXPENSE OF WINTER WOLLIES NOW. I'VE
GOT A POODLE MYSELF CALLED RICK! WHO I'M QUITE SURE
CAN PRODUCE THE GOODS.
PHOTO SHOWS:

       MISS EVE CHERRY, WITH HER PET POODLE
MARCUS BY HER SIDE, SPINNING THE WOOL TAKEN
OFF HER PET.

                 H1316
Industry - Textiles - Wool - NOT Sheep. Dogs, etc.

activity: Mr. Herbert picking mushrooms in a disused railway tunnel near Monmouth

te.text:
MONMOUTH . H/86

A NEW USE FOR RAILWAY TUNNELS .

Two Monmouth men, Mr. J.G. Herbert and Mr. G.B. Jakeway,
have started a novel venture by renting tunnels on a
disused branch of the G.W.R. near Monmouth for the growing
of mushrooms on an extensive scale. The dark damp tunnels
which maintain an even temperature are ideally suited for
the work. At present one 250 yards tunnel has been boarded
at the ends and contains about half a mile of mushroom beds.

Photo shows - Mr. Herbert, one of the partners picking
mushrooms in the tunnel near Monmouth.

TITHE " WAR " MEMORIAL IN SUFFOLK

A stonemason is building a cruious monument on the farm
of Mr. and Mrs. R.H. Rash at Wortham, near Diss, Suffolk.

" war " . It will be unveiled next Friday the anniversary
of the seizure of many cattle and pigs under the protection
of a large force of police. On this spot a deep trench was dug
and barbed wire barriers erected.

showing where the barbed wire barriers were erected.

te.text:
NEW FAMILY CAR IN PRODUCTION.

A new family car, the Standard Eight, is now in production
at the Canley, Coventry factory of the Standard Motor Company
Limited. Motorists and experts alike have greeted this
new "baby" car with an enthusiasm which has not been
accorded to a new car for many years, for this latest
model will provide comfort and economy at a price within the
means of the average person. The main features of the new
Standard Eight are that it is capable of over 60 miles per
hour, with a fuel consumption of 45 to 50 miles a gallon
at cruising speeds; it will seat four in comfort; has four
doors for easy access; ample accomodation for luggage and
it's compact overall dimensions make it easy to park in
confined spaces and easy to garage. This new model
will be on Show to the general public at the forthcoming
Motor Show which opens in London on October 21st.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS:  The "finished" end of the 8 h.p.
Standard production line at the Canley, Coventry factory
of The Standard Motor Company, Ltd., where this new "baby"
car is already coming off the assembly lines in volume
production to meet orders pouring in from all parts of the
world.

It has taken the Women's Land Army to find out
that Miss Littler, a volunteer in the employment
of the Flintshire War Agricultural Executive
Committee, possesses the gift of water divining.
Miss Littler joined the Women's Land Army March
1941 and is one of 9 girls employed on gang work.
Recently they were working on a piece of land which
was constantly being flooded by a hidden spring.
Mr.J.T.Richards, the Executive Officer of the
Flintshire War Agricultural Executive Committee,had
made extensive efforts to have the spring located.
Finally, he asked the 9 members of the Women's Land
Army, who were clearing the land, to try with a
hazel stick to see if they could divine this spring.
Miss Littler was found to be the only one who
possesses this unusual gift.
Since Flintshire farmers have heard of this there
have been many requests for her services,to help
in reclaiming flooded land and so save hundreds
of pounds in drainage. Also farmers wish to use
her to help to discover water for sinking wells.
O.P.S.1. The first step to becoming a Dowser is
to cut a forked twig from a hazel tree.
Miss Littler who is 19 years of age is seen on
right.

te.text:
"DIGGING FOR VICTORY"-- FOR COAL.

IT IS REALISED THAT COAL FORMS ONE OF THE
MOST IMPORTANT ARTICLES, FOR CARRYING ON A WAR, AND
THIS COUNTRY IS, LUCKILY ENOUGH, WELL SUPPLIED WITH
THIS IMPORTANT ITEM. THE WAR HAS BROUGHT THE MINER
INTO HIS OWN, THEIR LOT BEING MUCH BETTER THAT A FEW
YEARS AGO - PAY IS BETTER HOUSING IS BETTER-AND AN EVER
INCREASING BATTLE IS BEING WAGED IN THE LABORATORIES
TO MAKE THE JOB SAFER THAN EVER BEFORE. THE MEN OF THE
ARMY, NAVY AND AIR FORCE CONSTANTLY RECEIVE ACCLAIMATION
FOR THEIR GREAT WORK, BUT THE MINER, WHO IS JUST AS
ESSENTIAL, MUST NOT BE FORGOTTEN.

O.P.S. A MINER IN THE FOREST OF DEAN, USES THE MODERN
"AGROTONE" BATH AFTER COMING UP FROM THE MINE.
THE BATH IS ONE OF THE FEW IN THE COUNTRY WHICH
WAS PAID FOR BY THE MINERS AND INSTALLED AT A
COST OF £700 BY THE MINE OWNERS. IT IS A STEEL
CYLINDER, FIVE FEET DEEP, INSIDE WHICH IS A STEEL
SEAT. WATER IS SENT INTO IT BY MEANS OF SMALL JETS
AND IT IS AERATED. TEMPERATURE AND PRESSURE CAN BE
CONTROLLED . THE BATH IS ONE OF THE FINEST
PREVENTATIVE AND CURE FOR RHEUMATISM - A COMMON
COMPLAINT WITH MINERS.

PROPERTY OF

GERMANS HELPING TO BOOST BRITAIN'S COAL
OUTPUT: SINKING NEW SHAFTS IN WALES
March 31st 1954 PAR 41090-2 (PNR-R)

GERMANS HELPING TO BOOST BRITAIN'S COAL
OUTPUT: SINKING NEW SHAFTS IN WALES
A little bit of Western Germany has been
set down among the coal dumps of
South Wales.
Nearly 200 German mining experts are
now working there. They are sinking
two steel-and-concrete shafts, 2,000 feet
deep, for the National Coal Board's new
£7,500,000 colliery at Cynheidre.
The mine is expected to yield a million
tons a year of anthracite, one of
Britain's most valuable export commodities.
Germans were called in to do the job
because all British shaft-sinking
equipment was in use.
The Coal Board has estimated that the work
will take two years. But the Germans
themselves expect to do it in a much
shorter time.
PICTURE SHOWS:- HEINRICH KOSCHINSKI,
one of the German workers, operating the
levers of a winding machine on the
Cynheidre site.
March 31st 1954 PAR 41090-2 (PNR-R)
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION IN MORNING
PAPERS OF THURSDAY, APRIL 1st.
INDUS FUEL + POWER - COAL - PITS WELSH

te.text:
DEMAND FOR STEEL MEANS DEMAND FOR COKE
7.9.36.
The present demand for steel in the heavy industries caused by
the increase of armaments and shipbuilding gives interest to
the remarkable photographs taken at the new Coke oven plant
of the United Steel Companies at Workington, Cumberland, where
the fuel is produced to supply the needs of the combine. The plant
comprises a battery of 53 Woodhall-Duckham Becker coke ovens with
electrically-driven machinery for charging the ovens and discharging
the coke, and mechanical equipment for handling and preparing the
coal for carbonisation and for handling, quenching, cooling and
grading the coke. Tar, Ammonia and crude benzole are produced
the sale of these by-products contributing towards lower
manufacturing cost of the coke. The picture shows
the beautiful clouds of steam which emerge from the
quenching station as water descends on the glowing coke on
conveyer below.

PHOTOGRAPH BY
CENTRAL PRESS PHOTOS LTD.
INCORPORATING
Central News Illustrations Service,
119, Fleet Street, LONDON, E.C. 4.

activity: production of 'man-made lumber' (compressed sawdust bonded with resin) using high frequency radio waves at a research centre

te.text:
174891 LUD
BRITAIN CAN ROLL OUT 'MAN-MADE LUMBER' IN ANY LENGTH.

London:  'Man-made lumber' - compressed sawdust
bonded with resin - rolls from the machine
at the Camden Town (North West London) research
centre of the British Artificial Resin Company,
which - with the aid of high frequency radio waves,
infra-red heat, and electro-magnetic vibrations has
solved the problem of making this board in any
length.
Leading plastics scientists and teams of research
workers have been working ten years on the problem
of increasing the versatility of the board-making
plant. Previously, the board could be pressed out
only within certain sizes.
Now sawdust and resin are fed into a hopper, mixed,
heated by radio waves then passed under pressure with
the temperature maintained by infra-red waves.
The board produced is used for building, making
furniture and has applications in  shipping, road
rail and air transport. Negotiations are proceeding
for the sale of plant to     other countries,
involving amounts totalling £1½ million sterling.
It is estimated exports should earn over £3 million
sterling each year.
         September 16th 1948  PN.g.  US SK PAR

COPYRIGHT.
PLANET NEWS LTD

activity: Miss Freda Mason and her sister Ellen waiting under an improvised shelter at South Birtley colliery where seven miners are entombed.

te.text:
MINERS ENTOMBED AT SOUTH BIRTLEY COLLIERY. 14.3.51.
Rescue workers who have been hacking
their way through a wall of mud to seven miners
entombed in a small drift colliery at South
Birtley, Co. Durham, today made a small hole
in the remaining clay obstruction and passed
food and drink to the trapped men. The men
have been entombed for 20 hours.
PHOTO SHOWS:- MISS FREDA MASON (right),
fiancee of one of the trapped men, Thomas
Hook, waiting with her sister, ELLEN, under
an improvised shelter. They had been
there all night.
H/Keystone. 825/573230

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
RECD. 15 MAR 1951
PLEASE RETURN

activity: Bevin boys settling down to work and training at a colliery in Kent

te.text:
MINISTRY OF INFORMATION
BRITISH OFFICIAL
PHOTOGRAPH NO.

BRITISH OFFICIAL PHOTOGRAPH: DISTRIBUTED BY THE MINISTRY OF
INFORMATION.

BEVIN BOYS.
At collieries all over the country, the Bevin boy is settling down
to work.  In Kent, at a colliery near Canterbury which is also a
training centre, Bevin boys start work at 7 a.m.  At that hour they
begin their shifts in the mine which lasts until 10:30.  At 10:30
they come up to the pithead, and after a bath and change of clothes,
have an hours break for dinner in the colliery canteen.  After
that they attend a P.T. class and a lecture, then at 3 p.m., they
go back to their billet for tea and the rest of the day is their
own.  Trainees receive a weekly wage of £3, and there is no
deductions during the training period.  For the 1st week they are
given a settling in allowance of 24s. 6d.

activity: crowds gathered outside Ely Cathedral for a ceremony to proclaim Queen Elizabeth II

te.text:
228264   OCK

ELIZABETH PROCLAIMED AT ELY - AFTER ANCIENT
CITY INSISTED ON RIGHTS.

Isle of Ely: Crowds gathered outside Ely Cathedral
during a special ceremony held to proclaim Queen
Elizabeth II.
Other parts of Britain held their proclamations
over a month ago, but Ely, where Kings and Queens
for centuries have been proclaimed, was passed over
in favour of March, the seat of the Isle of Ely
Council some 20 miles away. Protests followed, for
March is regarded by citizens of ancient Ely as a
mere "mushroom" market town and railroad junction.
Ely felt it had been slighted when the proclamation
was read at March, so to-day the special ceremony
was held to make amends.
15th March, 1952   PN-d.

RCD. 17 MAR 1952
PLEASE RETURN

in Denmark from room-sized concrete units pre- cast
in Norwich. The units were transported to Woolwich where

position - after which plumbing - cupboards - doors etc.
are set..

activity: women breaking and processing eggs at the N. Reich & Co. factory in Stepney

te.text:
RON BURTON   SUN   29.4.65
THEY BREAK HALF A MILLION EGGS PER DAY.
At Reich & Co. in the East End women are employed to break as many as
hald a million eggs a day.   The company provide egg fluid to bakeries.

By JENNY REES
AUBURN-HAIRED
Shirley Griffiths went
to work on an egg yester-
day. Or, to be precise,
6,000 eggs.
For 29-year-old Shirley,
married to a Stepney
lighterman, is what is
known as a "breaker" in
the liquid and processed egg
business.
Every day Shirley
smashes 15 to 20 white,
brown or speckled eggs a
minute, for six hours.
For this she gets 4s. an
hour, plus a production
bonus. In a good week she
can take home £12.
Shirley works for N.
Reich, a Stepney firm who
break and process half a
million surplus eggs a day
for the Egg Marketing
Board.
The result — 5,000 to
6,000 gallons of pasteurised
liquid eggs — goes to Lon-
don's large bakeries for use
in cakes.
It could be called an
exclusive job. Applicants
have to pass strict tests for
cleanliness — and smelling
ability.
Said the firm's technical
director, Mr. Peter Win-
bolt: "It is definitely a
woman's job. Men are not
nimble enough." The firm
employ about 25 to 50
women, depending on the
FAST WORK — WITH SPECIAL EGG-CRACKING DRUMS
season, and they work in a
spotless, white-tiled room.
The eggs are broken and
emptied into a small tray,
then examined for smell
and condition, before being
emptied into bowls.
Top breaker is Mrs. Emily
Stannard, 55-year-old
mother of four.
She has been breaking
eggs for five years, and gets
through 1,300 an hour.
The women are intro-
duced to the job by super-
visor Mrs. Elizabeth Shire,
who has been working at
the plant for 17 years.
"Some women learn to
break eggs within minutes,"
she said. "The secret is to
grip the egg lightly — and to
make a clean break."

LONDON NEWS AGENCY PHOTOS LTD
PHOTO SUPPLIED BY
L.N.A.
TEL: CENTRAL 6521
46, FLEET STREET, LONDON, E.C.4.

ISSUED 18-11-32. SUPPLIED LNA

AMAZING SCENES AT DAGENHAM
POLICE FORCE ADMITTANCE TO HOUSE

      Police and bailliffs forced
an entry into the Dagenham house
this morning (Friday) which was barricaded
yesterday. 
      The occupant is stated to be
a war widow with six children, and
a number of men had made an expert
preparation for a siege, 

      ...shows policemen removing
the men into the garden.
      The centre constable
was badly injured in the head and
collapsed shortly after this
picture was taken.
      The widow, is seen lying
on ground on left.

te.text:
Saidman  ILL.  1/11/45
Welsh Girls train in London for new Industry.
25 Girls from Wales have arrived in London.
where they will train for three months in electric
bulb factories in Tottenham and Edmonton. Later
they will return to Merthyr to staff the new
factory which is being opened up as part of the
big scheme for the rehabilitation of the old
distressed areas.
3.)  Following their arrival and civic reception
the girls were entertained to tea. The
Mayors of Merthyr, Edmonton, and Tottenham give
a hand at tea.

activity: Members of a Medical Reclassification Board and a psychiatrist interviewing soldiers at a U.S. Replacement Camp dispensary.

te.text:
SAIDMAN (ILLUS)        6.12.43
U.S. REPLACEMENT CAMP.
OPS.7. Not only shipments from the States, but men
restored to active duty by General and Convalescent
hospitals, apprehended absentees, dental cripples,
and men no longer physically capable of fulfilling
their former duties, all meet here in the Depot
dispensary, with men turned up during lastnight's
medical inspection of the new shipment. Once an
individual record, independent of his previous
medical history, is initiated by the clerk, the
soldier is first interviewed by Capt. Daniel C.
Dawes, M.C., psychiatrist of the Depot Dispensary
Staff. Then man and form go separately before
each member of the Medical Reclassification Board.
Members of the board are found in the crowded
waiting room, [red strikethrough] where Capt. Dawes conducts his inter-
views. [/red strikethrough] Capt. Kenneth G. Burton, M.C., of Providence,
Rhode Island, is at left against door. Capt. Dawes,
of Boston, Mass., Lt. Adney K. Sutphin, M.C., of
Beckley, W.Va., Capt. Rudolph E. Warnecke, M.C.,
Depot Surgeon, (back to camera) of West Barrington,
Rhode Island, and Capt. R. H. Brown, M.C., of Kingsport,
Tenn.

te.text: Indus. Fuel + Power - OIL - From Seabed

FIRST BRITISH-BUILT OIL-DRILLING PLATFORM
ON 9,200-MILE TOW
February 21st 1959 PAR 75862-3 (PNR-R)
------------------------------------------------
FIRST BRITISH-BUILT OIL-DRILLING PLATFORM
ON 9,200-MILE TOW

Pictured from the air after leaving
Southampton towed by the tug THAMES (right)
to-day, Saturday, is the ORIENT EXPLORER,
the first mobile oil drilling platform to
be built in the United Kingdom.
It is to be towed, via Suez, a distance of
9,200 miles to British Borneo and, on hire
to the Brunei Shell Petroleum Company, will
be used to drill for oil in the bed of the
South China Sea.
The platform, which contains 3,000 tons of
steel and cost nearly £1 million, is fitted
with a helicopter landing stage and has
been constructed to withstand a wind force
of 100 miles an hour.
It has air-conditioned living accommodation
for 56 men, who will be ferried to and from
the mainland of Borneo by helicopter.
February 21st 1959 PAR 75862-3 (PNR-R)

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
23 FEB 1959
PLEASE RETURN
TO

PENZANCE, Friday.
THE egg that Biddy the hen

trict

Thompson says Biddy probably
has an ailment which affects
the shell-making "mechanism."

activity: Soldering a stained glass panel for St. Stephen's, Houses of Parliament, at John Hardman and Company's works in Birmingham.

te.text:
"THE PRIDE OF CRAFTSMANSHIP."
168404.(CHI). BIRMINGHAM STUDIOS RESTORING STAINED GLASS
FOR HOUSES OF PARLIAMENT.

BIRMINGHAM, ENG; A century ago, John Hardman, influenced by
the then foremost British architect Augustus Welby Pugin,
and urged by his son following the halting by the French
revolution of the import of religious articles from the
Continent, opened at Newhall Hill, here, a metal and glass
works to carry out Pugin's designs, laying the foundations
for a stained glass industry in this Warwickshire city.
To-day the studios employ descendents of the original
craftsmen employed by the first John Hardman, where hands
unaided by machines, except the cutting diamond and the
kiln, create the stained glass windows that lend dignity
to some of the most famous buildings in Britain, the
Commonwealth and the United States of America.
PHOTO SHOWS:- Soldering a panel for St. Stephen's,
Westminster, London, (the Houses of Parliament) at John
Hardman and Company's works at Newhall Hill.
Foreground is Mr Albert Langford, of Birmingham, aged 34,
who has been with the firm for twenty years.
Leading lights in background is Mr Stanley Robinson,
who has just completed 21 years in the trade.
24th March, 1948. PN-s. (List - 4.)

COPYRIGHT
PLANET NEWS LTD.
3 - JOHNSON'S COURT
FLEET STREET
LONDON - E.C.4.
TEL. CENTRAL 3671/2783

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY

activity: overloaded cargo sheds at London's Heathrow airport stacked with imports awaiting deposit payment due to new government controls

te.text:
DAILY HERALD
PLEASE RETURN TO
ART LIBRARY

THE scene is a cargo shed
at London's Heathrow
airport. From ceiling to
floor the shed is stacked
with imports. Three other
huge sheds at the airport
are also full. For 10 days
British European Airways,
the largest carriers of
freight into Britain, have
had to stop flying goods to
Heathrow. There is simply
nowhere left to put
them. The main reason
for the jam is the
Government's new import
controls. Importers have
to deposit half the value
of the imports before the
goods are allowed past the
Customs and into the
shops. The additional
paperwork accounts for
part of the delay. But in
some cases importers
simply haven't been able
to raise the money to pay
the deposit. Until the
money is found the goods
will have to remain at
Heathrow, or be returned
to their country of origin,
or perish.

SUN WARNER 31-12-68
B.E.A. Import Cargo sheds overloaded with goods awaiting deposit payment
O.P.S. Scene at B.E.A. import sheds.

I am always asked: What are workers 
at Fords really like? People assume 
that they are a different species from any

in industry. Some are mean, some kindly, 
some tough, some meek.

the workers AND the management.

te.text:
Esten      D.H.        18.6.43
Army Beats the U Boats. Not To Be Published Before
0030 Hrs. Monday 21st June 1943 .
The word waste is now taboo in the Army who are out
to beat the U Boat in their Salvage of Equipment Depot.
Everything that had been previously regarded as waste
is now returned to the Returned Stores Depot for
reclamation. This Depot has achieved remarkable results.
The following figures represent some of the stores
which are repaired in Returned Stores Depots in the
United Kingdom over a period of 12 months. They should
prove of great interest to the public, and should act
as a stimulant and help them to realise how the Army
is safe-guarding their interests:-
Tents enough to house the entire Army in the United
Kingdom
Dinner plates enough to supply the First Army
Steel Helmets enough to supply the whole of the A.T.S.
Respirators enough to supply all Canadian Forces
Suits of Battle Dress enough to clothe one half of the
Home Guard
Beds enough to supply one half of the A.T.S.
Food Containers enough to supply five Armoured Corps
Web Equipment One and a quarter millions of pieces
repaired
Stoves over thirty thousand repaired
Shovels and Spades 36,000 repaired
Slicing and Mincing machines 9,600 repaired
Hand Fire Pumps 20,000 repaired
Hurricane Lamps 60,000 repaired
Chairs and Forms 96,000 repaired
Blankets 420,000 repaired
Ground Sheets 174,000 repaired
Woollen Drawers 192,000 repaired
Woollen Vests 96,000 repaired
Shirts 60,000 repaired

back into stores for issue.

activity: Farmers Bernard Roe and Clyde Higgs examining grain in a barn being dried by a Trojan airator method in sack tunnels during a wet summer.

te.text:
INDUS- AGRIC. GRAIN - RUINED BY WEATHER ETC.
PERSONAL +

LN 360467  SKI  LONDON BUREAU
FARMER BEATS THE ENGLISH "SUMMER."
BROADCHALKE, HANTS:  FARMER BERNARD ROE, (LEFT) OF HUT
AND LODGE FARM, AND THE WELL-KNOWN FARMING PERSONALITY
CLYDE HIGGS, WHO FARMS ON A BIG SCALE IN WILTSHIRE,
WARWICKSHIRE AND TANGANYIKA, EXAMINE SOME OF THE GRAIN
IN FARMER ROE'S BARN, WHICH HAS BEEN DRIED, DESPITE THE WET
SUMMER, BY A NEW AIRATOR METHOD, IN SACK TUNNELS.  FARMER
ROE HAS 240 ACRES OF BARLEY, AND HERE PART OF HIS FIVE 30-TON
GRAIN-SACK TUNNELS IS SHOWN COUPLED TO THE AIRATOR WHICH IS BLOWING
HOT AND COLD AIR INTO IT; IT HAS TAKEN THE AIRATOR 100 HOURS TO
REDUCE THE MOISTURE CONTENT FROM 27-PERCENT TO 16-PERCENT,
THE SAFE STORAGE MINIMUM.  OTHER FARMERS IN THE DISTRICT
HAVE NOT BEGUN TO HARVEST-MR ROE HAS GOT IN 120 TONS.
THE AIRATOR MEANS THAT FARMERS NEED ONLY WAIT UNTIL THE
STRAW IS DRY ENOUGH TO CUT; THE AIRATOR DOES THE REST, SAVING
MONEY AND TIME AND LABOUR—EACH BAG IS MANHANDLED ONCE,
INSTEAD OF THREE TIMES.  IT IS TOO LATE THIS YEAR TO SAVE MILLIONS
OF TONS OF GRAIN AND HAY, BUT NEXT YEAR THE AIRATOR COULD SAVE
THE FORTUNES OF FARMERS THROUGHOUT THE COUNTRY.  THE AIRATOR
IS EXTREMELY MOBILE, AND CHEAP TO RUN ON DIESEL FUEL.  IT CAN
ALSO BE COUPLED TO VINTILATED BINS, SILOS, OR GRAIN-SACK PLATFORMS.
AND IT CAN ALSO BE USED AS A POWER UNIT, THE AIRATOR IS
MADE BY TROJAN-AN APT NAME FOR THIS HARD-WORKING MACHINE.
AUGUST 30TH 1958 PN-JJ

BOUVERIE STREET,
LONDON, E.C.4.
PHONE:- FLE. 3671/2/3.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY
1 SEP 1958

te.text:
MURPHY.   SUN.   19.12.67.   STORY DAVISON.
Marine Band plays out Aspro Nicolas Conference at the Mayfair Hotel.
Girls have banners - Aspro, Biotex and Rennies, etc.

PROPERTY OF
SUN
20 DEC 1967
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

THE SCENE is at the conclusion
of a sales conference of the
people who make Aspro, Rennies,
Radox, Lifebuoy and Biotex for a
world market. Girls in swimsuits
parade buoyantly wearing sashes
bearing the names of the firm's
products. The Band of the Royal
Marines, hired for £163, play with
fervour 'Hey, Look Me Over.' It
is a sight to swell the hearts of
the 175 salesmen at the end of
their two-day hard-sell never-
take - no - for - an - answer sales
conference. The Ministry of
Defence were not so pleased. An
official said: "I don't think we
would look too favourably on one
of our bands getting mixed up
with this kind of thing." Don't
the Ministry people give you a
pain? In the name of exports,
isn't it enough to make you reach
for an Aspro, or even a Rennie?

te.text:
THE OLDEST OF THEM ALL.
GK/7262-12. In spite of his 84 years, there is still
strength and skill left in his hands. He is John Beddow,
aged 84, and oldest worker in "The Sons of Rest". John has
been with the company for 41 years and before joining the
veterans, was a furnace worker.

THE OLD FOLK OF INDUSTRY.
GK/7262. Seeking to prove a man is "not too old at 70"
is the engineering firm of Rubery, Owen and Co., of Darlaston,
Staffs who have started an "Old Folks Workshop" which they
call "Sons of Rest". Situated about a mile away from the
noise and bustle of the main factory, twelve men, all over
the age of 70 work on their own with no young workers beside
them to give them an inferiority complex over their ages.
The veterans start an hour later than the main factory. They
do drilling and assembly work on office equipment and farm
implements for overseas markets. The experiment has been
going on for 10 months and has proved a great success. Doctors
who are urging more active employment for elderly people for
the benefit of their health support it. It is also a means
of saving for industry skilled hands vitally necessary these
days, which would otherwise be lying idle.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
RCD. 2 - MAY 1951
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

DAILY HERALD

FLEET ST. LONDON, E.C.4

activity: Mr. William Brett, a village cobbler, at work in his shop in Wonersh making a pair of gold-embossed shoes for the Pope.

te.text:
ENGLI SH VILLAGE COBBLER MAKES SHOES FOR THE POPE.

An Englishman makes the Pope's shoes.
He is Mr. William Brett, the village cobbler at
Wonersh, near Guildford, Surrey.
One day, Dr.Banfield, of the Roman Catholic seminary
in the village, asked Mr. Brett if he would make
some shoes for the Pope. The shoes had to be of
special design like a monk's, but with two straps.
The seams were inlaid with gold braid and the heel
was covered in gold. A gold cross was inlaid
in the toe-cap.
All the embroidery work was also done in the village.
Mr. Brett's family have been shoemakers at
Wonersh for nearly 200 years.
PHOTO SHOWS - Mr. William Brett at work in his
shop at Wonersh, Surrey.
AND January 13th 1938 PN.r.

COPYRIGHT
PLANET NEWS LTD
3, JOHNSON'S COURT,
LONDON, E.C. 4.

activity: Oil search at Formby, showing drilling superintendent John Gibson with earth sample boxes brought up from a boring.

te.text:
THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

D H White   13/7/49

Oil search at Formby

13 / Supt, of the Drilling operations
     is John Gibson seen here with sample
     boxes of earth brought up from every
     5ft of boring

SEARCH FOR OIL IN LANCASHIRE.
Somewhere beneath the sand-dunes of the Lancashire
[illegible strikeout] coast, seven miles from Southport, lies a huge
untapped supply of oil.
Sixteen engineers who have just sunk a bore hole hope
to find it before their instruments register 7,500 ft.
They cannot go any deeper than that with their present
equipment and if they have not found it at that depth
they will try somewhere else.
An official at the D'Arcy Exploration Co, who is doing
the work, said "for ten years we have been getting 400
tons of oil a year from eight 'surface wells' at
Formby, but those wells are only 100 ft deep and we are
confident that a large oilfield, much deeper is
supplying them".
They tried three times before at Scarisbrick and
Bickerstaffe, but although they went down to 7,600 ft
they could not find the source.
Pointing to a thick, pinky fluid oozing out of a large
pipe alongside the towering derrick on the new site,
John Gibson the drilling superintendant explained
"that is the circulating mud which we pour down the
centre of the drill pipe, It seeps through the drilling
bit and brings up the small pieces of rock formation".
After the formation has been sieved out, the mud goes
back down the drill pipe.

te.text:
18.12.63.
NEW COAL DISTRIBUTION CENTRE OPENED AT WEST DRAYTON.
MR. RICHARD WOOD, former Minister of Fuel and Power,
today opened a coal depot at West Drayton. The depot is
the first to instrument a new system of coal
distribution that has been worked out by LORD ROBENS,
Chairman of the Coal Board, DR. BEECHING, Chairman of
British Railways, and the Coal Merchants Federation.
Instead of the coal being brought from the collieries to
railway sidings for collection by merchants, it will
in future be carried in block trains and concentrated
in these large depots which will serve areas in London
and other large cities. The West Drayton depot takes
the place of 22 small depots within an eight mile radius.
PHOTO SHOWS.
A view of the hoppers where the coal
merchants fill and load the coal.
KT REID JW/764306

From the Public Relations Division of:

WOOD & WEBSTER LTD., ACME CHAMBERS, BRADFORD ST., WALSALL.

Telephone: Walsall 21618 (3 lines)
Written by ............
Publication Date ............

HOUSING DEVELOPMENT & CONSTRUCTION LTD.

PROTOTYPE HOUSES BUILT IN THREE WEEKS

The prototype of a new system of industrialised house
building has just been completed by Housing Development &
Construction Ltd. at Stratford-upon-Avon. It is a pair of
semi-detached, three bedroomed houses, designed and built
to the full Parker-Morris Committee Recommendations, and
to the specification of the local authority Stratford-upon-Avon
M.B. It only required three weeks of normal working with
a very small team of men to complete this pair of houses
for occupation. This is undoubtedly the fastest erection
time of any system of truly permanent housing for local
authorities yet developed.

Progress Picture Shows:

Close-up of a corner of the semi-detached pair of houses
showing the pre-cast reinforced concrete perimeter ring
beams being set upon the specially designed foundations.

te.text:
IN every big city of Britain last night squads of
hastily mobilised police were guarding power
stations, gasworks and reservoirs.
Urgent warning had been flashed to them from
Scotland Yard following a series of mysterious
bomb outrages in London, Enfield, Birmingham,
Manchester, Liverpool, Alnwick and Belfast.
Thirty detectives were sent to guard one power station
alone—that at Willesden, N.W. Liverpool’s nine miles of
docks were closely patrolled. Thames police watched the
river between Woolwich Arsenal and Barking power station.
Enfield Small Arms factory was under guard.
The outrages, Scotland Yard believes, are the work of
terrorist emissaries of the outlawed Irish Republican Army.

activity: The Mitchell-Hedges Trophy, a solid silver oval bowl for the National Coal Output Competition.

te.text:
The Mitchell-Hedges Trophy, to be
presented to the winning Division in
the National Coal Output Competition,
is a solid silver oval bowl, weighing
nearly one hundredweight, 27 inches
across and two feet high. It was
designed by John Flaxman, R.A.,
designer to George III, and was made
by Craftsman Paul Storr in 1815 - the date
of Waterloo. The citizens of Denbigh,
North Wales, presented the trophy to
Sir Watkin Williams Wynn, Bart. for
his military prowess.

The trophy was presented to
the mining industry by the Explorer,
Mr. F.A. Mitchell-Hedges.

The inscription in Welsh may
be translated as:

"This silver bowl in praise of
his military feats was presented
to the sweet and gentle Welshman, Sir
Watkin, foremost man of our land, in
salutation of him, and that his memory
may be cherished."

"An ever present help to the
Crown in the day of need was the
manly Sir Watkin - perfect knight in
the foremost line of descent, dear to
his country and his King".

BRITAIN'S FIRST BALLOON-SHAPED GASOMETER
BEING TESTED ON CANVEY ISLAND.

Britain's first balloon-shaped
gasometer is being tested on Canvey
Island (Essex).
It is designed to offer less resistance
to high winds, and if satisfactory
more of the same type will be built
in other parts of the country.
The gasometer is 45-feet in diameter
with a capacity of 500,000 cubic feet.
It has walls three-quarters of an inch
thick and will work at a pressure
of 50 pounds to the square inch.
PHOTO SHOWS:- Britain's first
balloon-shaped gasometer on Canvey Island.
CLEM July 3rd 1936 P.T.

activity: five typists from Colt Heating and Ventilation volunteering to work extra unpaid hours to assist the national economy

te.text:
FIVE TYPISTS [illegible] their firm yesterday that they would work an extra two and a half hours a week without pay to help Britain's financial position.
Within an hour all their 235 colleagues had volunteered to work the extra time too.
So from Monday the staff at the head office of Colt Heating and Ventilation in Surbiton, Surrey, will start at 8.30 am. each day instead of nine.
Several of the 500 workers at the firm's main factory in Havant, Hants., want to do the same, but they will have to get the approval of the Amalgamated Engineering Union.
Way to wealth
The work-harder move was made in response to a staff memo put out by Mr. Fred Price, the firm's marketing director.
The memo said that if everyone in Britain put in an extra unpaid half-day a week "our balance of payments problem would disappear overnight and very quickly we should once more become the wealthiest country in the world."
The five typists—Valerie White, aged 21, Joan Southwell, 20, Christine French, 17, Carol Fry, 16, and Brenda Mumford, 15, sent a memo back.
It said: "Let us be the first company to start the ball rolling."
The five girls, who earn around £10 a week and type an average of 100 orders daily, think they will manage an extra five orders a day in the extra half-hour.
Fabulous
Colt Heating and Ventilation, annual turnover £3-million, export 30 per cent. of their production.
Mr. Alan O'Hea, the firm's 41-year-old joint managing director, described the idea as "the most fabulous I could imagine." He added: "All the management will be at their desks with them at 8.30 am.
"At Havant we will have to wait for the A.E.U. If they decided to stand in the way that is the end of the matter as far as the factory is concerned."
At the AEU head office in London I was told last night: "There is no one here to make a comment. Everyone is on holiday until Tuesday."
er volunteers (from left): Brenda, Christine, Valerie, Joan and Carol

Copyright: Syndication International
27 Floral Street, London, WC2

activity: the frozen food industry, specifically the promotion of frozen chips and peas

te.text:
DAILY
HERALD
RECEIVED
17 MAY 1962
ART LIBRARY

by BARBARA JEFFERY
LOOK out for a big sales war to get
you to eat frozen chips. Last year
£72million was spent on frozen
foods in Britain. But this is still less
than 2½d. in the £ of our total food
bill.
The frozen food firms believe that they
can double these figures. And they are
banking on the potato to do the trick.
So far peas are the runaway best-seller
in the frozen food market, accounting for
a third of the takings. Sales are still
increasing but there is a feeling in some
sections of the trade that saturation point
may not be far off.
What the industry need is another
basic food that can be promoted as peas
have been. And they think that frozen
potatoes — especially frozen chips — are
the answer.

activity: Miss Margaret Hornby trying out the first computerised homes-for-sale register at Plantation House

te.text:
3-1-68
HOUSE-HUNTING....BY COMPUTER.....

     The first ever computerised homes-for-
sale register is being made available to the public
from tomorrow -Thursday 4th. January. 1968.. With
32,000 houses and flats, valued at more than
£100,000,000 already programmed on the computer,
it is believed to be the largest and most comprehensive
single register of residential properties for sale
ever assembled at one central source. The service
is the brainchild of Homeseekers Computer Services of
7. Buckingham Gate, and initially covers properties
in the Great London Area; and 11 surrounding counties-
Bedfordshire; Hertfordshire; Berkshire; Buckinghamshire;
Essex; Hampshire; Kent; Middlesex ;Oxfordshire; Sussex
and Surrey. Three hundred and forty Estate Agents are
participating. Details of their properties are fed into
the computer. Househunters give details of their
requirements. These details are fed into the computer
and the applicant receives in the post information
on the ten properties most closely corresponding to
his requirements. The computer is an I.C.T. 1900
series owned by Assets Computer Services Ltd..

KEYSTONE PHOTO SHOWS:- MISS MARGARET HORNBY, a
director and Secretary of the Company - with the
questions ..and answers.. as she tries out the first
computerised homes-for-sale register, at Plantation
House, Mincing Lane, this afternoon.
          JSS/KEYSTONE      C/13239-2. /4

CENTRAL OFFICE OF INFORMATION PHOTO GRAPH :

NEW JOBS FOR THE RHONDDA.

(See Feature Set Intro. No. 251).

New jobs have come to the Rhondda as 23 new factories
have been opened in the valley. During the depression
of the 1930's there was one collier to every 2.7 of the
total population and four men out of ten suffered up to
15 years of unemployment. Now the ratio is one collier
to every 7.6 of the total population and there are
alternative jobs. Not only is the economic future of
the Rhondda on a broader and safer base, but jobs are
available to those who fall victim to the dreaded dust
diseases which can turn a man from the pits at any age
from 20 until he retires.

D.48408. (12). A mid-European industry, the making of cast aluminium,
spoons, and forks, has been brought to the Rhondda by
the firm of Celnik and Power, Ltd., of Tonypandy.

title: A photographic print of Industry, Iron & Steel, Miscellaneous
activity: Ravenscraig steelworkers in Motherwell celebrating a record output week with cigars supplied by the management.

te.text: Industry - Misc - Workers - Gen - NOT Working Scenes

6 col x 7" DEEP.
( CUT OUT AS
SHOWN. )

nscraig steelworkers celebrate their output record . . cigars supplied by the management
Picture by JACK HAMILTON

1N RUSSIA they would probably have got
the Order of Lenin, or the title "Hero of
Labour." But not in Britain. Notably not
at the Ravenscraig steelworks in Mother-
well, where yesterday the furnacemen
were celebrating their achievement of a
record week's output. There the manage-
ment were quick to reward each of their
workers with the symbol of capitalist
success: a fat cigar.

They could, when you consider it, have
chosen something equally symbolic to
distribute — like yachts, fast cars or
blondes — but there is a limit to what
can be expected from even the most
grateful management.

In one sense, though, the holders of
the Order of the Fat Cigar have some-
thing in common with the Heroes of
Labour. In Motherwell, the management
have rushed in bearing gifts. In Russia,
the state adds a few more names to the
Marxist honours list. And in neither case
does anyone mention money. In Russia,
because it is a deviationist snare. In
Motherwell, perhaps because they have
to work it all out in relation to the wage
freeze. Still, there is always the pure
satisfaction of success, and being (for a
day anyway) a man with a big cigar.

te.text:
By DENNIS NEWSON
A FOUR-STOREY block of flats which could house
100 people in comfort is standing empty only a
stone's throw from the Houses of Parliament. It has
been empty for more than FIVE YEARS.
Homeless London families have
eyed the block enviously. Scores
of M Ps have made inquiries,
for it is near enough to the
Commons for them to get home
for a meal and back in time for
a division.
And opposite the building on
the corner of Great Smith-street
and Great Peter-street, West-
minster, is another, smaller
block.
For the past 12 months only
one of its 13 flats has been
occupied.
Action was promised last night
by the Westminster City Coun-
cil's assistant town clerk, Mr.
Ronald Chamberlin.
He was meeting bearded 26-
year-old Mr. Henry Pelham, a
director of the Veribest Manu-
facturing Company which leased
the properties just after the war.
A council official said: " We
understand that Mr. Pelham has
consulted architects about reno-
vating the smaller block and
later letting it.
"If this is not done quickly,
the council may well use its
powers of compulsory purchase."
Mr. Pelham's firm was refused
permission to convert the flats
into offices.
It says it will have to spend
£20,000 on the smaller block.
Renovation of the larger block
might not be commercially
worthwhile as the lease has
only 14 years to run.

EMPTY for five
years .. This
is the block of
flats in Westmin-
ster which could
house 100 fam-
ilies. The council
may take action.

TANNER.              D.H.                22.11.61.
EMPTY FLATS. Story:- Newson.
A large block of flats at the junction of Great Smith
Street, & Great Peter Street, Westminster, big
enough to house 60 homeless people has been vacant
for 5 years.
O.P.S. General view of the vacant Mansionss.

activity: Laying out squares of Swiss quartzite in London for use on the Queen Mary's swimming bath.

te.text:
GOLDEN QUARTZITE, STONE THE PHARAOHS USED, 
PREPARED IN LONDON FOR THE QUEEN MARY. 
 
Golden quartzite, a stone that was used 
in the days of the Pharaohs to line 
the tomb of King Tutankhamen, is 
being prepared by a London firm of 
marble craftsmen for use in the pavements 
around the super swimming bath of the 
giant new liner Queen Mary. 
Quartzite is the seventh hardest 
material known. It is non-slip and the 
colour is permanent. For centuries 
quarrying of it stopped but in the 18th 
century, the monks in the Alps began 
to work it again. 
This is the first time in history that 
golden quartzite has been used for a ship. 
Three hundred tons of onyx from North 
Africa and marble from Malta are being 
made into chimneypieces for the Queen 
Mary. 
PHOTO SHOWS:- Laying out squares of 
Swiss quartzite in London for use on 
the Queen Mary's swimming bath. 
      G January 11th 1936 PN.r.

COPYRIGHT.
PLANET NEWS LTD
3, JOHNSON'S COURT,
LONDON, E.C. 4.

carrot beak, feet; cloves for eyes. Potat o hedgehog

Russian salad.  Half potatoes represent boats with
lettuce sails.

he took tray home. He was going to eat all the
potatoes.

HE WINS THE 6TH. INTERNATIONAL TUNA CUP....
AMERICA TEAM WINS IN THREE DAY CONTEST....

     HUGH RUTHERFORD of Mill Neck N.Y., Captain
of the United States Fishing team receives congratulat-
ions from Nova Scotia's Minister of trade and industry,
the Hon. Harols CONNOLLY, and receives the ALTON B.
SHARP trophy for winning the 6th. International Tuna
Cup match at Wedgeport, Nova Scotia.  The Americans
caught 19 of the 72 bluefin tuna taken in the three
day contest, defeating teams from Brazil, Cuba, Argentina
and the British Commonwealth....

te.text:
222536     DAW
NEW THAMES REFINERY.

Isle of Grain:  Construction work in progress at
the new oil refinery being built on the Isle of 
Grain in the Thames Estuary.
Being built by the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company,
which created the mighty Abadan (Persia) plant,
this new £30,000,000 refinery is being built on 
what was once salty marshes.
Four million tons of crude oil will be processed
here a year.  Work began in the middle of 1950,
and the first part is due to be commissioned in
the first six months of 1952.
When completed the refinery will employ some 1,500.
     November, 1951   PN-d.

activity: A mannequin, Marie McGowan, wearing an Ermine cape trimmed with Silver Fox during a preview of furs for export to Canada to help the war effort.

te.text:
SAIDMAN (ILLUS.)
MANNEQUIN AND FURS.
MISS MARIE MCGOWAN, 26 year old free lance mannequin and
photographers' model lives in the suburbs and goes by tube
daily to her work in the West End where appointments have
been made for her to display models. One day Miss McGowan
took part in the special pre-view of the FURS FOR EXPORT
TO CANADA to help the War effort.  The collection
was made from furs supplied by various parts of the
Commonwealth and Fashioned in London by the British Fur
Industry.  On this occasion Miss McGowan wore fur coats
to the value of many hundreds of pounds.
6.O.P.S. Miss McGowan wearing an Ermine cape trimmed with
           Silver Fox.

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION MONDAY'S
DAILIES, 24TH JANUARY, 1966

BIGGEST SHIP TO BE BUILT ON THE TYNE WILL
BE LAUNCHED NEXT MONTH
NCP5 J1565 24.1.66.
THERE'S A CERTAIN MAGIC ABOUT HITTING THE TON.
MOTOR CYCLISTS LIVE AND DIE FOR IT. OLD MEN OF
99 PRAY THAT THEY WILL HANG ON FOR THE PRIDE OF
BEING 100 NOT OUT. CRICKETERS' CAREERS RISE AND
FALL BY IT.
BUT NOWHERE IS THE ACHIEVEMENT SO PROUDLY AND
COMPETITIVELY MEASURED TODAY THAN IN SHIPBUILDING.
BUILD A SHIP OF 100,000 TONS OR MORE AND YOU CAN
SAY YOU ARE IN THE BIG LEAGUE, EVEN BY JAPAN'S
GIGANTIC STANDARD. NOW, THE TOUGH, TRADITIONAL
SHIPBUILDERS OF THE RIVER TYNE ARE PUTTING THE
FINISHING TOUCHES TO THEIR FANFARE ENTRY INTO
THE 'BIG LEAGUE.'
A THOUSAND MEN AT THE WORLD-FAMOUS YARD OF
SWAN, HUNTER AND WIGHAM RICHARDSON, WALLSEND-ON-TYNE, ARE SCURRYING OVER AND BELOW THE GIGANTIC
DECKS OF THE 100,000-TON 'BRITISH ARGOSY'
GETTING HER READY FOR LAUNCHING ON FEBRUARY 7TH.
THE VESSEL IS BEING BUILT FOR THE BP TANKER
COMPANY. SHE WILL BE THE FIRST BRITISH-BUILT
SHIP TO ENTER 'BIG LEAGUE' THIS YEAR AND IS THE
BIGGEST SHIP EVER BUILT ON A RIVER RENOWNED FOR
PUSHING THE BOAT OUT IN A BIG WAY.
FIFTEEN YEARS AGO, PRINCESS MARGARET WENT TO
SWAN HUNTERS TO LAUNCH THE THEN BIGGEST SUPER
TANKER OF THE DAY, THE 28,000 TON 'VELUTINA'.
THE BRITISH ARGOSY MAKES THAT LOOK LIKE A ROWING
BOAT. SHE STANDS LIKE AN ENDLESS STRETCH OF
ELASTIC 917FT. LONG, 128FT. WIDE AND 66FT. DEEP,
WITH ENOUGH ROOM ON HER DECKS TO SWALLOW UP NEARLY
THREE FOOTBALL PITCHES.
EVERY SINGLE PIECE OF DRAG CHAIN ON THE WHOLE
OF THE RIVER TYNE, 1 250 TONS OF IT, IS BEING
BEGGED AND BORROWED TO CONTROL HER GRAND SLAM
ENTRY INTO THE RIVER WHEN LAUNCHED BY LADY
BRIDGEMAN (WIFE OF SIR MAURICE BRIDGEMAN, CHAIRMAN
OF BP). EVEN THEN SHE WILL HAVE ONLY 25 YARDS -
LITTLE MORE THAN A CRICKET PITCH LENGTH - IN WHICH
TO AVOID HITTING THE RIVER'S OPPOSITE BANK.
THE BRITISH ARGOSY WILL BE ONLY THE SECOND
BRITISH SHIP OF 100,000 TONS TO BE LAUNCHED TO
DATE. HER SISTER SHIP, BRITISH ADMIRAL, WAS
LAUNCHED FROM VICKERS-ARMSTRONG'S BARROW YARD LAST
YEAR BY THE QUEEN.
PHOTO SHOWS: AN AERIAL VIEW OF THE GIGANTIC
"BRITISH ARGOSY" (100,000 TONS D.W.) WHICH WILL
BE LAUNCHED ON FEBRUARY 7TH.

te.text:
SOUTH WALES.    AW/RI
LOCUSTS MAKE MORE WORK FOR WELSH INDUSTRY.
Plagues of locusts in South America are being fought with a
new idea, incorporating Welsh tinplate. Before the locusts
gain the stage in which they can fly, their only means of
transport is to hop. A barrier of hundreds of miles of sheet
tin, manufactured at Llanelly, is to be built, in front of
which will be a deep trench in which it is hoped to trap the
locusts. The slippery tinplate barrier will prevent them from
getting out, and men with flame throwers can effectively destroy
them.
Photo shows-    Sheets of tinplate coming out of the [illegible]
galvanizing machine at the Llanelly factory.
Fox July 29th. 36.

te.text:
DURHAM PRODUCES DOLLAR-SAVING PIPELINE       D/TAE

One of the biggest contracts for large diamter steel
pipes ever placed in Britain has just been secured by
South Durham Steel and Iron Company, an old established
Teeside firm. The order, from the Basrah Petroleum Co.
(an associate of the Iraq Petroleum Company) is for the
manufacture of 80 miles of 24-inch pipe, weighing 17,000
tons, to be laid next year from the Zubair oilfields in
Southern Iraq to the port of Fao, on the Persian Gulf
near Basrah. In addition to opening new and increasing
markets for the British steel industry, the £900,000
order will mean a saving of some 2 1/2 million dollars, as
hitherto most large diamter oil piping has been obtained
from the United States.

PHOTO SHOWS: A workman at the South Durham Steel and
Iron Company's works, seen grinding the inside seam of
the weld 6" back, as required for pipe laying.

activity: Signor Massa, Labour Attache at the Italian Embassy, speaking to miner trainees at Maltby regarding the National Coal Board's decision to suspend recruiting Italian labour.

te.text:
Some will
go home
THE recruiting of Itali-
an labour for
the mines has
been suspended.
Men already
here and not
placed in jobs
will be repatri-
ated by the
National Coal
Board if they
wish to go
home.
The NCB
announced this
yesterday, and
said that Board
officials and
Italian Govern-
ment represen-
tatives were seeing the men to
explain the position.
In the picture above Signor
Massa, Labour Attache at the
Italian Embassy, is telling miner
trainees at Maltby, Yorks, of the
Coal Board's decision.
The Board said that the scheme,
which began last year, had re-
sulted in about 1,200 men being
taken into the pits. About 1,000
more had been brought here and
were in training centres.
For some months there had been
increasing difficulty in placing
Italians, owing to the unwilling-
ness of miners' lodges to accept
them.
The NCB was trying to over-
come the objections, but for the
time being there were few places
open to Italians.
The 31 Italians who were sus-
pended from underground work at
Bullcroft Colliery, near Doncaster,
several weeks ago will not be re-
instated, but will be treated in the
same way as others who cannot
be placed in the mining industry.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
16 MAY 1952
PLEASE RETURN
ART LIBRARY

te.text:
"NYLONS BY THE MILLIONS"
NEW BRITISH FACTORY IS EVERY GIRL'S DREAM    DG/M3

Ten thousand nylon stockings each day, or enough
samples of sheer leg appeal to last a girl a lifetime
if she threw away her stockings every Friday night,
is the target of a high speed modern factory which has
just been opened at Enniskillen, Northern Ireland.
The factory is the result of a combination of
English, Irish, American and Canadian enterprise. It is
equipped with the latest American knitting machines,
though the operatives are mainly Co. Fermanagh
men and women. Fermanagh girls are reputed to
be the most beautiful in the United Kingdom.

PHOTO SHOWS:- "No leg to stand on". Folks who
say there's a shortage should see these gleaming
nylons drying on heated moulds after dyeing,
at the new factory in Enniskillen. Most
of these are, however for export.

activity: aftermath of a fire and explosion at the Ironbridge Metal Company works in Madeley

te.text:
MYSTERY BLAST
KILLS TWO
HERALD REPORTER
IRONBRIDGE, Shropshire, Friday.
A MANAGING DIRECTOR and a woman employee are
believed to have perished in a mystery explosion which
blew the roof off a metal works at Madeley today.
Thirteen others—five women employees and firemen—were
injured.
The three-storeys factory of the
Ironbridge Metal Company was
destroyed by fire.
It was engaged in smelting down
aluminium foil dropped by the
RAF to upset enemy radar—the
stuff German children called
angel's hair.
Families evacuated
More than 100 firemen are
standing by tonight, unable to use
water for fear of causing thermite
in the factory to explode.
They are concentrating on pre-
venting the blaze from spreading
to near-by cottages, from which
families have been evacuated.
Soldiers and firemen had to stop
work about midnight because of
the threat of another explosion.
Clouds of black smoke from the
building indicated that a diesel oil
tank had caught fire.
It was only tonight, after the
police had checked names of
injured at scattered hospitals,
that it was discovered that Mrs.
Kate Healey, of Ironbridge, had
apparently been trapped.
The managing director
is Mr. Ferdinand Fraenkel, who
was an Austrian refugee.
Blitz-like blaze
Troops called out to assist
firemen search the burning
debris after the metal works
explosion yesterday.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
RCD. 15 MAY 1950

activity: A residential building (Housing Flats) where a fatal accident occurred involving a child, Eugene O'Toole.

te.text:
Secret 
dread of 
a proud 
mother 
Herald Reporter 
LITTLE Eugene was 18 
months old, the youngest 
of the five strapping O'Toole 
brothers. A fine, strong 
baby. 
Other mothers smiled enviably 
when Mrs. Ann O'Toole told 
them: "He weighs 35½lb. al- 
ready." But Mrs. O'Toole was 
nagged by a secret dread. 
For when she took him out to 
Wandsworth Common little 
Eugene would play for hours 
and not be tired. Dad used to 
get tired first. 
Shoes? He took size seven. And 
last Saturday Mrs. O'Toole 
bought him two new shirts - 
meant for a boy of three. 
She was proud—yet afraid. And 
yesterday her fear materialised. 
A climb 
Eugene dragged a heavy chair on 
to the balcony of their fourth- 
storey flat in St. Ives House, 
East Hill Estate, Wandsworth, 
and climbed on it. 
Then mothers in the flats opposite 
screamed as he plunged 50ft. to 
the concrete below. He died in 
hospital. 
Last night, 40-year-old Mrs. 
O'Toole, whose other sons are 
aged nine to 21, said: "He was 
so strong, I always feared he 
might do something like that 
when I was not looking. 
I was in another room for only 
second or two. 
He was such a fine baby . . . but 
feel he was sent to break our 
hearts."

DAILY HERALD 
Photograph 
BY L. GARNADE 
NUMBER...1957.728-1

PROPERTY OF 
DAILY HERALD 
- 4 JUN 1957 
PLEASE RETURN 
TO 
ART LIBRARY
